visits.text: Faro Cidade Velha: Moorish ramparts still containing a real lived-in old town, not an open-air museum. The Sé cathedral (13th century, rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake) is worth a climb up its bell tower to see the lagoon stretching to the horizon. The municipal museum in the Nossa Senhora da Assunção convent displays Roman mosaics from Ossonoba.

Storks have nested in the Arco da Vila towers ever since they chose these battlements as a breeding site. The neoclassical arch dates from 1812, commissioned by Bishop Francisco Gomes do Avelar. It marks the entrance to the fortified city from the Jardim Manuel Bívar. Below, the old Moorish gate from the 11th century—one of Portugal's oldest preserved horseshoe arches.

Sixty kilometers of lagoons, sandbanks, and barrier islands—the Ria Formosa stretches from Faro to Cacela Velha. A protected natural park, one of Europe's most important for migratory birds. Ilha Deserta, accessible by boat from the port, is genuinely deserted: an Atlantic beach in its raw state.

Bills clatter overhead as storks nest atop the Arco da Vila, the main gateway to the Cidade Velha, Faro’s old town. Bishop Francisco Gomes do Avelar commissioned this arch from Italian architect Francisco Xavier Fabri. It was inaugurated in 1812. Once you have walked through, turn around: behind the facade is a much older gateway, a horseshoe arch from the Muslim period, probably dating to the 11th century.

The best view of Ria Formosa, the lagoon fringed by sandy islands along Faro’s coast, takes some effort: about 68 steps lead to the top of the tower of the Sé, the cathedral. Construction began in 1251, two years after the Christian reconquest of the city. In 1596, English troops under the Earl of Essex looted and burned it. Admission costs €5. Visit on a weekday: on Sundays, the church is generally reserved for services.

Discovered in 1926 beneath two streets in Faro, a Roman mosaic of Oceanus, the sea deity, is the highlight of the Museu Municipal de Faro. It is classified as a national treasure. The museum occupies the Convent of Nossa Senhora da Assunção, where construction began in 1519. Its cloister, completed in 1548, is one of Portugal’s earliest Renaissance-style cloisters. The convent is also in the old town: combine your visit with the Sé.

“Stop here and consider that you too will reach this state”: the inscription above the entrance to the Capela dos Ossos, the Chapel of Bones, sets the tone. Opened in 1816 behind the Igreja do Carmo, it is lined with the bones of more than a thousand Carmelite monks, including 1,245 skulls. The room measures just 4 m by 6 m. Visit on a weekday: on Saturdays, it is only open in the morning.

activities.text: If you have an afternoon, take the boat to Ilha Deserta from the Porta Nova pier. The crossing takes 20 minutes. On the island: a beach stretching several kilometers, one restaurant at the end, the Atlantic on the other side of the dunes. Nothing else. The return with the sunset behind Faro is worth the trip.

Ilha Deserta: white sand, turquoise water and the Atlantic horizon. The restaurant at the end of the island serves fresh seafood at reasonable prices. Arrive early to get a place on the terrace before the day-trippers from the Algarve arrive in force.
Head to Faro Airport on the morning of your departure. Allow extra time to return the rental car.

visits.text: Discover Albufeira, the most popular tourist resort in southern Portugal offering something for every type of traveler. From scenic coastlines and long sandy beaches to a charming old town with traditional architecture, this central Algarve hub provides excellent access to attractions throughout the region. The old fishermen's neighborhood and clifftop old town are particularly atmospheric areas to explore.

Visit Praia da Falésia, one of the world's most unique beaches, stretching over 6 kilometers between Vilamoura and Albufeira. The impressive red sandstone cliffs change colors depending on the weather and light, creating breathtaking scenery worth visiting in any season. The most beautiful stretch near Olhos de Agua features particularly spectacular cliff formations that photograph beautifully.

Explore the picturesque Chapel of Nossa Senhora da Rocha in Porches, approximately 18 km from Albufeira, a 25-minute drive away, dramatically perched on coastal cliffs above the ocean. Although the little chapel itself is charming, the main attraction is the spectacular coastal scenery visible from the paths heading west. This popular sunset spot rewards visitors with beautiful views of the Algarve coast.

activities.text: Go kayaking from St Rafael Beach in Albufeira, paddling along the beautiful coastline to discover hidden caves and secluded coves. Water sports enthusiasts will find parasailing, jet skiing, and countless other activities available throughout the summer season. The beaches around Albufeira like Praia dos Arrifes and Praia São Rafael offer some of the most scenic coastal swimming in the central Algarve.

places.name: Alcácer do Sal

visits.text: Alcácer do Sal comes from the Arabic Al-Qasr—the fortress—and sal for the salt pans that have made its fortune since antiquity. The castle atop the hill was conquered by Afonso Henriques in 1158, then taken and retaken until 1217. The castle is now converted into a pousada, and its keep and ramparts remain open to visitors. Unobstructed views over the Sado estuary and rice fields.

The historic center of Alcácer slopes gently from the castle down to the river. White houses with blue or yellow trim, several Baroque churches. A natural lunch stop on the road between Beja and Lisbon.

activities.text: Have fried eels or shad soup with garlic and coriander for lunch in a tavern on the banks of the Sado. Local specialties tied to the river, best sampled in the cool season (October–March).

visits.text: At the heart of the Mosteiro de Alcobaça are two tombs in the transept, the part of the church that crosses the nave. They hold King Pedro I and Inês de Castro, his companion, who was murdered in 1355 on the orders of Pedro’s father. After becoming king, Pedro had her remains moved here. The two tombs face each other so that at the end of time, when the dead rise according to Christian belief, each will see the other first. On Pedro’s tomb, look for the inscription “Até ao fim do mundo,” meaning until the end of the world.

A channel diverted from the Alcoa River still runs through the kitchen of the Mosteiro de Alcobaça. The monks drew water and washed fish here without going outside. Above it, the enormous chimney rests on eight iron columns. The monastery, Portugal’s first Gothic building, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1989. Its Claustro do Silêncio, commissioned by King Dinis in the late 13th century, was where the monks walked without speaking. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes, including the dormitory and the Hall of Kings.

activities.text: Finish your visit to Alcobaça with a sweet treat on the monastery square. Convent sweets, made with egg yolks and sugar, originated in convent kitchens. Try a cornucópia, a crisp pastry horn filled with egg custard, or trouxas de ovos, rolls of egg threads in syrup. Every November, the town hosts an international exhibition of convent sweets and liqueurs.

visits.text: The Moorish castle of Aljezur fell in 1249, among the last Moorish strongholds conquered in Portugal—the Reconquista ended here very late. The ruins dominate the valley from a basalt crag. From the summit, views over the inland valley and the Atlantic in the distance. Free access to the climb, with a marked path from the main square.

The Museu Municipal de Aljezur is tiny—but the local Reconquista is carefully recounted there, with Islamic ceramics and campaign maps to illustrate it. This is where you understand why this coast held out longer than the rest of the country. Tickets cost a few euros; allow 45 minutes for a visit.

activities.text: Walk the castle trail on foot: from Praça da Liberdade, the path climbs in 10 minutes to the ramparts. View over the Aljezur valley and the Bordeira dunes in the distance. Descent through the alleyways of the historic quarter.

visits.text: Almeida's star-shaped fortress has 12 points, on a plan inspired by Vauban but adapted to the local topography, built in the 17th and 18th centuries. The walk around the bastions is 4 km and takes 2 hours. Less famous than Elvas (a UNESCO site)—the tour buses have not found it yet.

On August 26, 1810, a French shell landed in the fortress courtyard, ignited a powder trail left by a poorly closed barrel, and triggered a chain explosion of the main depot. Hundreds of defenders killed in seconds. The town capitulated the next day. The crater is still visible today.

activities.text: Walk around the bastions first thing in the morning—4 km, 2 hours, free entry. The whole walking circuit follows the outer ramparts and passes every bastion of the star.

places.name: Alter do Chão

visits.text: Sixty mares go out into the field every morning at the Coudelaria de Alter Real: that's the moment to see. This royal stud farm founded in 1748 by King João V to supply haute école horses to the Lisbon court is one of the world's oldest stud farms in continuous operation on its original site. 800 hectares, pure Lusitano breed.

The Coudelaria de Alter Real stud farm was founded in 1748 by King João V, who purchased the bloodline's first mares in Andalusia. The on-site museum tells the history of this breed and displays saddles, bits, and harnesses from the 16th century. Remarkable collection of baroque equipment.

activities.text: Depending on the season, classical riding demonstrations take place at the Coudelaria—ask at the entrance. Outside demonstrations, you can watch the stallions training in the indoor riding arenas. A call ahead is recommended before making the detour: +351 245 619 060.

visits.text: In 1809, soldiers and residents of Amarante defended the Ponte de São Gonçalo against Napoleon’s troops for fourteen days. The current bridge dates to 1790: it replaced an older bridge swept away by a flood of the Tâmega in 1763. Traces of the fighting are still visible on the stone. Walk across, then sit on a bench in one of its four small semicircular overlooks, facing the river and São Gonçalo Church.

The facade of the Igreja de São Gonçalo is worth looking up at. The Varanda dos Reis, the “balcony of kings,” displays statues of four 16th-century monarchs, including Philip I, king of Spain, who also became king of Portugal in 1581. Inside, a statue of the saint, who died in 1262, stands on his tomb. São Gonçalo is believed to help single women find a husband: many still come to pray or leave flowers. Allow time for the neighboring cloister, which houses the municipal museum.

Amarante is a small town, but its museum tells the story of a modern painter with ties to the Cubists whose recognition reached as far as New York. The Museu Municipal Amadeo de Souza-Cardoso, housed in the cloister of the former convent, honors this painter, born in Amarante in 1887 and a friend of Modigliani in Paris. In 1913, he sold seven of the eight paintings he exhibited at the Armory Show, a modern art exhibition in New York. He died of the Spanish flu in 1918, at age 30. The museum is closed on Mondays and between 12:30 p.m. and 2 p.m.

activities.text: Egg yolks, sugar, and almonds: this trio gives the cakes at Confeitaria da Ponte their sweetness. Opened in 1930, it is Amarante’s oldest pastry shop. Its recipes come from the town’s former convents. Try the lérias (egg yolks and almonds), foguetes (egg-filled puff pastries), and brisas do Tâmega (small boat-shaped pastries filled with egg cream). Expect to pay one to two euros apiece, to take out or enjoy on the terrace.

visits.text: Probably founded around the beginning of the Christian era, the Roman city of Ammaia has only been identified and excavated since 1994–1995. The site covers its original twenty hectares, of which only a tiny fraction has been uncovered: forum, baths, south gate. Classified as a National Monument since 1949, it lies in the same municipality of São Salvador da Aramenha as Marvão. Entrance €3, open 9 AM–12:30 PM and 2–5:30 PM.

Small museum, big surprise: the Roman glassware collection from Ammaia at Quinta do Deão is one of the most remarkable on the Iberian Peninsula. Cups, flasks, unguentaria—nearly intact forms after two thousand years. The staff speaks English and explains the context enthusiastically.

activities.text: Walk to the south gate to understand the extent of what was once a city of several thousand inhabitants—far more populous than Marvão is today. The contrast between the forgotten Roman city below and the medieval village visible on the ridge to the north says it all about the shift from one civilization to another.

places.name: Arcos de Valdevez

visits.text: Oval on the outside and octagonal on the inside, the Igreja da Lapa in Arcos de Valdevez plays with shapes. Completed in 1767, it is attributed to André Soares, the architect of Braga’s Arco da Porta Nova. Beneath its lofty dome, look at the Rococo altarpieces, the large carved wooden panels behind the altars, and the ornate grilles. Step inside if the door is open: 15 minutes is enough.

The Paço da Giela, a national monument on the outskirts of Arcos de Valdevez, combines a 14th-century tower with 16th-century living quarters. Its windows are Manueline, a Portuguese decorative style from the early 16th century. An earlier fortification already stood on the site in the 11th century. The rooms display objects found during excavations and trace the building’s development. Opening hours vary by season: check with the tourist office before visiting.

activities.text: In 1140, on the banks of the Vez, Afonso Henriques and King Alfonso VII of Castile faced each other in a tournament, a contest between knights governed by rules, rather than a pitched battle. This Recontro de Valdevez is seen as a step toward Portugal’s independence. Spend 30 minutes strolling along the banks of the Vez. Farther upstream, the Ecovia do Vez, a 32 km greenway, follows the river to the village of Sistelo. Before leaving, try rebuçados dos Arcos, large local candies.

visits.text: Explore the Arouca UNESCO Global Geopark, a protected landscape renowned for extraordinary geological heritage including the famous giant trilobites of Canelas. This territory surrounded by the Freita, Montemuro, and Arada mountain ranges represents millions of years of Earth's history preserved in remarkable rock formations. The geopark offers adventure activities amid dramatic natural scenery.

Walk the Passadiços do Paiva, a spectacular 8-kilometer wooden walkway zigzagging along the Paiva River gorges. This engineering marvel passes thundering waterfalls, steep cliffs and pristine natural pools carved into the rock. The walkways provide safe access to one of Portugal's most dramatic river landscapes, previously inaccessible to visitors. Allow for a round trip by car during the day from Arouca to reach the start of the walk.

activities.text: Cross the 516 Arouca, one of the world's longest pedestrian suspension bridges, stretching 516 meters above the Paiva River gorges at a height of 175 meters. This thrilling walkway offers breathtaking views of the valley below and the surrounding mountain landscape. Advance tickets are required for this unforgettable adventure experience. Allow for a round trip by car during the day from Arouca, followed by a walk to the bridge.

Challenge yourself with white water rafting on the Paiva River, considered one of Portugal's premier destinations for river sports. Rapids range from gentle to demanding, with professional guides leading expeditions through spectacular gorge scenery. Kayaking and canyoning adventures provide different ways to experience this remarkable waterway.

visits.text: Visit the distinctive Circular Castle of Arraiolos, a defensive structure that is unique in Portugal for its rounded shape. From atop its walls, enjoy spectacular views over the green landscapes of the Alentejo and the historic village below.

Explore the Arraiolos Carpet Interpretive Center, an interactive museum that tells the story of this centuries-old art considered one of Portugal's earliest crafts. Arraiolos carpets are world-famous, and this tradition permeates every street corner in the town.

Wander through the historic center of Arraiolos, discovering the Arraiolos carpet paving in a central square with cafés and craft shops. The village preserves its picturesque character with white houses and cobblestone streets typical of the Alentejo.

activities.text: Visit the Monte da Ravasqueira wine estate, which offers wine tourism experiences including tastings and a visit to the Private Carriage Collection. Discover the stories behind the wines of this prestigious Alentejo estate.

visits.text: Embark on a ride in a traditional moliceiro boat through the picturesque canals of Aveiro, a city often dubbed the Venice of Portugal. These colorful vessels, once used for seaweed harvesting, now glide past stunning Art Nouveau facades and charming bridges. Each boat features vibrant paintings depicting local humor and maritime traditions, offering a unique window into the city's cultural heritage.

Explore the Museu de Aveiro housed in the former Convento de Jesus, where Saint Joana, a princess, spent her final years. This remarkable collection showcases sacred art spanning centuries, including the ornate baroque tomb of the princess herself. The museum building alone, with its gilded woodwork and azulejo tiles, represents a masterpiece of Portuguese religious architecture.

Wander through Aveiro's Art Nouveau quarter, a treasure trove of early 20th-century architecture centered around the former ceramics factory. Marvel at the elaborately decorated facades featuring the iconic Portuguese azulejo tiles, intricate ironwork balconies, and organic motifs that define this distinctive architectural style.

activities.text: Paddle through the Ria de Aveiro by kayak, discovering the vast lagoon ecosystem with its salt pans, diverse birdlife, and traditional fishing villages. This protected wetland offers a peaceful escape into nature just minutes from the city center.

Visit the Marinha da Troncalhada Ecomuseum to discover the ancient art of salt harvesting that shaped Aveiro's economy for centuries. Watch as workers use traditional techniques to extract salt from the crystalline ponds, continuing a practice dating back to Roman times.

visits.text: Avenida dos Aliados is the grand avenue in central Porto, laid out beginning in 1916. Its name honors the Allied countries of World War I. At the top stands Porto City Hall, the Paços do Concelho. Along one side, the former Café Imperial now houses a McDonald’s that humor website 9GAG dubbed “the most beautiful in the world.” Continue down the avenue to Liberty Square: São Bento station is just a two-minute walk away.

Few train stations are worth a detour without a train ticket: São Bento station is one of them. Its entrance hall is covered with around 20,000 azulejos, painted by Jorge Colaço between 1905 and 1916. The large blue panels depict Portuguese history, including the arrival on horseback of King John I and his English wife, Philippa of Lancaster, in Porto in 1387. A colorful frieze also shows the country’s past modes of transportation. The hall is still part of a working station: admire the walls while leaving room for travelers to pass.

visits.text: A roasted rooster that crows to save an innocent man: that is the legend behind the Cruzeiro do Senhor do Galo, an 18th-century stone cross. According to the story, a Galician pilgrim on his way to Santiago de Compostela was wrongly condemned. To prove his innocence, he declared that the roasted rooster served to the judge would crow. The rooster crowed, and the man was saved. The cross is displayed in the ruins of the Paço dos Condes de Barcelos, a free open-air museum. Work on this palace began in the 15th century under Count Afonso, who also built the palace in Guimarães.

The Ponte Medieval de Barcelos, a Gothic bridge over the Cávado, was built between 1325 and 1328 on the orders of Count Pedro Afonso. Its five unequal arches connect the town to the suburb of Barcelinhos on the opposite bank. Pilgrims on the Portuguese Way to Santiago still cross it today. Right beside the palace ruins, the Igreja Matriz, the main church, combines Romanesque and Gothic architecture. Cross the bridge for the view of town, then head back up to the church.

In December 1504, according to tradition, a cross outlined in black earth appeared on the ground at Campo da Feira. To shelter it, Barcelos built the Igreja do Senhor Bom Jesus da Cruz, a Baroque church dating to 1710 and decorated with azulejo tile panels. Every May 3, the Festa das Cruzes, the Festival of the Crosses, draws crowds here. The church borders the market square: visit on a Thursday between browsing the stalls at the fair.

You’ll get a sweeping view of Barcelos from the top of the Torre de Porta Nova, a 15th-century tower. It is the only one of the five gates in the old town wall still standing. It houses the tourist office and a permanent exhibition of local crafts. Admission is free. On weekdays, the tower is open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

The Museu de Olaria, the pottery museum, is worth a visit even if you don’t collect anything. Opened in 1963, it brings together nearly 10,000 pottery objects from Portugal and Portuguese-speaking countries. Barcelos is known for its figurado, humorous clay figurines with exaggerated features depicting farmers, musicians, and Nativity figures. This craftsmanship has earned it UNESCO Creative City status for Crafts and Folk Art. Admission to the museum is free.

activities.text: Live animals, wicker baskets, cured meats, and piles of clothing: every Thursday, the Feira de Barcelos fills Campo da República, which locals also call Campo da Feira. Its origins date back to the 15th century. You’ll find fruits and vegetables, pastries, shoes, and crafts from Minho: basketry, tinware, embroidery, and woodwork. Come in the morning and keep some change handy for small purchases.

places.name: Batalha

visits.text: The Mosteiro da Batalha began with a vow: King João I had it built to thank the Virgin Mary for his victory over the Castilians at Aljubarrota in 1385. Construction lasted from 1386 to 1517. The Capela do Fundador is Portugal’s first royal pantheon, meaning its first burial chapel for kings. João I and the English queen Philippa of Lancaster rest beneath its star vault. One of their sons, Henry the Navigator, rests along the south wall. The monastery opens at 9 a.m. year-round.

Between 1448 and 1477, the Claustro Real at the Mosteiro da Batalha took on its Gothic form. Later, architect Mateus Fernandes added delicate stone screens between the arches in the Manueline style, Portugal’s decorative style of the early 16th century. Their motifs alternate between the cross of the Order of Christ and the armillary sphere, an astronomical instrument made of interlocking rings. Walk slowly around the cloister to spot these two motifs.

Two motionless sentries stand guard in the Sala do Capítulo, the chapter house of the Mosteiro da Batalha. They watch over the tomb of two unknown soldiers killed during World War I. Look up: the star vault spans about 19 m without a central pillar. It held only on the third attempt, and architect Huguet is said to have spent a night beneath it to prove its strength. Remain silent near the honor guard.

The most surprising part of the Mosteiro da Batalha was never completed: the Capelas Imperfeitas, the “Unfinished Chapels.” King Duarte began them around 1434 as a pantheon for his family, with seven burial chapels. The central vault was never built, leaving the space open to the sky. The tomb of Duarte and Queen Leonor was installed here in the 1940s. The entrance is outside the church; bring an umbrella if it rains.

activities.text: Between Alcobaça and Batalha, stop at the Centro de Interpretação da Batalha de Aljubarrota, on the São Jorge plateau. This is where the army of João I and Nuno Álvares Pereira defeated the Castilian army on August 14, 1385. A multimedia show lasting about 30 minutes tells the story of the battle. Near the neighboring chapel, a mass grave yielded nearly 2,900 bones damaged by arrows and crossbow bolts, which are short projectiles. The center is open from 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. and is closed on Mondays.

visits.text: Nobody comes to Beja on purpose. That's precisely what makes it interesting. A discreet district capital, Roman (Pax Julia), Visigothic, Moorish, it has survived everything without ever becoming famous. The Praça da República at the center, lined with whitewashed houses with colorful trim, is one of the finest squares in the Alentejo without appearing on any guidebook cover.

The keep of the Castelo de Beja rises 40 meters—the Torre de Menagem, built entirely of marble, features an eight-pointed star vault at the summit, characteristic of the region's medieval military architecture. From the battlements, views stretch endlessly across the Alentejo plains. Small admission fee.

A 15th-century convent houses Portugal's most famous love correspondence. The Museu Rainha Dona Leonor, installed in the former Convento da Conceição founded in 1459, is where the nun Mariana Alcoforado allegedly wrote her five letters to a French officer in 1666—published in Paris in 1669 as Lettres portugaises. Real or fake, the debate has never been settled. Check hours before visiting: the main convent is sometimes closed for renovations.

activities.text: Settle in at the Praça da República and order a plate of migas alentejanas or carne de porco à alentejana at one of the restaurants around the square. Beja's cuisine comes from a town that feeds on its own fields: no frills, direct flavors.

The town of Beja breathes Alentejo gastronomy right into its bakeries: local sweets made with nata (cream) and almonds can be found in the downtown pastelarias. A late-afternoon stop for coffee and bolo de mel beats a restaurant dessert.

visits.text: Too beautiful to be true, yet everything is authentic: the Mosteiro dos Jerónimos is a masterpiece of Manueline style, financed by a 5% tax on the spice trade with India. Built from 1501 onwards by order of Manuel I, it houses Vasco da Gama's tomb. UNESCO-listed since 1983 along with the Torre de Belém. Closed Mondays.

Standing on the Tagus since 1519, the Torre de Belém looks like a stone wedding cake. This Manueline river defense tower, built by Francisco de Arruda between 1514 and 1519, guarded the harbor entrance. A rhinoceros sculpture on the west façade recalls that a living rhino was gifted to King Manuel I - the animal drowned in a shipwreck before reaching Rome. Long queues in summer, arrive early.

Cotton was spun here in 1846; since 2008, designers and restaurants have been moving in: LX Factory occupies 23,000 m² of former factories belonging to the Companhia de Fiação e Tecidos Lisbonense, under the 25 de Abril bridge. The Ler Devagar bookstore, in a former printing house, has shelves reaching to the ceiling and a bicycle suspended in mid-air. Sunday morning flea market.

activities.text: Only a few master pastry chefs know the original recipe for Pastéis de Belém - kept secret since 1837 when monks from the neighboring monastery started selling their tarts to survive after the closure of convents. The Fábrica de Pastéis de Belém, Rua de Belém 84-92, is the only one authorized to use this name. Long queue, but it moves quickly. Order them sprinkled with cinnamon.

Finish with the Padrão dos Descobrimentos in late afternoon: 52 meters of white concrete shaped like a ship's prow, inaugurated in 1960. Controversial, kitsch for some, but the view from the top over the Tagus and the Jerónimos justifies the €4.

visits.text: The story of Belmonte's crypto-Jews is barely believable and perfectly documented. Expelled in 1496, they practiced Judaism in secret for over four centuries—no synagogue, no books, by oral transmission, mainly through the women. Revealed in 1917 to a passing Polish engineer. The Museu Judaico de Belmonte, opened in 2005, has received some 400,000 visitors in twenty years. Closed Mondays.

Belmonte Castle stands on the Morro da Esperança at 650 m altitude. Pedro Álvares Cabral grew up here—he was the son of the castle's alcaide, born in Belmonte around 1467. He reached the coast of Brazil on April 22, 1500, commanding a fleet of 13 ships sent toward the Indies by King Manuel I.
The Museu dos Descobrimentos is disconcertingly modern for this village: 16 interactive rooms on Portuguese expansion and Cabral's legacy in Brazil. Much more immersive than expected. Allow 45 min.

activities.text: Allow an hour and a half for the Jewish Museum alone—that's the minimum to do the permanent exhibition without rushing. If you're coming with family, the witness videos are subtitled.

Climb to the viewpoint above the castle to see the Cova da Beira—the valley wedged between the Serra da Estrela and the Serra da Gardunha. The cherry orchards below bloom in March-April; in May-June, the harvest draws visitors from across the district.

days_plan.itin_title: Portugal: Historic Villages & Serra da Estrela in 8 Days

visits.text: The Michelin Guide ranks Praia da Marinha among Europe's ten most beautiful beaches, and the view from the clifftop makes it easy to see why. The sandy beach is framed by orange limestone cliffs that the sea has carved into rock formations. It is near the hamlet of Caramujeira, in the municipality of Lagoa. The path down to the beach is steep: keep your closed-toe shoes on and take in the panorama from above first.

activities.text: Since August 2024, new rules have governed visits to Algar de Benagil, a sea cave with a large round opening in its roof. Between Lagos and Albufeira, it is the only cave carved by the sea from both the side and above: the ceiling collapsed, letting sunlight in. Landing on its interior beach or swimming into the cave is now prohibited. Kayaks may enter only with a guide, and each boat stays inside for just a few minutes.

Wear sturdy shoes for the Percurso dos Sete Vales Suspensos, the Seven Hanging Valleys Trail: 5.7 km along the cliffs between Praia da Marinha and Praia de Vale Centeanes. These small valleys end abruptly at the cliff edge, overlooking the sea. The trail passes above Benagil and Praia do Carvalho, then ends near Alfanzina Lighthouse. Stay well back from the edge and the algares, natural shafts carved into the limestone by water.

Algarve in 7 Days: Ria Formosa, Benagil, Lagos, and Sagres

visits.text: Portugal did not yet exist when Sé de Braga, the cathedral, was consecrated in 1089: the region was then part of the Kingdom of León. It is Portugal’s first cathedral. Count Henry and Countess Teresa, the parents of Afonso Henriques, are buried in the Chapel of the Kings. Go up to the coro alto, the choir loft, for a close look at the two gilded wooden organs from the 1730s. A ticket covering the cathedral, choir loft, and treasury costs about €5. Avoid Sunday mornings, which are reserved for Mass.

Boxwood trimmed into geometric patterns, sculpted cedars, and ruined stone arcades: the Jardim de Santa Bárbara runs alongside the east wing of Braga’s former archbishops’ palace. These arches are the remains of a palace wing destroyed by fire in 1866. The garden itself was only laid out in 1955, around a fountain topped with a statue of Saint Barbara. Admission is free. Allow 15 minutes, then head to Largo do Paço, the palace square, right next door.

Walk beneath the Arco da Porta Nova to enter Braga’s old town. This city gate was opened in 1512. The Baroque and Neoclassical arch visible today is attributed to André Soares, an 18th-century architect from Braga. He also designed the Church of Lapa, which you will see in Arcos de Valdevez. From the gate, continue on foot toward the cathedral.

The Palácio do Raio is more than 250 years old and has a facade covered in blue azulejos, the painted ceramic tiles typical of Portugal. This 18th-century Baroque and Rococo palace now houses an exhibition space devoted to the history of the Misericórdia, a charitable brotherhood in Braga. View the facade from the sidewalk across the street: it offers the best view of the decoration as a whole.

More than 570 zigzagging steps lead up to the Church of Bom Jesus do Monte, a sanctuary designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019, about 6 km from central Braga. The stairway forms a Way of the Cross, with chapels depicting the Passion of Christ. On the Stairway of the Five Senses, each landing has its own fountain, one for each sense, from sight to taste. The Neoclassical church at the top, begun in 1784, is the work of architect Carlos Amarante. Walk up early in the morning, before the tour groups arrive, and take the funicular back down.

For the widest view over Braga, head up to the Santuário do Sameiro, less than 2 km from Bom Jesus. Construction of this sanctuary dedicated to the Virgin began in 1863. A grand staircase of 265 steps leads to the basilica. The best viewpoint is at the top of its dome, overlooking the city and the Minho Valley. Come in the late afternoon for softer light.

activities.text: Braga’s most surprising ride lasts three minutes: the Elevador do Bom Jesus, the sanctuary’s funicular, which has been operating since 1882. It runs without electricity, powered by the weight of water. At the top, the tank of the car about to descend is filled with water. Now heavier, it descends and pulls the other car uphill, after that car’s tank has been emptied at the bottom. It is the world’s oldest water-counterbalanced funicular still in operation. In summer, it departs every half hour, at 25 and 55 minutes past the hour, from 8:55 a.m. to 7:55 p.m.

You can take a breather in Bom Jesus Park, with around 26 hectares of woodland and gardens at the top of the hill. You’ll find viewpoints, an artificial grotto designed by Swiss architect Ernest Korrodi, and a small lake with rowboats for rent. The shaded paths are pleasant during the hot hours of summer. Bring a picnic so you can enjoy the setting at your own pace.

days_plan.itin_title: Minho in 6 Days: Guimarães, Braga, Ponte de Lima, Caminha

visits.text: Discover the majestic Bragança Castle, a medieval fortress that has dominated the city since the 12th century. This imposing citadel with its keep offers an exceptional panorama over the old town rooftops and the surrounding mountains of Montesinho Natural Park. Don't miss the Domus Municipalis, a rare example of Romanesque secular architecture in Portugal.

Immerse yourself in history at the Iberian Museum of Mask and Costume, housed within the citadel walls. This fascinating museum presents the ancestral traditions of Trás-os-Montes Carnival festivals with their impressive ritual masks. Discover how these pagan ceremonies have survived the centuries in this remote region of Portugal.

Explore Montesinho Natural Park, one of Portugal's best-kept secrets. This UNESCO Biosphere Reserve is home to exceptional biodiversity including Iberian wolves, golden eagles, and preserved flora. The landscapes of mountains, oak forests, and traditional schist villages transport you to a forgotten Portugal.

Visit the authentic village of Rio de Onor; allow for a round trip by car from Bragança. The inhabitants still follow ancestral communal traditions, sharing land and herds. It is a living testimony to a rural way of life that has practically disappeared elsewhere in Europe.

activities.text: Stroll through the cobblestone streets of Bragança's historic center, where every stone tells the story of a city that was once the capital of a powerful duchy. Admire the noble facades, baroque churches, and let yourself be charmed by the authentic atmosphere of this border town that has preserved its medieval character intact.

Stop at Gimonde, a charming village crossed by the Onor River where a medieval bridge spans the crystal-clear waters. This picturesque hamlet is the ideal starting point for hikes in the natural park and offers total immersion in Trás-os-Montes rural life with its traditional houses and peaceful atmosphere.

visits.text: Sailors called this cape the "end of the world" - the last land before the open Atlantic, America beyond. The Cabo de São Vicente lighthouse entered service in 1846, built on the site of a convent destroyed by the corsair Francis Drake in 1587. Its current range exceeds 60 km. Free parking, free access to the surroundings.

The current lighthouse is one of Europe's most powerful. It stands on the ruins of a 16th-century fortress built to protect the Franciscan convent that stood there—destroyed in 1587 by Drake, rebuilt in 1606. A small museum inside traces the site's history. Open from 10am until 5pm or 6pm depending on the season, adult ticket €1.50.

activities.text: Arrive in late afternoon for the Atlantic sunset: the raking light on the 75-meter black cliffs is the simplest and most effective spectacle on the entire coast. Dozens of people converge here every evening - even in low season.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Lisbon and Southern Portugal Tour in 15 Days

places.name: Cabo Espichel

visits.text: The dinosaur footprints at Cabo Espichel weren't falsified by local devotion - they're perfectly real, dated to the Lower Cretaceous, about 145 million years ago. Several series of sauropod (giant herbivore) tracks are visible on the tilted slabs of Praia dos Lagosteiros and Baía dos Lagosteiros. The legend of Our Lady of the Cape, who allegedly appeared on the back of a mule, arose from medieval interpretation of these giant traces.

The Ermida da Memória, a small chapel of medieval origin, marks the exact spot of the Marian apparition that gave birth to the cult of Nossa Senhora do Cabo Espichel. The current sanctuary - commissioned by Dom Pedro II at the turn of the 18th century - has been under restoration via the Portuguese tourism Revive program since 2014.

activities.text: Walk to the northern tip of the cape to view the Baía dos Lagosteiros from above—vertical cliffs dropping 100 meters into a cove. The wind here is constant and often fierce. The paths near the edge are unmarked; keep your distance.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Lisbon and Southern Portugal Tour in 15 Days

map_keywords: Santuário de Nossa Senhora do Cabo Espichel

visits.text: Beneath the glass platform at Cabo Girão, a 580 m drop separates your feet from the ocean. Madeira’s tourism office describes it as Europe’s highest promontory. Below, Fajã do Rancho and Fajã do Cabo Girão, small patches of cultivated land at the foot of the cliff, look tiny. The volcanic stone used for Funchal Cathedral was quarried from this cliff. The viewpoint is open daily from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.; nonresidents over 12 pay an admission fee.

days_plan.itin_title: Madeira in 7 Days: Funchal, Levadas, and Pico Ruivo

visits.text: White storks nest twenty meters above the waves at Cabo Sardão - impassive beneath the gulls' cries, beaks turned seaward. Storks nesting on cliffs above the ocean: an extremely rare phenomenon, documented here since the 1980s. The nesting season runs from April to late August. Free access, parking at Cavaleiro village.

The Cabo Sardão lighthouse entered service in 1915: 17-meter square tower, built backwards according to local tradition - the entrance door faces the sea rather than the land. Its current range is 42 km. It's the westernmost point of the Alentejo coast.

activities.text: Park at Cavaleiro village and walk 20 minutes on the coastal trail to the lighthouse. The path follows the black schist cliffs and passes level with several stork nests visible to the naked eye. Bring binoculars in May—the chicks are in the nests.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Lisbon and Southern Portugal Tour in 15 Days

visits.text: The best of the Fortaleza de Cacela Velha is seen from outside. Its bastions overlook the lagoon beside the village’s small whitewashed center; focus on the panorama from the area around the fortress. Walk around the public spaces, then set aside a moment to observe the sandbars.

activities.text: If crossings are operating, head to Praia da Fábrica from the Fábrica area. The beach lies on the ocean side of a sand barrier, separated from the village by the lagoon’s channels, so access depends on water conditions. Ask locally and do not attempt to wade across a deep channel.

days_plan.itin_title: Algarve, Andalusia, and Alentejo Road Trip in 20 Days

places.name: Cais de Gaia

activities.text: Port wine takes its name from the city, but it ages across the river in the Vila Nova de Gaia wine cellars. In 1777, Gaia became the official wine storage location for all exporters. Port is a fortified wine: grape brandy is added to stop fermentation and preserve the fruit’s sugar. At Sandeman, on the quay, the short tour lasts 50 minutes and includes three ports (€23). At Taylor’s, on Rua do Choupelo, you explore independently with an audio guide on your phone: bring your headphones.

Caves Taylor's Vila Nova de Gaia

activities.text: Rust-colored water cascades beneath tree ferns: at Caldeira Velha, on the northern slope of the Fogo volcano, the color comes from iron in the thermal water. This natural monument has several pools. The water is around 25 °C beneath the waterfall and reaches 38 °C in the pools heated by fumaroles, vents that release volcanic steam. Admission is in time slots of 1 hour 30 minutes, with a maximum of 100 bathers. Tickets cost €10 with bathing and €3 without.

days_plan.itin_title: São Miguel in 6 Days: Sete Cidades, Lagoa do Fogo, Furnas

places.name: Calheta

visits.text: The building alone makes MUDAS, Madeira’s contemporary art museum in Calheta, worth a visit. Designed by architect Paulo David, it sits on a hill above town. Its collection of about 400 works, dating from the 1960s to the present, was displayed at the Fortaleza de São Tiago in Funchal until 2015. Open Tuesday through Saturday, with a break from 1 p.m. to 2 p.m.; closed Sundays, Mondays, and public holidays.

activities.text: Madeira rum is also made in the west: Engenho da Calheta, one of the island’s oldest sugarcane mills, produces rum and mel de cana. This “cane honey” is a dark syrup made from sugarcane juice. Taste both on-site, in small quantities if you’re driving.
You’ll end the day at Praia de Areia da Calheta, a sandy beach near the marina and one of the busiest on the west coast. After the levadas of Rabaçal, this is the place for a swim before dinner.

map_keywords: MUDAS Museu de Arte Contemporânea da Madeira

places.name: Câmara de Lobos

visits.text: Here, the colorful fishing boats bobbing in the bay of Câmara de Lobos are called xavelhas. The town takes its name from the monk seals, known as lobos-marinhos (“sea wolves”), that Zarco found in this bay in 1419; only a small colony remains in the Desertas Islands. In January 1950, Winston Churchill set up his easel at Miradouro do Espírito Santo to paint facing the sea. Head up there to see the view from his vantage point.

activities.text: If you try just one local drink, choose poncha, served in the bars of Câmara de Lobos. It combines aguardente de cana (a spirit distilled from sugarcane juice), honey, and lemon or orange juice. It’s stirred with a wooden stick called a mexelote. It’s strong: let someone else drive, or save it for the evening in Funchal.

visits.text: Outdoor café seating surrounds a fountain dating from 1551: the Praça do Conselheiro Silva Torres is the heart of Caminha. This Renaissance fountain, the chafariz, stands at its center. The Torre do Relógio, or clock tower, is a former keep in the ramparts. Around the square, see the 16th-century Igreja da Misericórdia and Casa Pita, a Neo-Manueline residence that imitates early 16th-century Portuguese decoration. The tourist office is on nearby Rua Direita, a cobblestone street with ornate balconies.

The finest detail of the Igreja Matriz de Caminha is above your head. Its coffered ceiling, made of recessed chestnut-wood panels, is attributed to Francisco Muñoz. Its decoration shows Mudéjar influence, meaning it was inspired by the art of Spain’s Muslims. Begun in 1488 by Basque builders and completed in 1556, the church blends Gothic, Manueline, and Renaissance styles. Spanish troops bombarded it in the 17th century during the Restoration War between Portugal and Spain. Look up as soon as you enter.

activities.text: Head to Foz do Minho, the river’s mouth, then to Praia de Moledo, a beach of white sand and rocks 4 km southwest of the center. Offshore, on an islet, the Forte da Ínsua occupies the site of a 14th-century Franciscan friary; King Manuel I had it rebuilt. Opposite, on the Spanish side, Mount Santa Tecla rises to 341 m. The beach attracts surfers and windsurfers: bring a windbreaker.

If you prefer walking, the Ecovia do Cristelo links Caminha to Moledo over 1.5 km. The Ecovia de la Foz do Minho follows the river’s mouth for about 1 km. These short paths for pedestrians and cyclists extend the greenway that follows the river upstream toward Vila Nova de Cerveira and Valença. Allow 45 minutes for each round-trip walk, including photo stops.

days_plan.itin_title: Minho in 6 Days: Guimarães, Braga, Ponte de Lima, Caminha

visits.text: Blue and white from the sidewalk to the roof: Capela das Almas, on Rua de Santa Catarina, is entirely covered in azulejos, the painted ceramic tiles typical of Portugal. There are 15,947 of them. They tell the stories of Saint Francis of Assisi and Saint Catherine. Designed by Eduardo Leite, this decoration dates to 1929: before then, the walls were simply plastered and painted white. Cross the street to take in the entire side wall at a glance. The chapel interior is only open at certain times.

days_plan.itin_title: Porto in 2 Days: Ribeira, Gaia Wine Cellars, and Foz do Douro

visits.text: Praia da Bordeira smells of salt and dried seaweed long before you see it. A freshwater lagoon borders the north of the beach, where the Bordeira river meets the ocean - fine sand dunes, lagoon, schist cliffs. Less known than Amado but more visually spectacular. Access from Carrapateira via a sandy path.
The Praia do Amado is beautiful in winter and summer alike, but the wind is constant and the swell strong. Surf schools operate on the beach.

activities.text: If you surf, the Praia do Amado offers regular waves and a sandy bottom. Surf lessons are available year-round through the village schools. Outside the peak season, allow €40-60 for a 2-hour lesson.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Lisbon and Southern Portugal Tour in 15 Days

visits.text: Explore Algar Seco in picturesque Carvoeiro, a unique coastal area featuring remarkable caves, grottos, and limestone cliffs sculpted by rain and sea over millions of years. Boardwalks make the views easily accessible, but adventurous visitors can explore pathways and staircases carved between the rocks, feeling as though they are navigating a natural maze. The most beautiful cave features two natural windows overlooking the coast and can be discovered by descending the stairs at the end of the parking lot.

Hike the famous Seven Hanging Valleys Trail, the most popular coastal walk in the Algarve, through breathtaking scenery between Praia da Marinha and Praia do Vale de Centeanes. Highlights along this 5.7-kilometer route include Benagil Cave, Benagil Beach, Carvalho Beach, and Alfazina Lighthouse. The trail provides easy access to one of the most scenic stretches of coastline in all of Portugal.

Photograph Praia da Marinha, where postcard-perfect views have made this one of the most recognizable beaches in Portugal. The clifftop paths overlooking the beach reveal the typical Algarve coastline featured in guidebooks worldwide. Walking westward from the viewpoint near the parking area reveals the most spectacular scenery along this stunning stretch of coast.

activities.text: Take a boat trip to the famous Benagil Cave, the largest and best-known sea cave in the Algarve accessible only from the water. This cathedral-like cavern is so massive that several boats can enter simultaneously, with sunlight streaming through its collapsed roof. The entire coastline here is dotted with sea caves creating spectacular scenery whether explored by speedboat or kayak.

days_plan.itin_title: Portugal Grand Tour: Algarve, Lisbon and the North

visits.text: Visit Sintra, a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape where romantic palaces rise from wooded hills; allow for a round trip from Cascais. Explore the Palácio Nacional with its distinctive conical kitchen chimneys and remarkable interiors covered in azulejos. Go up to the flamboyant Palácio da Pena by public transportation or on foot from Sintra, as private cars are not permitted: a 19th-century fantasy combining Gothic, Manueline, Moorish and Renaissance elements in an explosion of color.

Stand at Cabo da Roca, the westernmost point of mainland Europe, where dramatic cliffs plunge into the Atlantic beneath a historic lighthouse; allow for a round trip by car from Cascais. This windswept headland marks the place where Europe meets the ocean, creating a profound sense of standing at the edge of the world.

activities.text: Conclude in elegant Cascais, a beach resort attracting aristocrats since Portuguese royalty made it their summer playground. The charming old town features cobbled streets, whitewashed buildings, and a picturesque fishing harbor still in use. Sandy beaches and relaxed atmosphere provide the perfect transition before heading south.

days_plan.itin_title: Portugal Grand Tour: Algarve, Lisbon and the North

visits.text: Marvel at the Episcopal Palace Garden of Castelo Branco, a masterpiece of Portuguese landscape art commissioned by the Bishop of Guarda D. João de Mendonça around 1720. This Baroque garden features pools, balconies with stone balustrades, and statues of the kings of Portugal, with those of the monarchs from the period of Spanish rule deliberately made smaller.

Discover the Barrocal Park, a unique natural space integrated into the UNESCO Naturtejo Global Geopark. Inaugurated in 2020, this 40-hectare park allows you to appreciate a granite landscape shaped over hundreds of millions of years. Explore the Lizard Tunnel, the Bee-eater Observatory, and the suspension bridge to the São Martinho viewpoint.

Visit the Cargaleiro Museum, opened to the public in 2005, which displays a remarkable collection of paintings, ceramics, sculptures, and tapestries. In addition to works by visual artist Manuel Cargaleiro, a native of Vila Velha de Ródão, you can admire works by national and international artists.

Explore the Castelo Branco Embroidery Interpretation Center, where you can watch craftswomen producing new pieces of this centuries-old art on their looms. Castelo Branco Embroidery is a magnificent artistic expression with unique characteristics, preserved with the same dedication shown by previous generations.

Visit the Francisco Tavares Proença Júnior Museum, the CCCCB - Contemporary Culture Center of Castelo Branco, and the House of Memory of the Jewish Presence. These museums reveal the collective identity of Albicastro, preserving regional memory from archaeology to contemporary art.

Explore the Textile Museum and the Stonemason Museum, spaces dedicated to the traditional arts and crafts of the region. From embroidery to granite, these museums preserve age-old knowledge that has long been part of the collective imagination of Albicastro.

Discover the Olive Oil Route by visiting a traditional olive mill such as Fio da Beira. Olive oil from Beira-Baixa, where olive trees have been planted since 1359, now has PDO status and has won national and international awards for its exceptional quality.

activities.text: Explore Castelo Branco's historic heritage on foot: the Castle and its walls, São Miguel Church, São João Calvary, Clock Tower, Palace of the Viscounts of Portalegre, and Convento da Graça. Climb to the São Gens Viewpoint for a panoramic view over the city.

Discover the urban art and murals of Castelo Branco, including works by Vhils and the impressive mural alluding to the French Invasions. These artistic expressions represent historical episodes, traditions, and experiences of the region's people, transforming the streets into open-air museums.

Walk the hiking trails of the region: the 9.6 km PR2 - Schist Path, the 14.8 km PR1 - Gardunha Route or the PR3 - Sarzedas Schist Path. These trails start from villages around half an hour's drive from the stopover town. Look out for the more than 150 bird species that live in the district, including vultures, eagles and black storks.

Cool off at the Castelo Branco Pool-Beach, open from June to September, or at the river beaches of Almaceda and Sesmo, around half an hour's drive from the stopover town. Stroll through the City Park, the Devesa Civic Center and the Violets Park, green spaces ideal for moments of relaxation.

days_plan.itin_title: Beira Interior: Serra da Estrela, Schist Villages and Historic Cities
Beira Interior: Serra da Estrela, Schist Villages and Historic Cities
Portugal: Historic Villages & Serra da Estrela in 8 Days

visits.text: The Castelo de Almourol occupies a rocky islet in the middle of the Tagus. It can only be reached by boat, as there is no bridge or walking route. According to the inscription above the gate, the Knights Templar rebuilt it starting in 1171 under the direction of Gualdim Pais, the founder of Tomar. The castle guarded the river during the Reconquista, the recapture of lands from Muslim rule. The boat leaves from the Cais de Almourol, facing the castle, with no reservation required; tickets cost €4.

activities.text: To learn about the castle’s history before or after the crossing, stop by the Centro de Interpretação Templário de Almourol (CITA). It is located in the cultural center in Vila Nova da Barquinha, about 4 km away. This center is devoted to the Knights Templar and their defensive line along the Tagus. Admission is included in the castle ticket. Hours vary by season and day: confirm them in advance.

days_plan.itin_title: Óbidos, Nazaré, Alcobaça, Batalha, and Tomar in 6 Days

visits.text: Built in the 14th century and identified thanks to a stone tabernacle rediscovered in the 1970s, the medieval synagogue of Castelo de Vide is one of only two pre-expulsion synagogues preserved in Portugal—the other is in Tomar. The surrounding Judiaria welcomed Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 and retains its original layout with pointed-arch doorways and mezuzah marks. Free entrance, closed Mondays.

Locals have been fetching water here continuously since the 16th century: the Fonte da Vila is a Mannerist fountain at the heart of the Judiaria, at the corner of Rua da Fonte and Rua da Judiaria. Modest, almost forgotten by tourists. That's precisely why it deserves a stop.

Climb up to Castelo de Vide Castle to see Marvão on the northeast horizon, perched on its ridge five kilometers away. The two fortresses had faced each other for centuries. Castelo de Vide's medieval castle controls the Sever valley; clear view over the Serra de São Mamede.

activities.text: The Judiaria is small: that's its strength. Ten or so alleys are enough to get lost in the medieval Jewish quarter, one of the best preserved in Portugal. Every pointed-arch doorway is a document. Pick up a map at the tourist office—the signage doesn't provide enough information to understand the houses.

If you visit on a Friday morning, Castelo de Vide's main square comes alive early with a local market—vegetables, cheeses, and honey. The villages of Upper Alentejo have weekly markets that survive despite depopulation.

days_plan.itin_title: Portugal: From Aveiro's Canals to the Fortified Villages of Alentejo
Lisbon and Upper Alentejo Fortresses in 8 Days

visits.text: Two granite boars greet you at the main gate of Castelo Mendo. They are verracos—Celtic-Iberian animal sculptures associated with the Vettones, a people who inhabited the region before the Romans. Similar verracos are found throughout the western Iberian Peninsula. Allow 10 seconds to understand why they're there, 30 minutes for the rest of the village.

The walls inside Castelo Mendo date partly to the reign of Dom Sancho II (13th century), the second enclosure to Dom Dinis. Inside, Manueline houses, a medieval judiaria, and in the stones of the old Paço do Concelho, two carved figures face each other: Mendo and Menda, whose story is unknown.

activities.text: Look in the stones for the figures of Mendo and Menda—two carved faces watching each other from opposite sides of the alley, from different buildings. No one knows who they were or who had them engraved. Local tradition would have them as lovers condemned to see each other without touching.

days_plan.itin_title: Portugal: Historic Villages & Serra da Estrela in 8 Days

places.name: Castelo Rodrigo

visits.text: This village faces Spain: the border is 5 km away. From the top of the promontory, the Spanish ridgeline is visible in clear weather. The political isolation explains Castelo Rodrigo's strange history—a village more loyal to Madrid than to Lisbon for sixty years.

The ruins of the Palácio de Cristóvão de Moura are the trace of a punished betrayal. Cristóvão de Moura was Philip II of Spain's chief diplomat for seizing the Portuguese throne in 1580. Named Viceroy of Portugal and Marquis of Castelo Rodrigo, he had his palace built here. In 1640, as soon as independence was restored, the people burned the building. Never rebuilt. The ruins are freely accessible.

The Manueline windows still standing on the village façades testify to Castelo Rodrigo's importance in the 16th century. The medieval cistern within the walls, whose horseshoe arch suggests 13th-century construction, is accessible and often overlooked by visitors.

activities.text: If you pass late in the day, the raking light brings out the golden stones of the burned palace. The ruins have been used for open-air concerts—the acoustics are good. The Manueline windows still standing on the façades give an idea of what the building once was.

Walk down to the terraced almond trees covering the slope below the village—the February-March blossom is photographed by visitors from all over the peninsula. Out of season, the dry-stone terraces are simply beautiful.

Douro in 5 Days: Quintas, Pinhão, and the Côa Rock Engravings

map_keywords: Palácio Cristóvão de Moura Castelo Rodrigo

places.name: Castro Daire

visits.text: Climb the Serra de São Macário, a mountain range offering some of the finest panoramic views in all of northern Portugal. The winding road to the summit is an adventure in itself, with narrow roads climbing through dramatic upland landscapes. At the top, sweeping views extend over valleys, villages and distant mountain ranges in every direction. Allow for a round trip by car during the day from Castro Daire.

Visit Aldeia da Pena, one of northern Portugal's most isolated and picturesque traditional stone villages, hidden at the bottom of a valley. Narrow cobbled streets covered with straw wind between roughly hewn stone houses that seem to emerge from the landscape. Goats roam freely, their bells mingling with the murmur of a stream, creating an atmosphere unchanged for centuries. Allow for a round trip by car during the day from Castro Daire.

activities.text: Admire the sunset from the summit of the Serra de São Macário, where peace and spectacular scenery create truly magical moments. The elevated viewpoint often offers complete solitude, with the surrounding landscape bathed in golden light. Hiking trails radiate from the summit through forests and across high moorlands for further exploration. Allow for a round trip by car from Castro Daire, returning in the evening.

days_plan.itin_title: Portugal Road Trip: From Lisbon to the Wild North
Trás-os-Montes and Douro: Heritage, Nature and Centuries-Old Traditions

map_keywords: Serra de São Macário hiking trails

visits.text: The steppe stretches as far as the eye can see from Castro Verde: cereal crops, scattered cork oaks, immense sky. This Special Protection Area is classified by BirdLife International as one of Europe's most important areas for steppe birds—little bustards, pin-tailed sandgrouse, lesser kestrels. The LPN (Liga para a Protecção da Natureza) manages several reserves accessible to the public.

The Basílica Real de Nossa Senhora da Conceição preserves an 18th-century azulejo cycle recounting the Battle of Ourique of 1139 - mythical battle of Portugal's founding, where Afonso Henriques allegedly saw Christ appear to him. The exact location of the battle remains contested by historians, but the building marks the traditional site.

activities.text: If you're here in March–April, little bustards perform courtship displays at sunrise in the fields around Castro Verde. The LPN organizes guided birdwatching outings—information at the Castro Verde nature center. Binoculars essential.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Lisbon and Southern Portugal Tour in 15 Days

visits.text: Discover the famous Chaves Thermal Baths, whose thermal waters emerge at over 70°C. These thousand-year-old baths, already appreciated by the Romans, are renowned for their healing properties for muscular and digestive ailments. Taste the water at Fonte do Povo, a unique sensory experience even if the taste may surprise you!

Cross the remarkable Roman Bridge of Trajan, an impressive 140-meter monument that has spanned the Tâmega River for nearly 2,000 years. This 12-arch bridge, one of the best preserved on the Iberian Peninsula, bears witness to the genius of Roman engineers and the strategic importance of Chaves on the road between Braga and Astorga.

activities.text: Stroll through the historic center of Chaves, admiring the keep of the medieval castle and the Fort of São Francisco, now a charming hotel. Taste the famous pastéis de Chaves, meat-filled puff pastries that have earned this welcoming spa town its culinary reputation.

days_plan.itin_title: Trás-os-Montes and Douro: Heritage, Nature and Centuries-Old Traditions

visits.text: Explore the University of Coimbra, one of Europe's oldest and most prestigious academic institutions, founded in 1290. This UNESCO World Heritage Site crowns the city's hilltop, its magnificent baroque Joanina Library housing over 200,000 old volumes beneath gilded ceilings and exotic wood shelving. The ceremonial halls and historic classrooms transport visitors through centuries of scholarly tradition.

Visit the Sé Velha, Coimbra's Romanesque Old Cathedral built in the 12th century during the tumultuous period of the Reconquista. This fortress-like church, with its crenellated walls and narrow windows, represents one of Portugal's finest examples of Romanesque architecture. Inside, the Gothic cloister and Renaissance altarpiece showcase the evolution of Portuguese religious art.

Wander through Coimbra's historic center, where narrow medieval streets wind between ancient stone buildings. The city's unique geography creates two distinct zones: the Baixa with its bustling commercial streets and the Alta where centuries of academic tradition permeate every cobblestone.

activities.text: Discover the Monastery of Santa Cruz, final resting place of Portugal's first two kings, Afonso Henriques and Sancho I. This 12th-century monastery features an ornate Manueline portal, Renaissance sacristy, and stunning azulejo panels depicting the life of Saint Augustine.

days_plan.itin_title: Portugal: From Aveiro's Canals to the Fortified Villages of Alentejo

visits.text: Discover the iconic striped houses of Costa Nova, known locally as palheiros. These charming wooden structures, painted in vibrant reds, blues, greens, and yellows, were originally fishermen's huts used to store equipment. Today they stand as one of Portugal's most photographed coastal landmarks, creating a rainbow of color against the Atlantic backdrop.

Climb the Farol da Barra, Portugal's tallest lighthouse standing at 62 meters. Built in 1893, this striking red and white tower offers panoramic views across the Atlantic Ocean and the Aveiro lagoon. The ascent rewards visitors with breathtaking vistas of the coastline stretching toward the horizon.

activities.text: Relax on the golden sands of Costa Nova do Prado beach, a favorite destination for surfers and sunbathers alike. The powerful Atlantic waves make this an excellent spot for water sports, while the long stretches of sand invite peaceful walks along the shore.

days_plan.itin_title: Portugal: From Aveiro's Canals to the Fortified Villages of Alentejo

places.name: Covão da Ametade

visits.text: Covão da Ametade is a glacial basin at the source of the Zêzere—a granite cirque at 1500 m altitude, fed by winter snowfields. It's the birth of the river that crosses all of Beira before joining the Tagus. The water comes out cold and clear even in August.

The trail from Manteigas to Covão da Ametade follows the glacial valley for 7 km one way. The elevation gain is moderate and the path marked. At sunrise, the waters are still and the reflection of the granite wall in the lake is crisp.

activities.text: Set out on foot from Manteigas at dawn—the Zêzere glacial trail is one of the finest in the Serra. 14 km round trip, about 3.5 hours. Hiking boots required: the trail gets rocky after the first 500 m.

places.name: Covão dos Conchos

visits.text: Covão dos Conchos is an artificial spillway at the bottom of a mountain lake—a circular funnel that swallows water in silence and diverts it under the mountain to another basin. Went viral on social media for its “portal to the depths” effect. The hydraulic reality is simpler, but the visual effect delivers.

The trail between Lagoa Comprida and Covão dos Conchos runs about 5 km round trip from the Lagoa parking lot. The high moorlands of the Serra da Estrela crossed along the way are among Portugal's most open landscapes.

activities.text: Do the Lagoa Comprida - Covão dos Conchos loop early in the morning to see the spillway without the photographers. After 10 a.m. in summer, it's crowded. The morning light on the water is better anyway.

visits.text: Begin your Covilhã exploration at Santa Maria Maior Church, a stunning 16th-century Baroque edifice in the heart of the historic center. Marvel at the exquisite blue and white azulejo tiles adorning its exterior, beautifully depicting scenes from the life of the Virgin Mary, showcasing centuries of Portuguese religious artistry.

Climb to Portas do Sol Viewpoint for panoramic vistas stretching across Covilhã's rooftops to the majestic Serra da Gardunha mountain range. This elevated terrace features a historic sundial and several remarkable street art murals from the WOOL Urban Art Festival.

Explore Praça do Município, the vibrant heart of Covilhã where the imposing Town Hall, ornate Misericórdia Church, and elegant Municipal Theater surround a statue honoring Pêro da Covilhã, the legendary 15th-century explorer sent by King John II to discover the spice routes to India and Ethiopia.

Visit the Wool Museum documenting Covilhã's heritage as one of Portugal's main wool producers. Housed in the historic Real Fábrica de Panos and Real Fábrica Veiga, the museum showcases the traditional textile processes that once powered hundreds of local factories.

Journey to Varanda dos Carqueijais viewpoint, just 10 minutes from Covilhã, offering one of Serra da Estrela's most spectacular panoramas. The distinctive metal viewing platform has become an iconic photography spot, framing the dramatic mountain landscape in a unique architectural gesture.

Ascend to Torre, mainland Portugal's highest point at nearly 2,000 meters elevation. This dramatic summit, just 30 minutes from Covilhã, attracts visitors year-round seeking snow in winter and cool mountain air in summer. Portugal's only natural ski resort operates here during the coldest months.

Discover Covão d'Ametade, one of the most enchanting glacial valleys in the Serra da Estrela, around thirty minutes by road from Covilhã. This fairy-tale landscape of spectacular rock formations, crystal-clear streams and alpine meadows captivates visitors in every season, whether blanketed in snow or carpeted with wildflowers.

activities.text: Embark on the WOOL Urban Art Route, an extraordinary open-air museum featuring works by international artists including Bordalo II's iconic recycled material owl, Third's massive heart mural, and Daniel Eime's intricate portraits. This annual festival has transformed neglected walls into vibrant canvases throughout the historic center.

Cool off at Unhais da Serra river beach, a pristine natural swimming spot surrounded by lush mountain vegetation. The well-maintained facilities and crystal-clear waters make this an ideal escape from summer heat, just 30 minutes from Covilhã.

visits.text: Almost nothing: an arch and three granite pillars. The Varanda do Grão-Prior is all that remains of the palace of the Knights of the Order of Malta in Crato. An emblem of the town, as locals say. It's from this loggia that the prior asserted his power over the Priorado, a vast territory that extended over a good part of central Portugal.

Dom Manuel I married Eleanor of Austria here in 1518: Crato's Praça do Município has seen kings pass through. Today it's a quiet provincial square, with the municipal museum in a baroque palace, the symbol of the Maltese Cross carved everywhere, and cats on the windowsills.

activities.text: Have a glass of Alentejo red wine in Crato's square—Portalegre wines have body and a high-altitude freshness rare in Alentejo. The town is sleepy, but service at the bars on the square is good. A well-deserved break before Flor da Rosa.

days_plan.itin_title: Lisbon and Upper Alentejo Fortresses in 8 Days

visits.text: The Cromeleque dos Almendres is 15 km from Évora, but this megalithic circle of 95 granite monoliths—dating back about 6,000 years—is one of the best-preserved megalithic ensembles on the Iberian Peninsula. Dirt road for the last 2 kilometers. Free visit, always deserted on weekdays before 10 a.m.

About 2 km from the cromlech, the Menhir dos Almendres stands alone among the olive trees: a standing stone over 2 m tall, older than the circle itself. A sign marks it beside the track leading to the cromlech, followed by a few hundred meters on foot.

activities.text: You can combine the megalithic visit with a short walk through the montado—the cork oak forest typical of the Alentejo. The estate around the cromlech is open, with abundant wildlife in spring.

places.name: Elvas

visits.text: Marvel at the grand Amoreira Aqueduct, stretching 7 km with 843 arches, built by architect Francisco de Arruda, who also designed Belém Tower. This impressive monument marks the entrance to the world's largest bastioned fortification, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Explore the fortifications of Elvas, whose star-shaped defensive structures with a perimeter of about 10 km are a unique testimony to the evolution of military strategy up to the 19th century. The complex includes Islamic and medieval walls, the 17th-century fortified enclosure, and the Forts of Santa Luzia and Graça.

Visit the former Cathedral, now the Church of Nossa Senhora da Assunção, the Church of the Dominican Nuns with its distinctive octagonal floor plan, the Manueline pillory, and the Fernandina Tower. In the streets of the historic center, identify the arches that mark the old entrances through the walls.

Discover Praça da República, the city's living room, paved with Portuguese cobblestones, spacious and airy, with welcoming outdoor seating areas. This is the heart of Elvas, where residents and visitors meet to enjoy the tranquil atmosphere of this border garrison town.

activities.text: Visit the museums of Elvas: the Contemporary Art Museum, the João Carpinteiro Photography Museum with cameras from 1898 and prints dated 1860, the Sacred Art Museum, and two military-themed museum spaces.

Explore the Church of São Domingos, the Third Order of São Francisco Church, and outside the walls, the Sanctuary of Senhor Jesus da Piedade where the famous annual pilgrimage takes place in September, coinciding with the São Mateus Fair.

places.name: Estremoz

visits.text: Visit the Medieval Castle of Estremoz from the 13th century, now transformed into the Pousada Rainha Santa Isabel. The Tower of the Three Crowns, so called because three kings participated in its construction (Afonso III, Sancho II, and Dinis), offers splendid views over the marble region.

Explore the Professor Joaquim Vermelho Municipal Museum, located opposite the keep, with exhibitions on Alentejo life and the region's famous ceramics. The traditional globe-shaped moringa jugs from Estremoz are particularly remarkable.
Admire the elegant Church of Santa Maria, a 16th-century hall church in late Renaissance style that replaced a medieval church. This monument impresses with its monumental scale and rich decoration.

Visit the 18th-century Chapel of Senhor Jesus dos Inocentes, near the statue of Saint Elizabeth, Queen of Portugal. The statue pays tribute to the wife of King Dinis, famous for her charity and the miracle of the roses, who died in Estremoz.

activities.text: Stroll through Rossio Marquês de Pombal, the main square dominated by the twin marble towers of the former 17th-century Convent of the Congregados. Climb the tower for glorious views over Estremoz and visit the Sacred Art Museum.

Discover the Living Science Center in the former 15th-century Convent of the Maltese Sisters, with its beautiful cloister and exhibitions on Earth and Geology. The T-Rex skeleton replica is a must-see attraction for all ages.

Explore the Porta de Santarém, the main entrance to the medieval village enclosed by the 13th-century wall, and the 17th-century Porta dos Currais. Also admire the Manueline pillory and Lago do Gadanha with its iconic statue.

places.name: Évora

visits.text: Discover Praça do Giraldo, the beating heart of Évora, with its iconic arcades, the Church of Santo Antão, and the historic fountain that served for centuries as one of the population's main sources of water. The square's name pays tribute to Geraldo Sem Pavor, a semi-legendary figure in the reconquest of the city from the Moors.

Marvel at the Roman Temple of Évora, dating from the 1st century, the main vestige from when Ebora Liberalitas Iulia was one of the most notable Roman cities in Lusitania. Contrary to popular belief, this temple was likely dedicated to the imperial cult rather than to the goddess Diana.

Visit the imposing Évora Cathedral, the largest medieval cathedral in Portugal, built between the 12th and 13th centuries. Don't miss the cloisters, the main chapel, the Sacred Art Museum, and climb to the rooftop for a breathtaking panoramic view over this UNESCO World Heritage city.

Enter the 15th-century Church of São Francisco, in Manueline-Mudéjar and Renaissance styles, which once had the Royal Palace as an annex and was closely connected to Portugal's maritime expansion. Inside, the famous Chapel of Bones will remain forever etched in your memory.

Visit the College of the Holy Spirit, the main building of the University of Évora founded by Cardinal Dom Henrique in the 16th century. The grand cloister is a must-see, bearing witness to the historical importance of this centuries-old educational institution.

Discover Portas de Moura square and its fountain. One of the most emblematic squares in the 16th-century city, it is surrounded by noble mansions belonging to the most important families of the era. This square preserves the aristocratic atmosphere of Renaissance Évora.

Admire the Renaissance facade of the 16th-century Church of Graça, a fine example of architecture on Largo da Graça. This church demonstrates the richness of Évora's religious heritage, found throughout the city.

Visit the Art and Culture Center, the former Palace of the Inquisition, now a venue run by the Eugénio de Almeida Foundation dedicated to arts and culture with a special focus on contemporary art. A fascinating contrast between the building's dark history and its current cultural purpose.

Discover the Almendres Cromlech, built around 7,000 years ago, the largest megalithic complex on the Iberian Peninsula and one of the oldest in the world. This prehistoric monument bears witness to human occupation of this region since time immemorial. The site lies about thirty minutes by road from the town for this stage of the itinerary.

Just over 1 km from the cromlech, visit the Almendres Menhir, another impressive megalithic monument that complements this extraordinary archaeological complex. These monuments are unique testimonies to the civilizations that inhabited the Alentejo thousands of years ago.

activities.text: Explore Largo Conde Vila Flor, home to some of the city's main buildings: the stunning Church of the Lóios with its blue and white azulejo tiles at their finest, the 15th-century Convent of the Lóios now a pousada, the Palace of the Dukes of Cadaval, and the Évora Museum with nearly 20,000 objects.

Stroll through the magnificent Public Garden built in the 19th century, where you'll find the 15th-century Palace of Dom Manuel, the place where Vasco da Gama was appointed commander of the fleet that would discover the maritime route to India. Don't miss the charming mock ruins with their peacocks.

Discover the imposing Walls of Évora surrounding the entire historic center and the grand Silver Water Aqueduct, inaugurated in the 16th century to supply the city. Look for the houses built between its arches, a secret that not all visitors discover.

Climb to the Windmills of Alto de São Bento for the best panoramic view over Évora. This viewpoint offers a unique perspective of the World Heritage city, with its monuments and walls silhouetted against the Alentejo plain.

Visit the Cartuxa Winery, one of the most prestigious in Portugal, where you can taste the renowned Alentejo wine and olive oil. This wine tourism experience is essential for those wishing to discover the authentic flavors of the region.

Travel the Évora Ecovia - Mora Branch on foot or by bicycle, an alternative way to discover the Alentejo landscape. This route allows direct contact with nature and the golden plains that characterize this region.

visits.text: Discover the unique Castle of Évora Monte, erected by King Dinis in the 14th century atop Roman fortifications, in a spectacular position on a steep hilltop. The almost triangular structure with five towers and an imposing keep is a unique example of Portuguese military architecture.

activities.text: Explore the small village of Évora Monte where the Convention of Évora Monte was signed in 1834, ending the Portuguese civil war. Legend has it that the signing took so long that only stale bread was left to eat, leading to the invention of the Alentejo açorda.
