visits.text: The Convention signed here on 26 May 1834 brought the civil war to an end. The Castelo de Evoramonte, rebuilt after the earthquake of 1531 in a Renaissance style inspired by Italian palace architecture, with four round towers girdled by Manueline rope moldings, has been a national monument since 1910. Small entrance fee.

The Alentejo spreads beneath Evoramonte's ramparts to the horizon without interruption. The village perched at 481 meters on the Serra de Ossa is tiny—one main street, white houses with blue shutters, pottery at the doorsteps. What Monsaraz has become touristy, Evoramonte remains preserved.

activities.text: Walk the castle's wall-walk circuit in under an hour. The views over the olive groves and cork oaks of the Serra de Ossa are particularly beautiful in late morning, before the heat raises a haze.

activities.text: Twisted trees with strange shapes stand apart from one another: in Fanal, many of the til trees (Ocotea foetens, a species of laurel) are more than a century old. This forest existed before the Portuguese arrived. It is part of the Laurissilva, Madeira’s UNESCO-protected laurel forest: a remnant of the forests that covered southern Europe 15 to 40 million years ago. In winter, a pond forms in an ancient crater. The site is designated an area for rest and silence: keep your voice down.

days_plan.itin_title: Madeira in 7 Days: Funchal, Levadas, and Pico Ruivo

activities.text: Walk to the end of the Molhe de Felgueiras, the breakwater built at the mouth of the Douro. Here, the river completes an 897 km journey that began in Spain and meets the Atlantic Ocean. The small, hexagonal, 10 m lighthouse, Farolim de Felgueiras, dates from 1886. Its light has been inactive since 2009, and it now retains only an audible signal for boats. Then walk along Avenida Dom Carlos I, facing the waves. In rough seas, stay well away from the end of the breakwater, which is exposed to waves.

days_plan.itin_title: Porto in 2 Days: Ribeira, Gaia Wine Cellars, and Foz do Douro

visits.text: The Capelinha das Aparições, a small chapel at the heart of the Santuário de Fátima, marks the spot where three shepherd children said they saw the Virgin Mary in 1917. These apparitions took place from May 13 to October 13 of that year. Local residents began building the chapel in 1919. On the esplanade, some pilgrims move on their knees along a long strip of marble to fulfill a vow. On May 13 and October 13, crowds approach a million people: choose another date to move around freely.

The crackling of hundreds of candles accompanies your walk toward the Basílica de Nossa Senhora do Rosário, the white church with a colonnade on the esplanade. Its cornerstone was laid in 1928, and it was consecrated in 1953. It houses the tombs of the three children: Francisco and Jacinta Marto, who died of the flu in 1919 and 1920, and their cousin Lúcia, who died in 2005. Near the chapel, worshippers throw their candles into a large fire; expect to pay €0.50 to €2.70 per candle.

More surprising than beautiful at first glance, the Basílica da Santíssima Trindade is an immense modern circular hall on the other side of the esplanade. Dedicated on October 12, 2007, it measures about 125 m in diameter and 18 m in height. Each of its twelve bronze doors, around 9 m tall, bears a phrase from the Bible. Behind the altar stands a 3 m statue of the Virgin Mary in white Carrara marble. Visit outside service times to appreciate the scale of the space.

You will then walk to Aljustrel, the hamlet where the three children were born, just over 2 km from the sanctuary. Allow about 30 minutes on foot. The homes of Lúcia and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta have been preserved and are free to visit. They open daily from 9 a.m. to 12:45 p.m. and from 2 p.m. to 5:45 p.m. Nearby, a monument at the Poço do Arneiro, an old well, marks the spot where, according to the children’s account, an angel appeared to them in 1916.

visits.text: Founded in 1356 by the Order of the Hospitallers, with half of it now converted into a pousada: the Monastery of Santa Maria de Flor da Rosa is one of the most accomplished examples of a fortified monastery on the Iberian Peninsula. Its founder, Dom Álvaro Gonçalves Pereira, father of the famous constable Nuno Álvares Pereira, is buried on site. The church has been classified as a National Monument since 1910.

Single nave, no side windows: the darkness inside Flor da Rosa church contrasts starkly with the harsh Alentejo light outside. Designed as much as a fortress as a place of worship—high crenellated walls, massive buttresses, defensive corbels. Closer to a watchtower than a Gothic cathedral.

activities.text: If your budget allows, have lunch at the monastery restaurant: eating in the former monastic outbuildings of a 14th-century building has a particular flavor. Otherwise, picnic in the courtyard—the grass is mowed, the chairs are there.

places.name: Funchal

visits.text: The finest feature of Sé do Funchal, the cathedral, is above your head. It is a cedarwood ceiling in the Mudéjar style, a decorative style that originated among Muslim artisans in Christian Spain. Construction began in 1486 using volcanic stone from Cabo Girão, a cliff you will see near the end of your trip. In the choir stalls, the wooden seats reserved for the clergy, look for bananas and wineskins carved among the prophets. Visit outside Mass times.

Doors turned into paintings line Rua de Santa Maria in the heart of Zona Velha, Funchal’s old town. Funchal’s first inhabitants settled in this neighborhood. The Arte Portas Abertas project (“open-door art”) had around 200 doors of abandoned houses and shops painted. Walk past Capela do Corpo Santo, a 15th-century chapel. A little farther on, Fortaleza de São Tiago, a fort begun in 1614, protected the city from privateers. In the evening, the street’s outdoor dining areas come alive.

The Museu de Arte Sacra do Funchal occupies the former bishop’s palace, founded in 1594. Its surprise is a collection of large-scale Flemish paintings, uncommon in European museums. From the 15th century onward, Madeira’s sugar was sold in Bruges and Antwerp. Enriched by this trade, the island’s plantation owners and merchants commissioned expensive works in Flanders. Allow 1 hour; the museum is closed on Sundays and closes at 1:30 p.m. on Saturdays.

The family of Zarco, the navigator who claimed Madeira for Portugal, had their second home at Quinta das Cruzes in Funchal. Converted into a museum in 1953, the house displays 17th-century Portuguese furniture carved from exotic woods imported mainly from Brazil. It also holds Chinese porcelain from the Qing dynasty, China’s last imperial dynasty. Allow 1 hour, including the garden; open Tuesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.

activities.text: Deliberately heated, Madeira wine can keep for more than 200 years in the bottle. Heat and air, which damage other wines, make this wine very stable, even after the bottle is opened. At Blandy’s Wine Lodge, in cellars dating from the 17th and 18th centuries, you will learn how this method originated: in the past, wine crossed the tropics in ships’ holds and returned tasting better. Fine wines, meanwhile, age without heating in warm rooms, using the canteiro method. Taste a Sercial, the driest, followed by a Malvasia, the sweetest.

If you visit just one market in Madeira, choose Mercado dos Lavradores, Funchal’s farmers’ market. The building, inaugurated in 1940 and designed by architect Edmundo Tavares, blends Art Deco and modernism. On the facade and in the fish hall, large panels of azulejos (painted ceramic tiles) by João Rodrigues depict scenes from the island. The fruit stalls are set up outdoors in the inner courtyard.

visits.text: Explore the Historic Center of Fundão, which combines traditional streets, local shops and renovated cultural spaces. Stroll across the Town Hall Square, visit the main parish church and discover the Town Hall building.

Discover Castelo Novo, one of Portugal's most beautiful Historic Villages, in the municipality of Fundão. The granite houses, the Manueline pillory, the castle, and the extraordinary central square form a medieval setting preserved with rare harmony. Climb to the castle in late afternoon to watch the sunset over the mountain.

Visit the José Monteiro Archaeological Museum, which brings together finds from the region that explain human occupation of the area since prehistoric times. Also explore Moagem - City of Engineering and Arts, a dynamic cultural space housed in a restored former factory.

activities.text: Hike the panoramic trails of Serra da Gardunha, such as PR7 or the climb to Racha da Penha, through woods, streams, and plateaus with views over the Zêzere valley. In spring, the slopes covered with flowering cherry trees transform the landscape into a unique spectacle.

Discover the Cherry Route of Fundão, Portugal's capital of this fruit. Between May and June, several estates open their doors for visits, pick-your-own sessions and food experiences. The Cherry Festival is one of the most popular events, with producers' stalls and plenty of entertainment.

days_plan.itin_title: Beira Interior: Serra da Estrela, Schist Villages and Historic Cities

visits.text: The smell of sulfur, steam, and bubbling water right in the street: in the village center, the Caldeiras das Furnas bring together around thirty hot springs and fumaroles, vents that release volcanic steam. Each spring has its own temperature and composition. Temperatures range from about 15 °C to over 95 °C at the hottest spring, Água Santa. Vendors cook ears of corn in the steam: try one. Admission is free.

Lunch has been cooking underground since dawn: on the northern shore of Lagoa das Furnas, pots of cozido, a boiled meat stew, are buried in the hot ground early in the morning. They cook there for 6 to 7 hours before being dug up around noon. This heat comes from the Furnas volcano, one of the island’s three active volcanoes. Its last eruption, in 1630, killed about 200 people. Come around noon and follow the safety signs: the water in the small pools reaches 66 to 93 °C.

The neo-Gothic chapel of Nossa Senhora das Vitórias, beside Lagoa das Furnas, was born of a vow. The intellectual José do Canto, who spent his summers by the lake, had it built in the hope that his seriously ill wife would recover. Inaugurated on August 15, 1886, it also serves as a tomb: both are buried there. The interior can only be viewed through the entrance gate. There is an admission fee for the surrounding garden.

You can visit our favorite garden on the island in a swimsuit: Parque Terra Nostra, in Furnas, covers 12.5 hectares of gardens and woodland. Thomas Hickling, the U.S. consul, built his summer home here in 1775. Its large thermal pool, with water between 38 and 42 °C, is orange-brown because of the iron. Wear a dark swimsuit, as the water stains light fabrics, and spend no more than 30 minutes in the water. Admission is €17 per adult, with opening hours from 10:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

If the sky is clear, head up to Miradouro do Pico do Ferro, about 5 km from the village by road. This viewpoint, at an elevation of 570 m, overlooks the caldera, the village, and Lagoa das Furnas. On a clear day, the view stretches to the ocean. Come early in the morning or late in the afternoon to avoid groups.

activities.text: Try cozido das Furnas for lunch at one of the village restaurants that serve it. The dish has cooked in the ground all morning, without a flame, using volcanic heat alone. In high season, reserve your table in advance. By evening, there is often no cozido left: request it a few hours ahead.

If you’re staying in Furnas, save Poça da Dona Beija for the evening. Its five pools of iron-rich thermal water, at around 39 °C, open daily from 8:30 a.m. to 11 p.m. Last admission is at 9:30 p.m., and you must leave the water by 10:30 p.m. Tickets are sold online only, with no exchanges or refunds: buy them as soon as your evening plans are set.

days_plan.itin_title: São Miguel in 6 Days: Sete Cidades, Lagoa do Fogo, Furnas

visits.text: Enter Peneda-Gerês National Park, Portugal's only national park, protecting a wilderness of mountains, ancient forests, and cascading waterfalls. The park encompasses the Peneda, Soajo, Amarela, and Gerês mountain ranges reaching 1,545 meters at their highest point. This remarkable landscape harbors diverse wildlife in pristine environments deserving Portugal's highest level of protection.

Visit Soajo, a traditional mountain village serving as an excellent hiking base, known for its unique espigueiros - historic stone granaries raised on granite pillars. These distinctive structures, used for centuries to store and dry corn, create one of the park's most photographed scenes. Stone houses and old churches reflect the enduring traditions of this isolated mountain community. Allow for a round trip by car during the day from Gerês.

Discover the Mourela plateau, rising to around 1,000 meters and recognized as one of the national park's leading birdwatching locations. This upland moorland habitat supports diverse bird species thriving among heather, grasslands and marshy ground. The plateau's open landscapes provide excellent visibility for spotting birds of prey and migratory species throughout the year. Allow for a round trip by car during the day from Gerês.

activities.text: Hike the trails of Peneda-Gerês including the adventurous Grande Rota traversing the park's most spectacular scenery. Shorter circular walks pass through forests, past waterfalls, and to scenic viewpoints. The park's five 'gates' offer visitor information centers with detailed hiking maps and guidance.

Seek adventure at waterfalls where canyoning and cliff jumping trips provide adrenaline-fueled ways to experience dramatic water features. Professional guides lead expeditions through gorges, alongside waterfalls, and into crystal-clear pools surrounded by granite cliffs. Swimming and sunbathing at natural pools offer refreshing rewards after hiking.

Relax in the natural thermal waters of Caldas do Gerês, a spa village famous for hot springs since Roman times. The therapeutic waters emerge at temperatures ideal for soothing tired muscles after active days in the mountains. This traditional wellness destination provides the perfect complement to outdoor adventures.

visits.text: The same family has been producing tea at the Fábrica de Chá Gorreana on the north coast since 1883. It is Europe’s oldest tea factory still in operation. Tea growing took hold here after a disease destroyed the island’s orange trees in the mid-19th century. In 1878, specialists from Macau taught locals how to process the leaves. The self-guided tour takes you past British machinery from the 19th and early 20th centuries, then ends with a free tasting. The factory opens daily.

activities.text: You can then walk among Gorreana’s tea bushes on the PRC28 SMI Chá Gorreana trail. This 3.4 km loop takes about 1 hour. Tea is harvested from April to October. Factory admission, parking, and the tasting are free: you pay only for purchases in the shop.

visits.text: Discover the Casa da Torre in Gouveia, a 16th-century building designated a National Monument in 1928. This beautiful example of Manueline style is one of the most important architectural landmarks of this mountain town, situated on the western slope of Serra da Estrela at an altitude of about 700 meters.

Visit the Abel Manta Municipal Museum, housed in the 18th-century Palace of the Counts of Vinhó and Almedina. This museum holds an important collection of works by the illustrious painter born in Gouveia, as well as works by artists such as Vieira da Silva, Joaquim Rodrigo, Júlio Resende, Júlio Pomar, Paula Rego, and other masters of Portuguese art.

Explore the Gouveia Town Hall, a former Jesuit College, and the Vergílio Ferreira Municipal Library, housed in the Serpa-Pimentel Palace. These grand buildings reflect the rich heritage of this city, which retains traces of the Castro, Roman, and Muslim civilizations.

activities.text: Climb to Monte Calvário with its 18th-century temple and enjoy an excellent panoramic view over the Mondego Valley. Also visit the Miradouro do Paixotão and the Gouveia Zoological Park, green spaces that make this city a favored destination for nature lovers.

Discover the Pedra da Orca Dolmen in the parish of Rio Torto, a megalithic monument dating from the late Neolithic period. This archaeological remains is the most significant example of ancient human occupation in this region, bearing witness to thousands of years of history.

visits.text: A cool temperature of around 17 °C welcomes you inside the Grutas de Mira de Aire, in summer and winter alike. Four local residents descended into the caves in 1947 in search of water. The caves opened to the public in 1974. The network extends for more than 11 km, but the tour covers about 600 m. You descend 683 steps to around 110 m underground, passing through chambers lit by colored lights. An elevator then takes you back to the surface. Tours start at 9:30 a.m., every day except December 25.

visits.text: Discover the majestic Sé Cathedral of Guarda, an imposing edifice whose construction began during the reign of King John I and was completed in 1517. This emblematic cathedral presents a fascinating blend of Gothic and Manueline styles, standing as one of the most remarkable religious monuments in Portugal's interior. Its grandeur reflects the historical importance of this city founded by King Sancho I.

Explore the Castle of Guarda, situated in a commanding position at an altitude of 1,056 meters, the highest point of any Portuguese city. Although only remnants of the walls and keep remain, this historic site evokes the times when Guarda was a strategic defensive point, explaining its nickname as the strong city.

Stroll through the old Jewish Quarter of Guarda, located within the walls near the Porta D'El Rei. This Jewish community was for centuries one of the most important and oldest in Portugal, leaving a historical and cultural legacy that can still be discovered in the narrow alleyways of this medieval neighborhood.

Admire the Misericórdia Church of Guarda, whose construction dates back to the 17th century. The portal is framed by two bell towers and displays an image of Our Lady of Mercy. The interior is dominated by the Baroque style, both in form and decoration, with King John V's coat of arms above the main portal.

Admire the Statue of Sancho I in Praça Luís de Camões, a bronze monument dedicated to the king who granted city status to Guarda on November 27, 1199. This tribute celebrates the founder of the city of the 5 Fs: Forte, Farta (abundant), Fria (cold), Fiel (faithful), and Formosa (beautiful).

Visit the Mileu Archaeological Site, discovered in 1953 during construction work. This important cluster of archaeological ruins, located about two kilometers from Guarda, features various Roman residential structures near the Chapel of Nossa Senhora de Mileu.

activities.text: Visit the Guarda Museum, founded in 1940, which houses a remarkable collection including archaeology, numismatics, sacred sculpture from the 13th to 18th centuries, sacred painting, arms and armor, ceramics, and contemporary art. Housed in a historic building, this museum preserves the memory and identity of the Beira region.

Enjoy the Rio Diz Urban Park, an impressive 21-hectare space with an 11,400-square-meter body of water, a playground, green areas, a partially covered entertainment area, and a toy library. Also stroll through the Municipal Garden with its curious hedge maze.

places.name: Guimarães

visits.text: Medieval in appearance, yet rebuilt in the 20th century: that is the paradox of the Paço dos Duques de Bragança, the Palace of the Dukes of Braganza. Afonso, Count of Barcelos and later the first Duke of Braganza, began having it built in the 1420s. The dukes later moved to Vila Viçosa, and the palace became a barracks in 1807. It was rebuilt from 1937 to 1959 under the Estado Novo, the authoritarian regime of the time. This highly interpretive restoration remains controversial. The palace is open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.: admission is €10, or €13 including the castle.

According to tradition, Afonso Henriques, Portugal’s first king, was born at Castelo de Guimarães, the castle crowning the hill above the city. Countess Mumadona Dias had the first tower built here in the 10th century to protect a monastery. Right next door, the small Church of São Miguel do Castelo preserves the baptismal font where the future king is said to have been baptized. During the ongoing restoration, only the inner courtyard is open to visitors: the wall walk and keep are closed. Admission is €5.

Houses with granite ground floors and wooden upper stories, an olive tree amid the cobblestones: this is Largo da Oliveira, the heart of the historic center designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. According to tradition, a withered olive tree here turned green again in 1342, three days after a cross was placed beside it. The neighboring church took its name from the tree: Nossa Senhora da Oliveira, Our Lady of the Olive Tree. In front stands the Padrão do Salado, a small monument dating from 1340 that commemorates the Battle of Salado, won that year by King Afonso IV, who had come to Castile’s aid. Return in the evening, when the outdoor cafés come alive.

One object in particular makes a visit to the Museu de Alberto Sampaio worthwhile: King João I’s gambeson. This padded garment was worn beneath armor. The king wore it at the Battle of Aljubarrota on August 14, 1385, a victory that helped secure Portugal’s independence. He later offered it to the Virgin of Guimarães. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. A combined ticket with the Palace of the Dukes and the castle costs €17.

“Aqui nasceu Portugal,” meaning “Portugal was born here,” appears in large letters on the Torre da Alfândega, a tower in Guimarães’s old city walls. It recalls the Battle of São Mamede, fought near the city on June 24, 1128. That day, Afonso Henriques defeated the troops of his own mother, Countess Teresa. This victory is presented as the birth of the country. Step back a little to take your photo.

Leather was still being worked in the Zona de Couros, the old tanners’ district south of the old town, as recently as 2005. Hides soaked in vats, then in a bath of tannin extracted from oak bark: this substance turns hides into leather. Since 2023, the district has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site. Walk among the old vats and the tall brick chimney, between the Alameda gardens and the train station.

activities.text: If the sky is clear, head up Mount Penha on the Teleférico de Guimarães, the cable car linking the city to the summit. The cabin travels nearly 1.7 km and climbs 366 m in less than eight minutes. At the top, at 617 m, enormous fallen granite boulders form small caves, one of which has become a chapel. The Penha sanctuary, in the center of the park, was inaugurated in 1947. Hours vary by season, and the cable car stops running in bad weather: check turipenha.pt before setting out.

visits.text: Sixty inhabitants. Two millennia beneath your feet. Idanha-a-Velha, founded under Augustus as Civitas Igaeditanorum, became a Visigothic episcopal seat before falling to the Moors in the 8th century. The Sé Catedral—an early Christian basilica turned Visigothic—preserves two baptisteries, including a cruciform one with traces of original paint. Unique in Portugal. Visit before the midday heat.

The cathedral looks modest from outside, but the Torre dos Templários is built on the podium of a Roman temple: the 13th century resting on the 1st. A few meters away, the Manueline pillory and ongoing excavations complete the reading of the layers.

activities.text: Walk slowly: recent digs continue to unearth remains. The tourist office hands out an annotated map. One hour covers the whole village, no more.

visits.text: Outside, a restrained Gothic church; inside, almost everything is gilded. The Igreja de São Francisco, or Church of Saint Francis, completed around 1425, was covered in carved and gilded wood during the 17th and 18th centuries, from the pillars to the ceiling. It is nicknamed the “golden church.” Look for the Tree of Jesse, a carved family tree commissioned in 1718: it depicts Jesus’s ancestors, including twelve kings of Judah. The ticket (€9) also includes admission to the catacombs, where monks lie buried beneath the floor. When you leave, tram 1 departs right next door from the Infante stop.

visits.text: It is called the Casa Escondida, the “hidden house”: a house barely more than a meter and a half wide, wedged between Carmo Church and the Carmelites Church. According to tradition, it separated the two churches so their religious communities would not live under the same roof. The Igreja do Carmo, built between 1756 and 1768, is recognizable by the large azulejo panel covering its side wall, installed in 1912. It depicts the founding of the Carmelite religious order. View it from the street. You can visit the hidden house with a ticket costing a few euros.

visits.text: Discover the Janeiro de Cima River Beach, one of the most beautiful in the region, surrounded by schist houses and traditional boats. This riverside village offers a welcoming setting where tradition meets unspoiled nature.

Visit the neighboring village of Janeiro de Baixo, which retains the same authentic riverside atmosphere. The schist houses, cobblestone streets, and connection to the river make this village a haven of tranquility in the heart of Beira Interior.

Explore Barroca, which offers rock art, hiking and authentic contact with rural life. This village preserves ancestral traditions and unique geological landscapes that bear witness to millions of years of natural history.

activities.text: Venture into the Tejo International Natural Park, where you can watch vultures, eagles and black storks on the rocks. Take a boat trip on the Rio Tejo at Vila Velha de Ródão and admire the Portas de Ródão, imposing cliffs that form one of the most spectacular landscapes in Portugal. These two sites are far away: allow for a round trip within the day from the stopover town.

visits.text: If the old tram 1 has rattled you around for a good half hour along the Douro, Jardim do Passeio Alegre is the place to catch your breath. This garden in Foz do Douro, the neighborhood at the river’s mouth, was designed by landscape architect Émile David. It features two 18th-century obelisks by Nicolau Nasoni, the architect of Clérigos Tower. A fountain designated a national monument completes the setting. Tram 1 terminates here: check the last departure time before strolling around, as service is reduced in winter.

places.name: Lagoa do Fogo

visits.text: São Miguel’s wildest lake, in our opinion: Lagoa do Fogo, the “Lake of Fire,” fills a volcanic crater in the center of the island. Its last eruption was in 1563. The Miradouro da Lagoa do Fogo viewpoint sits at an elevation of 776 m, about 200 m above the lake. In summer, from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m., visitors’ cars can no longer drive up to the viewpoint: a shuttle leaves from the free parking lots at Caldeira Velha and Casa da Água. In fog, you won’t see anything.

activities.text: You can hike down from the viewpoint to the beach at Lagoa do Fogo, which is made of pumice, a very lightweight volcanic rock. It was voted Portugal’s best wild beach in the Portuguese 7 Wonders of Beaches competition. The trail is steep: allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours 30 minutes for the approximately 4 km round trip, as the climb back up is harder than the descent. In April and May, gulls nest near the shores and defend their territory: keep your distance.

visits.text: Golden-yellow rock pillars, some reaching 20 m high, rise from the sea below Ponta da Piedade Lighthouse, which dates to 1913. The headland is about 3 km from central Lagos, a 40-minute walk along the coast. A staircase with more than a hundred steps leads down to the water. Come early in the morning or at sunset: in summer, the free parking lot is full between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m.

Behind its plain facade, Igreja de Santo António hides an interior covered in carved, gilded woodwork known as talha dourada. Damaged in the 1755 earthquake, the church was restored in 1769, when its blue-and-white azulejos and dome were installed. Six paintings depict the miracles of Saint Anthony. Entry is through Museu Dr. José Formosinho, open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. and 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. Admission costs €3, or €5 including the slavery museum.

In 1444, a Portuguese expedition sold 235 African captives in the square where the Mercado de Escravos de Lagos now stands. They were the first African slaves sold in Europe in the modern era. Henry the Navigator, who financed the expedition, received one-fifth of their value. The current building, dating to 1691, houses the Rota da Escravatura museum, the route of slavery. The visit is brief and sober: allow 45 minutes.

To understand Lagos, follow its 16th-century ramparts from Praça do Infante, where the statue of Henry the Navigator stands. In the 15th century, the city was the center of Portuguese maritime exploration, and Henry lived here most of the time. Gil Eanes, a sailor from Lagos, was the first to sail past Cape Bojador on the African coast, in 1434. Allow 30 minutes for a walk along the ramparts.

Head down to Praia Dona Ana, a sandy cove surrounded by rocks sculpted by the sea. At high tide, the cliffs divide it into several small coves. A little farther toward Ponta da Piedade, a wooden staircase leads to Praia do Camilo. Come at low tide to walk from one cove to another.

activities.text: If the sea is calm, take a boat tour of the Ponta da Piedade caves from Lagos. Allow 60 to 90 minutes and €25 to €40 per person, depending on the boat and trip length. Boats enter several of the caves carved into the cliffs. For a quieter outing, guided kayak or paddleboard trips depart from Praia da Batata year-round, costing around €35 to €50.

visits.text: Climb the 686 steps of the baroque stairway at the Sanctuary of Nossa Senhora dos Remédios, Lamego's emblem and one of the most impressive monumental ensembles in Portugal. Azulejo panels, allegorical fountains like the Fountain of the Giants in the Patio of Kings, and breathtaking panoramic views punctuate this ascent culminating at the sanctuary dedicated to the city's patron saint.

Visit Lamego Cathedral, which dates back to the 12th century and combines original Romanesque elements with Gothic and Renaissance additions. The Manueline triple portal, the most significant work in this region, stands out, as do the baroque high altar inside and the vaults over the nave and two aisles, covered with colorful Old Testament frescoes.

Discover the Lamego Museum, housed in the former baroque Episcopal Palace. It possesses one of the finest religious art collections in Portugal, including works by Grão Vasco and Flemish tapestries. Prepare to be utterly amazed by the gilded wooden altars transferred in their entirety from the Chagas Monastery.

Walk the Port Wine Trail in the parish of Samodães, a must for hiking enthusiasts and simply one of the best trails in Portugal. The landscapes of the Douro wine region are sublime with their terraces sculpted into the hillsides, creating a natural amphitheater where the vine has reigned since time immemorial.

Visit the Raposeira Cellars and treat yourself to a refreshing break with the elegant sparkling wine of Lamego. Discover how Cistercian monks developed the ancestral rituals to achieve the perfection of this refined wine, celebrating the winemaking tradition that makes Lamego one of the cradles of Portuguese sparkling wine.

activities.text: Explore Lamego Castle and its fascinating Cistern, one of the best-preserved castle cisterns in Portugal. Climb the 12th-century keep with its fun, interactive explanations. Don't miss the Gate of the Fig Trees with its two turrets and the Archaeological Center with its treasures from Roman times.

Indulge in Lamego's gastronomy: roast kid, lean ham renowned since ancient times, sausages and smoked products. For pastries, taste the traditional convent pastries known as Grades de Lamego and the very sweet Tarte de Lamego. Visit A Presunteca for a tasting platter accompanied by wines from the region.

visits.text: Climb up to Leiria Castle, a medieval fortress perched spectacularly above the town, with origins dating back to the 12th century. The castle's romantic ruins, including the royal palace and the Gothic loggia, offer views sweeping across the pine forests to the Atlantic.

Stroll through Praça Rodrigues Lobo, Leiria's elegant main square surrounded by arcaded buildings and charming cafés. This bustling gathering place showcases the city's architectural heritage, including fine examples of Art Nouveau design by architect Ernesto Korrodi.

Visit Leiria Cathedral, a 16th-century Mannerist masterpiece dedicated to Our Lady of the Assumption. This unique hall church, with its nave and two aisles of equal height, stands as one of Portugal's finest examples of the hall church style, comparable to the Jerónimos Monastery in Lisbon.

activities.text: Explore the newly renovated Leiria Museum, housed in the former Santo Agostinho Convent. After 97 years of scattered collections, this comprehensive museum now tells the city's story through innovative displays spanning archaeology, art, and local traditions.

visits.text: The locals call it “Catedral do Parapente.” Linhares da Beira, at 820 m altitude on the western slope of the Serra da Estrela, is one of the most active paragliding sites in Portugal—launch right below the castle. Even if conditions are calm, you'll still see wings in the sky.

Linhares da Beira Castle, a National Monument rebuilt under Dom Dinis in 1291, retains two crenellated towers from which you see the Mondego valley open up below. The Igreja Matriz preserves three paintings from the school of Grão Vasco—the same painter you'll encounter again in Viseu.

activities.text: If conditions are right, try a tandem introductory flight with the village school—Aventura Linhares offers year-round flights. The aerial view of the castle and the Serra is unmatched.

days_plan.itin_title: Portugal: Historic Villages & Serra da Estrela in 8 Days

visits.text: Day 1: Begin your Lisbon adventure at the magnificent Praça do Comércio, the city's grandest square opening dramatically onto the Tagus River. This monumental waterfront plaza, rebuilt after the devastating 1755 earthquake, served as the ceremonial entrance to Portugal's capital for arriving dignitaries. The elegant arcaded buildings and triumphal arch create one of Europe's most impressive urban spaces.

Day 1: Stroll along Rua Augusta, Lisbon's vibrant pedestrian thoroughfare connecting the waterfront to the heart of the Baixa district. This lively street buzzes with outdoor cafés, traditional shops, and street performers beneath elegant 18th-century façades. Climb to the top of the Arco da Rua Augusta for sweeping views over the geometric streets of downtown and the glittering Tagus beyond.

Day 1: Ascend in the Elevador de Santa Justa, an extraordinary neo-Gothic iron lift designed by a student of Gustave Eiffel in 1902. This remarkable piece of urban engineering whisks passengers 45 meters up through an ornate wrought-iron tower to connect the Baixa with the Carmo neighborhood above. The viewing platform at the summit reveals a stunning panorama across Lisbon's terracotta rooftops.

Day 1: Explore the hauntingly beautiful ruins of the Convento do Carmo, a Gothic monastery left roofless since the catastrophic earthquake of 1755. The skeletal arches reaching toward the open sky create one of Lisbon's most atmospheric and photographed sites. Today the ruins house an archaeological museum with artifacts spanning from prehistoric times to the medieval period.

Day 2: Lose yourself in the labyrinthine streets of Alfama, Lisbon's oldest and most atmospheric neighborhood that survived the great earthquake largely intact. Narrow alleyways wind between ancient houses adorned with colorful azulejo tiles, while the melancholic strains of fado music drift from hidden taverns. This medieval quarter climbing from the waterfront to the castle preserves the authentic soul of old Lisbon.

Day 2: Conquer the heights of Castelo de São Jorge, the hilltop fortress that has watched over Lisbon for more than a millennium. Originally a Moorish stronghold before the Christian reconquest in 1147, the castle walls and towers offer the most spectacular panoramic views in the entire capital. Wander through archaeological remains, peaceful gardens, and ramparts overlooking the city's seven hills.

Day 2: Visit the Sé Cathedral, Lisbon's oldest church and a powerful symbol of the Christian reconquest, built on the site of a former mosque in the 12th century. This Romanesque fortress-church has survived earthquakes, wars, and centuries of history while accumulating Gothic cloisters, baroque chapels, and treasures from every era. The austere façade flanked by two bell towers creates an imposing presence in the heart of Alfama.

Day 2: Journey to the riverside district of Belém, where Portugal's Age of Discovery left its most magnificent monuments along the Tagus. This elegant quarter west of the center celebrates the era when Portuguese navigators charted unknown oceans and established a global maritime empire. Tree-lined avenues, manicured gardens, and waterfront promenades connect the area's UNESCO-listed treasures.

Day 2: Marvel at the Mosteiro dos Jerónimos, an extraordinary masterpiece of Manueline architecture and one of Portugal's most important monuments. This 16th-century monastery, built to commemorate Vasco da Gama's voyage to India, features fantastically ornate stone carvings combining maritime, religious, and royal symbols. The cloisters rank among the most beautiful in Europe, their delicate stonework a testament to Portugal's golden age.

Day 2: Stand before the iconic Torre de Belém, a fortified tower rising from the Tagus that has become the definitive symbol of Lisbon. Built in the early 16th century to guard the river entrance, this UNESCO World Heritage Site blends Manueline and Moorish architectural elements in its decorative stonework. The tower's position jutting into the river recalls the departure point for countless Portuguese voyages of exploration.

Day 3: Discover the MAAT (Museum of Art, Architecture and Technology), a stunning contemporary museum whose undulating rooftop merges seamlessly with the Belém waterfront. This architectural landmark hosts rotating exhibitions of national and international contemporary art within its futuristic interior spaces. The rooftop walkway offers unique perspectives over the Tagus and connects to the adjacent historic power station.

Day 3: Experience the creative energy of LX Factory, a former industrial complex transformed into Lisbon's most vibrant cultural hub. Abandoned textile factories now house independent boutiques, bookshops, art galleries, and creative studios beneath exposed brick and ironwork. This alternative neighborhood pulses with artistic energy and represents the contemporary, forward-looking side of the Portuguese capital.

activities.text: Day 1: Wander through the elegant Chiado district, Lisbon's traditional quarter of intellectuals, artists, and literary cafés where Fernando Pessoa once held court. This sophisticated neighborhood bridges the lower city with the bohemian heights of Bairro Alto, offering excellent shopping, historic theaters, and charming squares. The area's cultural significance and refined atmosphere make it perfect for an afternoon of exploration.

Day 2: Ride the legendary Tram 28, a vintage yellow streetcar that rattles through Lisbon's most picturesque neighborhoods on its winding route across the city. This living piece of transport history climbs impossibly steep streets, squeezes through narrow passages, and passes major landmarks from Alfama to Estrela. The journey aboard these century-old wooden trams provides an authentic and scenic way to experience the city's dramatic topography.

Day 2: Take in the view at the end of the day from the Miradouro de Santa Luzia, a romantic terrace overlooking the rooftops of Alfama and the glittering Tagus. Bougainvillea-draped pergolas, decorative azulejo panels and palm trees frame views stretching from the dome of the National Pantheon to the distant hills. This beloved viewpoint captures the essence of Lisbon's melancholic beauty as the city glows in the evening light.

Day 2: Photograph the Padrão dos Descobrimentos, a striking modernist monument celebrating the Portuguese explorers who opened new sea routes to the world. This 52-meter sculpture rising from the riverbank depicts Henry the Navigator leading a procession of historical figures toward the water. The monument's dramatic silhouette and waterfront position make it one of Belém's most recognizable landmarks.

Day 3: Explore the Bairro Alto, Lisbon's historic high quarter where bohemian spirit meets traditional neighborhood life. By day, quiet streets reveal vintage shops, fado houses, and neighborhood taverns serving traditional petiscos. After dark, the quarter transforms into the city's legendary nightlife district with countless bars spilling onto the narrow streets.

Day 3: Seek out Lisbon's famous miradouros, the scenic viewpoints scattered across the city's seven hills that reveal new perspectives at every turn. From the panoramic Miradouro da Senhora do Monte to the elegant terraces of São Pedro de Alcântara, each offers its own character and vista. These beloved gathering spots are essential to understanding how Lisbonites experience their dramatically vertical city.

visits.text: Book a time slot before stepping into Livraria Lello: admission requires a ticket, priced at €15.95 on the official website. Opened in 1906, the bookstore owes its fame to its staircase. It looks like carved wood, but it is one of Portugal’s first concrete staircases, painted to imitate wood. Its red color resulted from a painting mistake during the 1993 restoration, and it was kept. The ticket price is deducted from the purchase of a book published by Lello. Suitcases and large backpacks are not allowed.

visits.text: In 1419, João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira landed on Machico beach before claiming Madeira for the Portuguese crown. In 1440, Machico became the archipelago’s first captaincy: a territory entrusted to Tristão Vaz and his descendants by Prince Henry the Navigator. On this volcanic island, the pale sand of Praia de Machico is a surprise: it was brought from Western Sahara. Go for a swim after hiking PR8; the beach is a 15-minute drive away.

visits.text: The Zêzere Valley opens in a perfect U below Manteigas—one of the few genuine glacial valleys in Portugal, carved more than 20,000 years ago. Descending toward the village on the N338, the U-shape suddenly imposes itself. Flocks guarded by Serra da Estrela dogs graze the high pastures.

The Burel Factory revives a wool fabric that Manteigas workshops had produced since the 18th century. A local hotel-owning couple relaunched the old Lanifícios Império plant with its period machines. The visit is free and self-guided: you see the looms in operation, from raw yarn to finished cloth.

At the Termas de Manteigas, a few kilometers from the village, a soak in sulfurous water at 40°C after a day of walking is still an experience. Locals have come here for generations to ease their rheumatism.

The village itself is tiny, but its São Pedro church preserves a sober baroque interior on the main square—a useful counterpoint to all the bare granite from previous days. The 18th-century granite façade is worth a 10-minute stop.

Manteigas sits at the bottom of the Zêzere glacial valley. Look up: the two U-shaped slopes frame the sky. Look down: the river runs over the pebbles. A rare geography in Portugal, and legible from any point in the village.

activities.text: Take the glacial trail in the morning toward Covão da Ametade, an alpine basin at the source of the Zêzere. 7 km round trip from Manteigas, moderate elevation gain. The view of the granite wall opposite is worth every step.

If you are coming in summer, book accommodation in Manteigas early—the village is fully booked several weeks ahead in July and August. Casa de São Lourenço, 10 km above the village, is an option with a direct view over the glacial valley.
Sample the queijo da Serra da Estrela and the enchidos (smoked sausages) in one of the village taverns before continuing north. A real break before the string of frontier villages.

Portugal: Historic Villages & Serra da Estrela in 8 Days

visits.text: The citadel of Marialva is inhabited—but barely. The population left the walls in the 19th century when the castle lost its military utility. What you visit today is a power center emptied of its content: alleys without inhabitants, a ruined church, a castle open to the four winds. A few high-end guesthouses have since been installed. The atmosphere is out of time.

The castle, whose origins go back at least to the 12th century, was rebuilt by Dom Sancho I then by Dom Dinis. Excavations around the site have unearthed remains dating to the 6th century BCE—the Túrdulos, Lusitanian peoples predating the Romans.

activities.text: Take time to climb to the high point of the citadel to see the plain toward the Côa. The silence and absence of crowds—even in midsummer—give Marialva a quality of experience rare among the other villages in the network.

days_plan.itin_title: Portugal: Historic Villages & Serra da Estrela in 8 Days

visits.text: At 865 meters, Marvão locals say you see the backs of birds in flight: it's true. Marvão Castle, built on a quartzite ridge and refortified by Dom Dinis in the late 13th century, offers from its keep a view over the Serra de São Mamede to the south and the Spanish village of Valencia de Alcántara to the northeast on clear days. Park below—the Porta do Rodão only lets one car through at a time.

Refortified by Dom Dinis in the late 13th century, Marvão's ramparts encircle the village in a circuit of less than a kilometer. You can walk them in an hour, with views over both slopes at every tower. The granite ramparts merge with the rock to the point where you can't tell where nature ends and construction begins.

Hidden behind the castle, white, suspended above the void: Marvão's small cemetery is one of the quietest places in Portugal. A few dozen graves facing Spain, the wind, nothing else. Nobody goes there. That's why it's worth the detour.

This so-called “Roman” bridge served as a toll crossing to tax Jews expelled from Castile as they entered Portugal in 1492. The granite structure spans the Sever River and probably incorporates medieval or older foundations, despite its misleading nickname. The corner tower houses a memorial to those who crossed here.

An unobtrusive memorial in the Portagem tower: what looks like a simple border crossing was, for entire families, the end of a world. They crossed on foot in a few hours, leaving behind decades of ties to their homeland. The memorial recounts this history without exaggeration.

activities.text: Walk the complete circuit of the ramparts in an hour, starting on the east side to have the light behind you in late afternoon. There is little change in elevation. Bring water—there's nowhere to replenish supplies on the ramparts circuit.

If you stay overnight within the walls, the village empties at 6 PM and takes on another dimension: deserted alleys, golden light, not a sound. Rooms within the walls are very few—book two months in advance, especially for May and September.

The water of the Sever is icy even in July—Spaniards from the other side come to swim anyway. The Praia Fluvial de Portagem is a free natural pool in the riverbed, with trees for shade and a few benches. Ideal after climbing up to Marvão.

activities.text: Start your shopping at Mercado do Bolhão, the large covered market in central Porto. The building dates to 1914. It reopened on September 15, 2022, after more than four years of restoration. On the ground floor, stalls sell fish, meat, vegetables, and flowers. Upstairs, around ten restaurants offer a place to have lunch. Come on a Saturday morning: the market opens at 8 a.m. and is closed on Sundays.

visits.text: In Portugal, only two churches still contain an original mihrab—and Mértola is the only one where it remains fully visible. The Igreja Matriz, a former 12th-century Almohad mosque, was converted in 1238 without demolishing its niche oriented toward Mecca or its five Muslim naves. The stucco decoration is still legible. Free visit.

This castle defends a confluence, but the real interest lies beneath the cobblestones. The Castelo de Mértola, perched on a rocky spur above the Guadiana and Oeiras rivers, contains Roman, Visigothic, and Umayyad stratigraphic layers unearthed by archaeologists from the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola since the 1980s. The views over both watercourses more than justify the admission price.

The Museu de Mértola is spread across about ten sites throughout town—early Christian basilica, Roman house, Islamic workshop. Each room is a slice of superimposed centuries, making Mértola a rare archaeological case in Europe. Combined ticket available at the Tourist Office, best purchased first.

activities.text: Head down to the Guadiana riverbank in late afternoon, at the foot of the ramparts. The river forms a calm loop here, ideal for a 30-minute walk along the towpath. The late-afternoon light in the Baixo Alentejo is particularly intense—photographers know this well.

If the sun is still high, drive 18 km east to the Mina de São Domingos for a preview before tomorrow's visit. The panorama over the rust-colored hills in evening light is worth the trip even from the car.

places.name: Mina de São Domingos

visits.text: The red waters of the Corta da Mina sting your eyes at first sight: acidic, loaded with iron and copper, they've stained the bottom of the quarry a blood red that resembles nothing else. The São Domingos copper mine, exploited since Roman times then relaunched by a British company in 1855, closed in 1966. The landscape hasn't been decontaminated.

A separate English quarter survives at the end of the village - British managers lived apart from Portuguese miners, with their separate Protestant cemetery, their football club, their theater. Today some houses are still inhabited, others are open to the winds. One of Europe's most singular industrial archaeology sites.

activities.text: Walk through the ruins of the industrial complex: factory chimneys, mine headframe, disused power plant. The marked path starts from the central parking area and loops around the site in 45 minutes. Caution: the area around the Corta da Mina is marked as a toxic zone—don't touch the water.

places.name: Miróbriga

visits.text: Wild grass has reclaimed the seating tiers of Miróbriga's hippodrome—360 meters long, laid out in the hills. This 2nd-century Roman circus is one of the few identified in Portugal. Site managed by the Regional Directorate of Culture of Alentejo, open Tuesday to Sunday from 9am to 12:30pm and 2pm to 5:30pm.

A hippodrome in Portugal is rare—and Miróbriga has an almost intact one. But the rest of the site is just as substantial: two distinct bath complexes (one thought to have been for men, the other for women), a forum, tabernae and a single-arch Roman bridge. Founded in the Iron Age, the site remained inhabited until the 4th century. Ticket about €3, audio guide available at reception.

activities.text: If you have time, look for the single-arch Roman bridge below the main site: it's poorly signposted but intact. From the bridge, the path climbs back to the baths via a marked trail. Bring closed-toe shoes - the terrain is uneven.

visits.text: Monção’s ramparts are bastioned fortifications, with pointed projections that allowed defenders to fire along the walls. Construction began in 1656, following a design by French engineer Miguel de L’École, whose work you’ll see again in Valença. Besieged by the Spanish from October 1658 to February 1659, the fortified town eventually surrendered. Two of its five gates remain, including the Porta de Salvaterra. From the riverside ramparts, look across to Salvaterra de Miño, the Spanish town on the opposite bank.

In 1369, according to the accounts, the Castilians besieged Monção, and the town was starving. Deu-la-Deu Martins, wife of the alcaide, the castle governor, baked bread with the last of the flour. She threw it to the besiegers as though the storerooms were full. Discouraged, they lifted the siege. Praça Deu-la-Deu bears her name, and Monção’s coat of arms shows a woman holding a loaf of bread in each hand. Her tomb is in the Igreja Matriz, a 13th-century Romanesque church.

Before tasting, it helps to understand: that is the role of the Museu do Alvarinho, housed in the Casa do Curro on Praça Deu-la-Deu. This municipal museum presents Monção and Melgaço as the birthplace of Alvarinho, the grape variety behind the region’s reputation. It also explores the area’s landscapes, traditions, and historic houses. Allow 30 minutes; opening hours are published on the municipal website.

activities.text: Book a guided tour of the Palácio da Brejoeira, 5 km south of Monção: tours start at 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. and last around 1 hour 30 minutes. Work on this Neoclassical palace began around 1806 and took nearly thirty years. Its estate includes 18 hectares of Alvarinho vineyards, and its first wine went on sale in 1976. In 2025, the “Património” package (interior, gardens, chapel, and old wine cellar) cost €9.50. Add a tasting for €3 to €5.50.

days_plan.itin_title: Minho in 6 Days: Guimarães, Braga, Ponte de Lima, Caminha

visits.text: At 902 m, Fóia is the highest point in the Algarve, in the Serra de Monchique. The summit bristles with antennas and an air force radar station: the setting is hardly pristine, but on a clear day the view stretches to the Atlantic. Choose a cloudless day, or all you will see is fog.

Walk up through the narrow streets of Monchique to the Igreja Matriz, the town’s main church, dating from the 16th century. Its portal is Manueline, the Portuguese decorative style from the reign of King Manuel I. Here, it is carved with motifs drawn from nature. Inside, you will see 18th-century azulejos and a Baroque altarpiece, a large carved decorative structure behind the altar.

Water emerges from the ground at 32 °C in Caldas de Monchique, a small spa village about 6 km south of the town. These springs have been renowned for their beneficial properties since Roman times, and Portugal’s royal family used to spend the season here. Stop for a break on your way down to Silves.

activities.text: Medronho is the Serra de Monchique’s fruit brandy, distilled from the fruit of the strawberry tree, a shrub with small red berries. Try a small glass at a café in town. It is a strong spirit: if you are driving, limit yourself to a drop or take a bottle home.

days_plan.itin_title: Algarve in 7 Days: Ria Formosa, Benagil, Lagos, and Sagres

visits.text: The “most Portuguese village in Portugal”—title from a 1938 competition under the Estado Novo. What it actually means: the houses of Monsanto are built between multi-ton granite boulders. Some use the rock as a roof, others as a load-bearing wall. The Casa de Uma Só Telha—the one-tile house, whose single tile is a giant boulder—sums up the principle. Visit early to avoid the crowds.

Monsanto Castle was built on lands granted to the Order of the Temple around 1165 by King Afonso Henriques. The hill peaks at 763 m. The walk up from the village takes 30 min. Views across the Beira all the way to the Spanish frontier. The ruins are freely accessible.

The Romanesque chapel of São Miguel, wedged against the rocks halfway up, dates to the 12th century. Around it, tombs carved directly into the granite—medieval anthropomorphic graves, some with a niche for the head. The site is often deserted even in high season.

activities.text: If you set out on foot before 9 a.m., the village is deserted and the morning light falls on the granite. The goat bells you hear from time to time are included. Come back down for breakfast at one of the two cafés within the walls.

days_plan.itin_title: Portugal: Historic Villages & Serra da Estrela in 8 Days

visits.text: Discover Monsaraz, the graceful medieval village that won the Monument Villages category of Portugal's 7 Wonders. Made of lime and slate, this settlement suspended in time whispers stories of bold kings and Knights Templar, preserving its old-world magic like few places in the world.

Visit Monsaraz Castle, built by King Dinis in the 14th century and listed as a National Monument. The former parade ground has served as a bullring since 1830, hosting each year the traditional bullfight during the festivities of Our Lord Jesus of the Steps. From the castle, enjoy the views over the artificial lake of the Alqueva Dam.

Enter the 16th-century Parish Church of Nossa Senhora da Lagoa, built in Renaissance style from regional slate. Inside, admire the tomb of Gomes Martins Silvestre, a Knight Templar, first governor and founder of Monsaraz, sculpted in Estremoz marble with a funeral procession of seventeen figures.

Explore the Former Courthouses in Travessa da Cadeia, the old administrative headquarters and court of Monsaraz. Don't miss the medieval fresco The Good and the Bad Judge, a satire on corruption in the justice system of the era depicting two judges with contrasting demeanors.

activities.text: Walk along the walls past their four gates: Porta da Vila, protected by two towers with a plaque dedicated to the Immaculate Conception by King John IV in 1646, the Gothic-arched Porta d'Évora, and the Alcoba and Buraco gates. Admire the views over the Alentejo fields.

Discover the hidden treasures of Monsaraz: the Chapel of São João Batista known as Cuba due to its cubic Moorish-influenced shape, the ancient Cistern that may have been a mosque, the Inquisition House, Santiago Church, and the hermitages of São Bento, São Lázaro, Santa Catarina, and São Sebastião.

places.name: Monte

visits.text: Koi glide beneath pagodas and Buddha statues at Monte Palace Madeira, a 7-hectare tropical garden in the hills above Funchal. Along the paths is a collection of azulejos (painted ceramic tiles) dating from the 17th through the 20th centuries. Two permanent exhibitions round out the visit, one on Africa and the other on the treasures of nature. The Funchal cable car (Teleférico do Funchal) takes you up from Zona Velha in 15 minutes, climbing 560 m in elevation. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes; open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Austria’s last emperor rests in Igreja de Nossa Senhora do Monte, far from Vienna. Charles I died in exile in Funchal on April 1, 1922, at age 34. His body was placed in a chapel in this church, begun in 1741; his heart is kept in Switzerland. On August 15, the Feast of the Assumption, celebrated here since 1551, fills the square in front of the church. Visit the church just before the carros de cesto ride down from Monte.

Quieter than Monte Palace, Jardim Botânico da Madeira spreads across 8 hectares of terraces above Funchal. It opened in 1960 on the Reid family’s former estate, Quinta do Bom Sucesso. More than 2,000 exotic plants from every continent grow here. Viewpoints overlook the city. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes; the garden closes at 5:30 p.m.

activities.text: You will reach the botanical garden from Monte on the Teleférico do Jardim Botânico in 9 minutes. Over a distance of 1,600 m, the cabin glides over the wooded Ribeira de João Gomes valley, between 10 and 100 m above the ground. Buy a round-trip ticket: the carros de cesto leave from Monte, so you will need to go back up there after visiting the garden.

In Madeira, they are called carros de cesto, or “basket cars.” These wicker sleds on wooden runners have been traveling down the road from Monte to Livramento since 1850: about 2 km in around 10 minutes. Two carreiros, drivers dressed in white and wearing straw boater hats, push the sled and then brake with their rubber soles. Despite having no engine, it reaches nearly 38 km/h on the slope.

visits.text: Moura takes its name from the legend of a Moorish princess - Moura Saluquia, who is said to have thrown herself from the castle after seeing her fiancé killed by Christian soldiers. Legend or not, the town remained Moorish until 1232.

Climb to Moura castle for the view over the Alentejo plain stretching to Spain—the border is 12 km away. The keep dates from the 14th century. Below, the town's café terraces cluster around Praça Sacadura Cabral. Moura is also known for its olives and olive oil, produced on surrounding estates.

activities.text: The Mouraria of Moura retains its narrow streets near the castle. This neighborhood housed the Muslim population after the Christian conquest, rather than a Jewish community. Walk through its alleys to look at the white facades and the layout of the old neighborhood. Allow 30 minutes for the walk.

places.name: Nazaré

visits.text: Locals in Nazaré tell how, in 1182, the knight Dom Fuas Roupinho was hunting a deer in the fog when his horse stopped short at the edge of the cliff. He credited the Virgin Mary with saving him and had the small Ermida da Memória, the “Chapel of Remembrance,” built on the spot. Its interior is covered with 17th- and 18th-century azulejos. Right beside it, the Miradouro do Suberco viewpoint overlooks the entire beach. Head up early to enjoy the view before the tour groups arrive.

The Santuário de Nossa Senhora da Nazaré overlooks the large square in Sítio. King Fernando I had a large church built here in 1377. Between the 16th and 19th centuries, it was transformed into a Baroque building, with interior walls covered in azulejos. It houses the statue of the Virgin Mary associated with the legend of Dom Fuas, the knight saved at the edge of the cliff. In the square, women vendors sometimes wear the traditional outfit with layered petticoats, known as the “seven skirts.” Cover your shoulders to enter: this is a pilgrimage site.

If you visit between October and March, watch the swell from the Forte de São Miguel Arcanjo, above Praia do Norte. This is where Nazaré’s giant waves form. Offshore, an underwater canyon about 230 km long plunges to a depth of 5,000 m. It begins 1 km from shore and channels the swell toward this beach. In 2020, Germany’s Sebastian Steudtner surfed a 26.2 m wave here, about the height of an eight-story building. In rough seas, stay on high ground: visitors have drowned on the beach.

The smell of salt and fish signals your arrival at the Museu do Peixe Seco, on the waterfront promenade. This living, open-air museum showcases a Nazaré tradition: drying fish in the sun. Horse mackerel (fish related to mackerel), sardines, small sharks, and octopuses are gutted, washed, and salted. They then dry for two to three days on wooden racks called estendais. Stop by in the morning to see the whole process, and buy a bag from the women vendors for a taste.

activities.text: The Ascensor da Nazaré, which takes you to Sítio, the old neighborhood perched on the cliff, has been closed for maintenance since November 9, 2026. The closure is expected to last about a month; the operator will announce the reopening date. This funicular, in service since 1889, travels 318 m on a 42% grade, rising 42 m for every 100 m horizontally. During the closure, you can walk up and back down along the Ladeira do Sítio, the old path between the beach and Sítio. The advertised one-way funicular fare is €2.50 in 2026.

Praia da Nazaré retains a slightly retro charm that makes it endearing. On the sand, rows of small canvas tents called barraquinhas face one another instead of the sea, encouraging conversations between neighbors. Outside the cultural center, old fishing boats are displayed outdoors, free to view. One was used for xávega, a fishing method in which teams of men and women hauled a net in from the beach.

Next, head to Pederneira, Nazaré’s third neighborhood, a former village built on a hill. From the Miradouro da Pederneira viewpoint, the view takes in the beach, Sítio on its cliff, and the lighthouse fort in the distance. This is the reverse of the view from Sítio, seen from the other side of the bay. Save this viewpoint for the end of the day, after the beach.

The Mercado Municipal de Nazaré reopened in April 2026 after renovations. This is where you’ll find the freshest fish in town, alongside fruit and vegetable stalls. Look for the day’s catch so you’ll know what to order later at a restaurant. Go in the morning, when the stalls are best stocked.

places.name: Nordeste

visits.text: “Madrugada” means “early morning” in Portuguese. The Miradouro da Ponta da Madrugada, in Lomba da Pedreira, is said to offer the most beautiful sunrise on São Miguel, and some locals camp there to catch the first light. The viewpoint overlooks the Serra da Tronqueira and the coast, with picnic tables and flower beds. To catch the sunrise, leave Furnas well before dawn.

Palm trees, flower beds, and benches facing the ocean: the Miradouro da Ponta do Sossego is a garden covering more than 13,000 m², nearly the size of two soccer fields. Sossego means “tranquility.” Below, you can see Fajã do Araújo, a small stretch of level ground at the foot of the cliff, and Lombo Gordo Beach. It is very close to the Madrugada viewpoint, so visit them both in succession.

On November 26, 1876, the Farol do Arnel was lit for the first time: it was the first lighthouse built in the Azores. Its 15 m tower stands at an elevation of 66 m on the eastern tip of São Miguel. The narrow access road has no parking and descends at a 35% grade. Leave your car on the regional road and walk the last 500 meters. The lighthouse offers free visits on Wednesday afternoons, from 2 p.m. to 5 p.m. in summer.

The Ponte dos Sete Arcos marks the approach to Vila do Nordeste, the administrative center of São Miguel’s least populous municipality. This seven-arched stone viaduct was built in 1882 and 1883. Locals simply call it “o viaduto,” the viaduct. In the small town center, the Igreja Matriz de São Jorge stands beside Praça da República. To see the entire bridge, walk down into the garden below, as recommended by the Nordeste tourist office.

Less well known than its neighbors, the Miradouro da Vista dos Barcos is worth a stop. Near Lomba do Moio, it overlooks the coast, with the Arnel lighthouse in the distance. Its name means “view of the boats”: this was the first point on the coast from which ships arriving from the east could be seen. Fifteen minutes is enough.

visits.text: Blue-and-white tiles frame the small balcony of the Porta da Vila, the main entrance through Óbidos’s defensive walls. These Baroque-style azulejos (painted earthenware tiles) surround an oratory (a small prayer niche) dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Piedade, the town’s patron saint. This is a double gateway: you pass through two successive openings before entering the town. Go before 10 AM to photograph it without the crowds.

The best view of Óbidos is from the wall walk along the Muralhas de Óbidos, the walkway atop the defensive walls that encircle the entire town. You can walk for more than a kilometer above the rooftops and narrow streets. Looking outward, you’ll see the 16th-century aqueduct, built at the request of Queen Catherine of Austria. The castle, now a place to stay, is reserved for its guests. Take care: the walkway has no guardrails, so hold children by the hand and come down before dark.

In 1441, King Afonso V married his cousin Isabel in the Igreja de Santa Maria in Óbidos. The bride and groom were 9 and 10 years old. This church, the town’s main church, has walls covered in 17th-century azulejos. It also houses paintings by the Baroque painter Josefa de Óbidos and her father, Baltazar Gomes Figueira. Afterward, look at the embroidery sold in town: since the 1950s, it has reproduced the motifs on these tiles.

The Museu Municipal de Óbidos, on Rua Direita, tells the story of the town’s artistic and religious history. Opened in 1970, it mainly displays paintings from the 16th and 17th centuries. The highlights are works by Josefa de Óbidos (1630–1684), who adopted the town’s name as her name as a painter. The museum is open from 9:30 AM to 1 PM and from 2 PM to 5:30 PM, and is closed on Mondays.

A church filled with books: Livraria de Santiago occupies a former 12th-century church inside Óbidos’s defensive walls. This choice is no coincidence. Since 2015, Óbidos has been part of UNESCO’s Cities of Literature network, and the town has more than ten bookstores. Step inside to browse the shelves, even if you don’t buy anything: admission is free.

You’ll head outside the defensive walls to the Santuário do Senhor Jesus da Pedra, a Baroque church with a hexagonal, or six-sided, floor plan. Construction, overseen by Captain Rodrigo Franco, began in 1740 and was completed around 1747. The towers never received the pinnacles (small stone points) planned for their tops, giving the building its unfinished appearance. Inside, a stone cross carved with the crucified Christ gave the sanctuary its name. Allow for a short detour by car from the Porta da Vila.

activities.text: If you try just one specialty in Óbidos, choose ginjinha served in a small chocolate cup. Ginjinha is a liqueur made by steeping sour cherries in brandy. Once you’ve finished the drink, you eat the cup. The counters along Rua Direita serve it plain, in chocolate, or “com ginja,” meaning with a cherry at the bottom.

The Lagoa de Óbidos, northwest of town, forms the largest lagoon system on the Portuguese coast. A lagoon is a shallow body of water separated from the ocean by a sandbar: here, the average depth is no more than 2 m. Migratory birds stop mainly in the Barrosa arm to the east, and flamingos visit in winter. A trail, the Ecovia da Lagoa, follows its shores. Come late in the day with binoculars.

visits.text: Odeceixe is the last Alentejo village before the Algarve - the administrative border runs through the middle of the beach. The perched village overlooks the valley from a ridge, with a restored windmill clearly visible from the N120. A few low houses, a bakery, a crossroads for Rota Vicentina hikers.

The Ribeira de Seixe separates fresh water from salt water just 100 meters apart at Praia de Odeceixe. On one side the river, cool and calm; on the other the ocean, cold and rough. This mixed-lagoon phenomenon is rare in Portugal. The beach is protected by cliffs on both sides, ideal for families.

activities.text: Swimming in both fresh and salt water at Praia de Odeceixe is unlike anything familiar: choose your water to suit your mood, fresh water on the left or the Atlantic on the right. From the village, reach the beach on foot or by car along the local road.

places.name: Olhão

visits.text: Two matching red-brick market halls stand on the waterfront: these are the Mercados de Olhão, built in the early 20th century. One sells fish, the other fruit, vegetables, and cheese. A replica of the Bom Sucesso, a small sailing vessel, is moored nearby. In 1808, Olhão rose up against the French occupation. Seventeen men then sailed aboard it to Brazil, where the Portuguese court had taken refuge, to deliver the news. Arrive between 7:30 and 9 a.m. to see the morning catch.

Climb the bell tower of the Igreja Matriz de Nossa Senhora do Rosário, a 17th-century Baroque church built by fishermen: from above, Olhão looks like a set of white building blocks. These houses in the Bairro da Barreta, the oldest fishing neighborhood, have flat rooftop terraces known as açoteias. Families watched for returning boats, dried fish, and slept there in summer. This style is linked to historic exchanges with North Africa. There is a small fee to climb the bell tower.

activities.text: If you take just one boat trip in Ria Formosa, choose Ilha da Culatra. Ria Formosa is a natural park spanning 60 km of coastline, with five sandy islands forming a barrier against the ocean. Culatra is about 6 km long, has no cars, and is home to some 700 residents. At its western tip, the 46 m Santa Maria lighthouse offers free visits on Wednesdays from 2 to 5 p.m. The public ferry leaves from the dock beside the market halls: 30 minutes to Culatra, 45 minutes to Farol, the lighthouse hamlet.

Less well known than the islands, the Centro de Educação Ambiental de Marim, the natural park’s discovery center, deserves two hours of your time. It is about 3 km east of Olhão. A 3 km loop trail passes a tide mill, which ran on seawater held back at high tide and released at low tide. It also passes Roman fish-salting tanks and bird-watching blinds. Look out for the western swamphen, a large blue-purple bird with a red bill. Admission costs €3.20.

visits.text: In 1832, a fire destroyed the cloister of São Francisco Convent. On its ruins, Porto’s merchants began building the Palácio da Bolsa, or Stock Exchange Palace, in 1842. Beneath the glass dome of the Courtyard of Nations, painted coats of arms represent Portugal and its trading partners. The highlight of the visit is the Arab Room, inspired by the Alhambra, the palace of Granada’s Moorish kings. The guided tour lasts 30 minutes (€14). The group’s language, with French among the options, depends on the order of arrival.

places.name: Pegadas de Dinossáurios da Serra de Aire

visits.text: Around 175 million years ago, sauropods walked across a mudflat here, an expanse of mud along the water’s edge. These long-necked herbivorous dinosaurs left around twenty trackways at the Monumento Natural das Pegadas de Dinossáurios da Serra de Aire, in the Parque Natural das Serras de Aire e Candeeiros. The two longest measure 147 m and 142 m. The round footprints were discovered in 1994 in a former quarry. The site is about ten kilometers from Fátima.

activities.text: You will then follow the roughly 1.8 km loop around the Pegadas de Dinossáurios quarry, with panels explaining the history of the Earth along the way. Before you head down, a 17-minute film places the tracks in the context of their time. The site’s garden brings together “living fossils,” ancient plants such as ferns, cycads (which look like small palm trees), and ginkgo, all of which already existed in the age of dinosaurs. Bring walking shoes.

visits.text: From 1934 to 1974, the Fortaleza de Peniche served as a political prison under the Estado Novo, Portugal’s dictatorship. Nearly 2,700 political prisoners were held here. On January 3, 1960, Communist leader Álvaro Cunhal and nine fellow prisoners escaped by climbing down the walls on a rope made from sheets. Opened in the fortress in 2024, the Museu Nacional Resistência e Liberdade lets visitors explore the cells and visiting room. It is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 AM to 6 PM; admission is €10.

You’ll end the day at Cabo Carvoeiro, the western tip of the Peniche peninsula, facing the Berlengas islands. A 25 m lighthouse guides ships from this headland, known for its shipwrecks. Right beside it stands the Nau dos Corvos, an isolated rock whose name means “the carrack of the crows” (a carrack was a large sailing ship used in earlier centuries). Come at sunset, but stay well back from the cliff edges.

activities.text: The trip’s most beautiful excursion starts at the port of Peniche: the crossing to Berlenga Grande, the main island in the Berlengas archipelago, about 15 kilometers offshore. The boat takes 40 to 45 minutes. On the island, a staircase leads to the Forte de São João Baptista, a 17th-century fort connected to the island by a bridge. The archipelago has been a UNESCO biosphere reserve since 2011, a designation that protects its natural environment: stay on marked trails. The island is limited to 550 visitors at any one time; this is not a quota for the entire day. Book early.

places.name: Peso da Régua

visits.text: The Museu do Douro occupies the Casa da Companhia, an 18th-century building restored and turned into a museum in 2008. It belonged to the company established in 1756 to regulate Douro wine production. This company marked the boundaries of the wine-growing area with granite boundary stones to better control production. The permanent exhibition tells the story of this landscape through tools, bottle labels, and works of art. Finish on the garden terrace above the river. The museum is open daily, with admission costing €7.

activities.text: If you take just one boat trip, choose the cruise from Régua to Pinhão, which heads up the Douro in a little over two hours. The highlight is the lock at Bagaúste Dam. The boat enters a large chamber enclosed by gates, which is then filled with water: the boat rises about 27 m to the level of the river upstream of the dam. This passage takes half an hour. Departures are in the afternoon, at around €30 per adult.

Return from Pinhão to Régua on the Douro railway line, following the water for about 25 minutes. The first train arrived in Régua in 1879. The Portuguese rail company describes this line as the only one in the world linking three UNESCO sites: Porto’s city center, the Douro wine-growing region, and the Côa rock engravings. Buy your ticket at Pinhão station or on board.
