visits.text: Park almost at the summit: a road leads up to Pico do Areeiro, Madeira’s third-highest peak (1,818 m). On clear days, the view extends across the ridges of the central massif, Ponta de São Lourenço, and the steep-sided Curral das Freiras valley; in exceptionally clear weather, you can see Porto Santo. Sunrise draws photographers here when the weather allows. Parking costs €4 per hour, and the road can be icy in winter.

activities.text: Walk the first section of PR1 Vereda do Areeiro to the Pedra Rija viewpoint (Miradouro da Pedra Rija), 1.2 km from the summit. The trail follows ridges of volcanic rock between steep slopes. Allow about 1 hour round-trip.

days_plan.itin_title: Madeira in 7 Days: Funchal, Levadas, and Pico Ruivo

visits.text: A sea of clouds can surround Pico Ruivo, Madeira’s highest point at 1,862 m. On clear days, the view extends as far as Porto Santo and the Desertas Islands. North of the summit, the mountain hut, renovated in 2019, offers water and meals to hikers. Bring a warm jacket for the climb, even in summer.

activities.text: The shortest route to Madeira’s highest point is also the easiest: the PR1.2 Vereda do Pico Ruivo starts at the Achada do Teixeira parking lot and reaches Pico Ruivo in 2.8 km. At the start, look for Homem em Pé, the “standing man,” a pillar of rock. Shelters along the trail offer protection from sudden weather changes, which are common at this altitude. Allow about 1 hour 30 minutes round-trip, plus time at the summit.

days_plan.itin_title: Madeira in 7 Days: Funchal, Levadas, and Pico Ruivo

visits.text: Enter the Douro Valley, a UNESCO World Heritage landscape of steep terraced vineyards tumbling toward one of Europe's most picturesque rivers. Port wine has been produced here for centuries using traditional methods. The dramatic landscape of vine-covered slopes and whitewashed quintas creates Portugal's most iconic scenery.

Explore the Alto Douro Wine Region on foot, hiking through working vineyards and peaceful traditional villages perched on hillsides. Walking trails wind between terraced slopes cultivated since Roman times, passing ancient olive groves and almond orchards. Natural beauty, agricultural heritage, and warm hospitality make this an unforgettable hiking destination.

Travel along the historic Douro railway line, opened in 1887 and considered one of the world's most scenic train journeys. The tracks follow the river from Porto to Pocinho, passing through tunnels and over bridges spanning tributary valleys. This engineering marvel provides a relaxing way to absorb magnificent valley scenery.

activities.text: Cycle through the Douro Valley's hillsides covered with vineyards, orchards, and traditional villages, following riverside trails and mountain climbs. The steep terrain rewards cyclists with spectacular views from elevated roads. E-bikes are highly recommended for those less accustomed to hills, allowing everyone to enjoy this magnificent cycling landscape.

Paddle the slow-flowing Douro River by kayak or canoe, gliding beneath towering cliffs and past terraced vineyards reflected in calm waters. This peaceful experience allows stops at riverside beaches and local villages for food and wine. The river perspective reveals the full grandeur of this UNESCO-protected landscape.

visits.text: The village of Mosteiros, north of Ponta da Ferraria on the same western coast, faces islets of black volcanic rock rising from the sea. Because the coast faces west, the sun sets in front of you in clear weather. End your day here after swimming at Ponta da Ferraria. Allow 30 to 60 minutes here.

activities.text: Hot water amid the waves: at Ponta da Ferraria, a thermal spring emerges at over 60 °C beside a lava platform. This platform formed when a lava flow advanced into the sea. The spring mixes with the ocean in a natural pool, where the water averages around 30 °C during the swimming season. At low tide, less seawater enters, so the water gets much hotter near the spring. Hold on to the ropes in the pool when swells roll in, and skip the swim if the sea is rough.

activities.text: The PR8 Vereda da Ponta de São Lourenço trail starts at Baía d'Abra and follows the peninsula for 4 km to Casa do Sardinha. Look for the dark veins in the cliffs: lava that cooled in cracks in the rock. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes round-trip in full sun: bring water and a hat.

places.name: Ponta Delgada

visits.text: The Portas da Cidade, Ponta Delgada’s city gates, have moved. Built in 1783 from basalt, the island’s black volcanic stone, and white stone, these three arches stood at the entrance to the old quay and controlled arrivals by sea. In 1952, construction of the waterfront avenue prompted their relocation to the neighboring square. Just behind them, the Igreja Matriz de São Sebastião, built between 1531 and 1547, retains a Manueline doorway, in the highly ornate Portuguese Gothic style. Inside, look at the carved cedar woodwork.

Thick stone walls facing the ocean: the Forte de São Brás was built in the second half of the 16th century to defend Ponta Delgada. The military has occupied it continuously ever since. Today it houses the Museu Militar dos Açores, which displays weapons, uniforms, vehicles, and World War I memorabilia. The museum is open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., except on public holidays. Allow 1 hour for your visit.

In our view, the best introduction to the island’s produce is the Mercado da Graça, Ponta Delgada’s covered market, named after a former convent nearby. Farmers, fishermen, and donkeys once mingled in the town hall square. The municipality later brought this trade together under one roof. You’ll find island-grown pineapples, custard apples (fruit with sweet white flesh), fresh cheese, and fish caught that morning. Come on Friday or Saturday, the busiest days.

If it rains, head beneath the city: the Gruta do Carvão is a lava tube. This natural tunnel formed when the surface of a lava flow cooled while the still-liquid lava continued flowing underneath. Its known length reaches 1,650 m. Its walls are orange because the iron in the basalt rusted on contact with air. The short tour covers about 200 m in 30 to 45 minutes, with five departures a day, the first at 10:30 a.m. Expect to pay €11 per adult.

Greenhouse-grown pineapples in the middle of the Atlantic: that’s the specialty of Plantações de Ananás Augusto Arruda in Fajã de Baixo, on the outskirts of Ponta Delgada. Pineapples replaced oranges in the 19th century, when the island’s orange trade collapsed. A fruit takes an average of 18 months to ripen. The closed greenhouses are filled with smoke for about a week so that all the plants flower at the same time, allowing the fruit to be harvested together. From April through September, the greenhouses are open daily from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

The people of São Miguel venerate the statue of Senhor Santo Cristo dos Milagres, the “Lord Christ of Miracles.” It is kept in the sanctuary of the Convent of Nossa Senhora da Esperança in Ponta Delgada. According to tradition, Pope Clement VII gave it to the convent’s first nuns in the 16th century. On the fifth Sunday after Easter, its procession, the largest religious celebration in the Azores, draws about 50,000 people. Stop by late in the day.

activities.text: You’ll depart from Ponta Delgada’s marina for a whale- and dolphin-watching trip lasting about 3 hours. More than 20 species of cetaceans, meaning whales and dolphins, frequent the Azores. Sperm whales can be seen year-round. Fin whales, another large whale species, and blue whales pass through mainly in April and May during their migration. On the cliffs, lookouts stationed in former whaling lookout towers, known as vigias, spot the animals and guide the boats by radio.

On departure day, return your car at João Paulo II Airport in Ponta Delgada, about 2 km west of downtown. A taxi from downtown takes about 5 minutes, at a fixed fare of €6 during the day and €7 at night. The Aerobus also connects the city to the airport every 40 minutes, from 7 a.m. to midnight.

places.name: Ponte de Lima

visits.text: Roman on one side, Gothic on the other: the bridge that gave Ponte de Lima its name combines two eras. Roman arches survive near the right bank; the rest dates to the 14th century. Statues of Roman soldiers on the riverbank recall a legend. In the 2nd century BCE, the troops of General Decimus Junius Brutus refused to cross the Lima. They mistook it for the Lethe, the river that erases memory in Greek mythology. The general crossed and called each soldier by name from the opposite bank. The bridge is for pedestrians only.

Shaded by plane trees, Avenida dos Plátanos, nicknamed “the street of fantasy,” is the promenade in central Ponte de Lima. The town received its charter from Countess Teresa in 1125 and is considered Portugal’s oldest vila. Vila is an official Portuguese designation between a village and a city. Largo de Camões, at the entrance to the bridge, is laid out around a fountain, the Chafariz Nobre. Every other Monday, the town’s large market, one of the oldest in the country, sets up on the riverbank.

Plaques attached to the Torre da Cadeia Velha show how high the Lima’s major floods reached. This tower is one of two surviving towers from the ramparts, built between 1359 and around 1370. It now houses the town’s tourist information center: ask for a map here. Nearby, the Igreja Matriz, the main church, was built by local residents starting in 1425. Take a look at its Gothic portal.

For sacred art, the Museu dos Terceiros is the best place to visit in Ponte de Lima. It occupies two neighboring churches: Santo António dos Frades and the church of the Ordem Terceira, a lay confraternity. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. It is closed on Mondays.

activities.text: Walk along the Ecovia do Lima, the greenway that follows the river for around 70 km. A greenway is a path reserved for pedestrians and cyclists. From Ponte de Lima, a frequently recommended section heads upstream to Ponte da Barca, 15 km away. Take a 1-hour round-trip walk along the water, or rent a bike in town to go farther.

In Ponte de Lima, arroz de sarrabulho is nicknamed the “black gold” of local cuisine. The full version of this pork and rice dish comes with rojões, chunks of fried pork, and tripas enfarinhadas, tripe coated in flour and then fried. Pair it with vinho verde, the regional wine, made here from the Loureiro grape variety. Save it for dinner: it’s a hearty dish.

places.name: Ponte de Sor

visits.text: Discover Ponte de Sor, strategically positioned on the historic route linking Mérida to Lisbon since Roman times. Today this riverside town marks kilometer 435 of Portugal's iconic EN2 road connecting Chaves to Faro, making it an essential stop for travelers exploring the country's diverse landscapes.

Visit the Centro de Artes e Cultura, a multidisciplinary space featuring the world's largest cork mosaic, certified by Guinness World Records in 2014. Albanian artist Saimir Strati created this remarkable work celebrating one of the region's most important industries, housed in a former grain mill that preserves industrial archaeological heritage.

Explore Galveias and its José Luís Peixoto Interpretation Center, dedicated to one of Portugal's most celebrated contemporary writers. This literary route encompasses 22 points of interest connecting the author's work to the landscapes that inspired him.

activities.text: Head to the Montargil dam, around thirty minutes by road from Ponte de Sor, the municipality's main attraction nestled among rolling cork oak forests. This vast reservoir offers a water sports center, a river beach and breathtaking viewpoints. For the ultimate experience, take a hot-air balloon flight at dawn or dusk to enjoy the serene Alentejo landscape from the air.

activities.text: Cross Luís I Bridge on its upper deck: this bridge has two levels, and the upper one sits more than 45 m above the Douro. This metal bridge was inaugurated on October 31, 1886. It was designed by Théophile Seyrig, a former partner of Gustave Eiffel. Until 1944, pedestrians paid a toll of five réis, the former Portuguese currency, to cross from one bank to the other. Today, pedestrians share the upper deck with metro Line D: watch for approaching trains.

visits.text: Explore Portalegre's historic center, where baroque architecture and azulejo-adorned facades line winding medieval streets. The Palácio Amarelo and numerous noble houses testify to the prosperity brought by the textile industry that made this city famous throughout Portugal.

Visit Portalegre Castle, a 13th-century medieval fortress whose walls and towers still dominate the city skyline. From the ramparts, spectacular views extend across Portalegre to the rolling hills of Serra de São Mamede, while a small military museum preserves local martial heritage.

Discover the Portalegre Tapestry Museum and Manufactory, celebrating the unique weaving technique that put this city on the artistic map. Inspired by painter Jean Lurçat, Portalegre tapestries are renowned worldwide for their intricate detail and vibrant colors. Visitors can watch artisans at work continuing this living tradition.

Explore the Sé Cathedral, a 16th-century church dedicated to Our Lady of the Assumption. Its baroque facade gives way to a serene interior featuring crystal chandeliers, a sacristy decorated with azulejo tiles, and an impressive collection of religious art spanning centuries.

activities.text: Visit the José Régio House-Museum, former residence of one of Portugal's greatest 20th-century writers. Beyond his personal belongings, the museum houses an extraordinary collection of sacred art, religious statues, and folk icons reflecting Régio's passion for traditional Portuguese culture.

Swing above the Alentejo plains on the panoramic swing «Carreiras sem fim» located at Miradouro da Fonte dos Carvoeiros. This Instagram-worthy spot offers unparalleled photo opportunities with sweeping views across the golden landscape.

visits.text: Arrive in Porto, Portugal's vibrant northern capital where the historic center cascades down hillsides to the Douro River. The UNESCO World Heritage Ribeira district reveals layers of history in its medieval streets, baroque churches, and iconic azulejo-covered buildings. This atmospheric city serves as the gateway to the magnificent wine country and wild landscapes of the north.

Cross the iconic Dom Luís I Bridge, the double-deck iron arch spanning the Douro that has become Porto's most recognizable landmark. The upper level offers pedestrians spectacular views over the historic center and the port wine cellars of Vila Nova de Gaia opposite. This engineering marvel connects the old city with centuries of winemaking tradition.

Stroll from the Dom Luís I Bridge along the Douro River to the Felgueiras Lighthouse at Foz, where the river meets the Atlantic Ocean. This scenic waterfront walk passes through historic neighborhoods, riverside promenades, and traditional fishing communities. The lighthouse marks the dramatic meeting point of river and sea with spectacular coastal views.

activities.text: Experience the surf culture at Matosinhos beach just outside Porto, an excellent destination for surfers with gentle waves and a sandy bottom. Local surf schools offer lessons for all levels at this accessible beach break. The consistent Atlantic swells make it one of northern Portugal's most popular spots for riding waves.

Paddle along the Douro River on a kayaking or stand-up paddleboard excursion through the heart of Porto. Gliding beneath the city's six bridges provides unique perspectives on terraced hillsides and historic architecture. This tranquil urban paddling experience offers a different pace for exploring this atmospheric city.

places.name: Porto Covo

visits.text: Porto Covo is the best-kept village on the Alentejo coast: white houses with blue trim, paved alleys, nothing superfluous. The Largo Marquês de Pombal is its heart—a rectangular square with Pombaline proportions, built after the 1755 earthquake according to the reconstruction's urban planning principles. Stop by in the evening when residents bring out their chairs.

Built in 1603 by order of Philip II to defend the coast against pirate raids, the Forte da Ilha do Pessegueiro occupies the center of Pessegueiro islet, a few hundred meters offshore. Around it, the seabed reveals Roman salting vats for garum—the island had been an active port center since at least Carthaginian times.

activities.text: In summer, boats offer crossings to the Ilha do Pessegueiro from the beach (around €10 return). The seabed around the island is rich in Roman amphorae - snorkeling is possible, but access to the underwater ruins is unmarked.

places.name: Porto da Cruz

visits.text: Penha de Águia, the “eagle’s rock,” is an escarpment rising to 580 m above sea level that towers over Porto da Cruz. The village grew with sugarcane, which the first settlers were already cultivating. For a photo, head down to the village waterfront.

activities.text: If you visit between March and May, you will see the machinery running at Engenhos do Norte in Porto da Cruz. Built in 1927 with 19th-century machinery, this mill still produces sugarcane spirit, Madeira rum, using the original methods. During the rest of the year, screens explain how the machinery works. Afterward, sample a few rums at Casa do Rum, right next door.

visits.text: Save Aquário da Madeira, Porto Moniz’s aquarium, for a day with heavy swells. It occupies the Forte de São João Baptista, a fort built in 1730 to defend against pirate attacks and later restored by the municipality. Since 2005, its 12 tanks have showcased more than 90 species found around the archipelago; the largest holds 500,000 liters of seawater.

activities.text: Formed by lava that cooled at the ocean’s edge, the Piscinas Naturais do Porto Moniz are black rock pools with a constant flow of seawater. The water stays around 20 to 21 °C year-round. The developed complex, with pools about 2 m deep, offers changing rooms, a bar, and a children’s pool; admission costs €3. The pools beside the aquarium are free, but have no lifeguards.

visits.text: A steep-sided cove, red cliffs rising 50 meters, turquoise water between the rocks—the Praia da Arrifana is more dramatic than beautiful, and that is what makes it memorable. A recognized surf spot, with regular swell even in summer.

The ruins of Forte da Arrifana dominate the cove from the northern promontory. Built in the 17th century to monitor the coast, the fort now retains only its foundations and two wall sections. Views looking down on the surfers below.

activities.text: Walk down to the beach before sunset via the staircase carved into the rock—a 10-minute walk from the parking area. Allow 1 hour there. Use a headlamp for the walk back if you stay late.

places.name: Praia do Malhão

visits.text: Dune sand as far as the eye can see, clean waves without beach infrastructure: Praia do Malhão remains wild because access is deliberately long - 2 km of sandy track from the N393, impassable for low-clearance cars. In the Parque Natural do Sudoeste Alentejano, camping outside official zones has been prohibited since 2021.

The Trilho dos Pescadores from the Rota Vicentina follows the cliff edge between Malhão and Vila Nova de Milfontes for 7 km - the best section of the Alentejo coast for walking alone in the morning. Marked in blue and green, low elevation gain.

activities.text: Surf or swim early: Praia do Malhão faces due west, direct Atlantic swell. No lifeguards or buoys. No shops on site - bring water and food for the day.

activities.text: The PR6 Levada das 25 Fontes follows a levada, an irrigation channel carved into the mountainside. Madeira has more than 2,170 km of levadas, and their maintenance paths now serve as hiking trails. The trail runs for 4.3 km through the laurel forest, with views of the Ribeira da Janela valley. At the end, water flowing down from the Paul da Serra plateau emerges from 25 springs around a pool. Allow about 3 hours round-trip, returning along the same trail.

You’ll start from the same place for PR6.1 Levada do Risco, an easy 1.5 km trail that shares its opening stretch with PR6. At the end, Risco waterfall drops straight down, tracing a white line against the dark rock. On its own, the hike takes about 2 hours round-trip, but you can combine it with PR6 on the same day.

visits.text: Reguengos de Monsaraz is the wine capital of the Alentejo, anchored to the most productive region of Portugal's vineyards. The town itself is quiet, but the Largo do Município and the 18th-century parish church make a pleasant stop between cellars.

The cellars smell of oak and ripe fruit: Herdade do Esporão, a few kilometers from town, produces on an estate of over 700 hectares under organic farming. Its medieval Torre Esporão, a classified national monument, stands amid the vines—a curious blend of 14th-century stone and stainless steel tanks.

activities.text: Book a tasting at Herdade do Esporão in advance—guided tours in foreign languages are scheduled at fixed times. Budget 1 to 1.5 hours. The on-site restaurant offers lunch featuring estate products, recommended if timing allows.

places.name: Ribeira dos Caldeirões

visits.text: Five watermills line the river in the Parque Natural da Ribeira dos Caldeirões, in the parish of Achada. Three date from the 16th century and are protected heritage sites. One houses a small museum about rural life in the past. Admission to the park is free, and there are picnic areas and playgrounds, making it a good lunch stop.

The sound of water drowns out everything else: at the Parque Natural da Ribeira dos Caldeirões, a large waterfall tumbles amid tree ferns and hydrangeas. The park occupies the slopes of the Serra da Tronqueira, surrounded by laurisilva, a moist laurel forest. Follow the main path to the large waterfall. Then take the smaller side trails leading to more secluded falls.

places.name: Ribeira Grande

visits.text: Ribeira Grande, on the north coast, became a city on June 29, 1981. You can explore its center on foot, from city hall to the Igreja Matriz de Nossa Senhora da Estrela. Don’t miss the Ponte dos Oito Arcos, an eight-arch bridge built in the 19th century to supplement the older single-arch bridge on the main square. Allow 40 minutes for the walk.

A distillery, then a barracks, then a tobacco factory, and finally an art center: that is the story of Arquipélago in Ribeira Grande. This contemporary art center opened in May 2015 within the basalt walls of a late-19th-century distillery. Two new buildings stand alongside it around a central courtyard. The architects used basalt from São Miguel for the floors. Allow 45 minutes for the exhibitions.

visits.text: Arcades, cafés, and terraces right by the water: Ribeira is one of Porto’s oldest neighborhoods. The arcaded houses on Ribeira Square were rebuilt after a major fire in 1491. On the quay, a small memorial, the Alminhas da Ponte, commemorates the tragedy of 1809. That year, during the invasion by Napoleon’s troops, a bridge made of boats tied together collapsed, and many residents drowned. Save this neighborhood for late in the day, when the evening light bathes Luís I Bridge in gold.

visits.text: In our opinion, the prettiest route down from São Bento to the river is Rua das Flores. Work on the street began in 1521 on the site of the bishop’s vegetable gardens, which were full of flowers—hence its name, “Street of Flowers.” Goldsmiths traditionally kept shops here, especially on the north side. Along the way, the Church of Mercy (Igreja da Misericórdia), begun in 1559, is worth a look. Take your time walking down to Largo de São Domingos, a small square near the Stock Exchange Palace.

days_plan.itin_title: Porto in 2 Days: Ribeira, Gaia Wine Cellars, and Foz do Douro

visits.text: Visit the Cró Thermal Baths, located just over 10 km from Sabugal. These thermal baths, whose medicinal waters have been used since Roman times, have been modernized with a new thermal complex equipped with cutting-edge technology. The ruins of the old baths bear witness to the long spa tradition of this region.

activities.text: Explore Sabugal's historic center with its imposing medieval castle and pentagonal keep, unique in Portugal. This border town preserves a rich architectural heritage and offers panoramic views over the granite landscape of the Beira frontier.

days_plan.itin_title: Beira Interior: Serra da Estrela, Schist Villages and Historic Cities

visits.text: Discover Sabugueiro, at an altitude of about 1,050 meters near the Rio Alva. The village is said to have developed from the huts of shepherds who made use of the mountain pastures. Visit the parish church, the calvary, the blacksmith's fountain and the ethnographic museum, which preserves local traditions.

Admire the Fervença Waterfall and explore the ancient Covão Grande glacier. The engraving carved into the rock near Fonte do Canariz proves that people passed through these parts as far back as ancient times, giving Sabugueiro a historical dimension that complements its natural beauty.

Visit the small village of Cabeça, at an altitude of 530 meters, with fewer than fifty houses, some built of schist, a century-old cork oak and a vast pine forest. The village offers authenticity, an exceptional view and tranquility, and turns into a display of sustainable lights at Christmas time. Cabeça is close to an hour's drive from the stopover town.

activities.text: Hike the Lagoa dos Conchos Trail at over 1,500 meters altitude, discovering one of the mountain's most surprising locations. This lagoon with a huge artificial funnel through which the waters seem to disappear is an engineering marvel. The 5 km linear trail offers nature and sublime views.

Explore the lagoons and reservoirs of Serra da Estrela: Lagoa Comprida, Covão dos Conchos, Covão do Meio, Covão do Forno, and Covão do Curral. These places are ideal for taking in the Natural Park's landscape and enjoying refreshing swims at the river beaches.

days_plan.itin_title: Beira Interior: Serra da Estrela, Schist Villages and Historic Cities

visits.text: Henry the Navigator is said to have founded a navigation school here, but there is no evidence to support the story. Fortaleza de Sagres, on a clifftop plateau at the end of the headland, was indeed built in the 15th century on his orders. Henry died in Sagres in 1460. On the ground, the Rosa dos Ventos (compass rose), a large stone circle divided into 32 directions, may have served as a sundial. Admission has cost €10 since 2025: afterward, walk around the headland with a windbreaker on.

The wind blows hard, and the cliffs plunge 75 m straight into the Atlantic: at Cape St. Vincent, you are at the southwestern tip of mainland Europe. The Romans called it the sacred promontory. The lighthouse, built in 1846 on the ruins of a convent, casts its beam 60 km out to sea. The lighthouse tower is currently closed to visitors indefinitely. For sunset, arrive an hour early. Touristy but fun: a truck here sells a sausage billed as “the last one before America.”

Fortaleza do Beliche, a small fort between Sagres and the cape, once protected tuna fishermen from pirates. It dates to the reign of Manuel I or John III in the 16th century, and the English privateer Francis Drake attacked it in 1587. Its Santa Catarina chapel, which partly overhangs the cliff edge, is closed to visitors because of the risk of collapse. Below lies Praia do Beliche, a sandy beach between the cliffs: stop on your way to the cape.

activities.text: Board a boat at Porto da Baleeira, Sagres's fishing harbor, for a dolphin-watching trip. Trips aboard rigid inflatable boats last about 1 hour 30 minutes and run year-round, starting at around €40 per adult. Choose an operator with marine biologists on its team: they explain what you see. The water stays cool, from 15 °C in winter to 19 °C in summer, and the wind makes it feel even cooler out at sea.

Depending on the wind, Sagres offers a calm beach or a beach for surfers. South-facing Praia da Mareta, a few minutes' walk from town, is the most sheltered. Southeast-facing Praia do Martinhal suits families, with lifeguards in summer. West-facing Praia do Tonel gets the biggest waves and strongest currents: leave it to experienced surfers.

activities.text: You will land at Cristiano Ronaldo Madeira Airport, in the municipality of Santa Cruz, 13 km from Funchal. Its runway runs alongside the ocean: the extension, completed in 2000, rests on 180 columns around 70 m tall. Wind often disrupts air traffic here, so delays are possible. Pick up your rental car, then follow the expressway west: central Funchal is about 20 minutes away.

You’ll return the car at Madeira Airport in Santa Cruz, about 20 minutes from Funchal via the expressway. Arrive early and monitor your flight’s status: wind often restricts air traffic at this airport. If you have time before boarding, Machico’s light-sand beach is a few minutes’ drive away.

visits.text: Touristy but informative, the Casas Típicas de Santana show how farmers on the north coast once lived. Their thatched roofs, made from wheat and rye stalks, slope almost to the ground to shed rainwater; they are replaced every four to five years. Beneath the roof, the attic stored crops, while the ground floor housed a kitchen and a bedroom. The wooden facades are painted white, red, and blue. The entire municipality is designated a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve.

days_plan.itin_title: Madeira in 7 Days: Funchal, Levadas, and Pico Ruivo

visits.text: Three kilometers of hills separate Santiago do Cacém from the Miróbriga site - but the real shock is the medieval castle that dominates the coastal plain from a ridge. Founded in the 11th century with Moorish origins, restored by the Templars, it offers from its ramparts a view that extends to the coast. Free entrance, ten-minute climb from the center. Better before 11am, before the sun beats down.

The Santiago do Cacém railway station doesn't look like much from the street. Go in anyway: the platform walls of the Beja–Sines line are covered with azulejos depicting plowing scenes and local monuments. A series of tile panels created in the 20th century in the Pombaline tradition. A two-minute detour, no ticket needed.

activities.text: Climb to the medieval castle in late afternoon when the raking light brings out the golden stones of the ramparts. The descent into the old town passes some well-preserved low houses. Allow 45 minutes round trip from the center.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Lisbon and Southern Portugal Tour in 15 Days

visits.text: “A boat with its keel in the air”: Portuguese writer Miguel Torga saw this hill as an overturned boat hull in the middle of the valley. At the Miradouro de São Leonardo de Galafura, at an elevation of 640 m, an azulejo panel reproduces his text near the chapel. Below, terraced vineyards descend to the Douro. For a picnic, stone tables await in the shade a little farther down.

days_plan.itin_title: Douro in 5 Days: Quintas, Pinhão, and the Côa Rock Engravings

places.name: São Pedro do Sul

visits.text: Discover São Pedro do Sul, known for picturesque scenery of thick green forests, crystal-clear rivers, and charming villages inhabited since Roman times. Natural thermal baths used for healing since antiquity offer relaxation with sulfur-rich mineral waters. The sweet-scented eucalyptus forests and peaceful atmosphere make this region ideal for nature lovers.

Drive along the thrilling Estrada do Portal do Inferno (Gate of Hell Road), a dramatic mountain road with steep slopes and sheer cliff edges; allow for a round trip by car from São Pedro do Sul. This spectacular road crosses the most dramatic high-mountain landscapes of northern Portugal, with viewpoints offering panoramic vistas. The narrow, winding road requires care but rewards you with unforgettable scenery.

Head up to the Serra de São Macário for some of the finest panoramic views in northern Portugal, with road access to the summit; allow for a round trip by car from São Pedro do Sul. The winding road climbs through dramatic landscapes to panoramic vistas across valleys and distant mountain ranges. Visit the isolated village of Aldeia da Pena, where goats wander through cobbled streets and stone houses seem to have grown out of the landscape.

activities.text: Hike through the forests to discover hidden waterfalls and picturesque viewpoints along networks of paths winding through fragrant woods. The trails follow rushing streams and climb toward panoramic ridgelines, offering perfect opportunities to experience natural beauty in solitude. Sunset from the Serra de São Macário creates magical moments with landscapes bathed in golden light; allow for a round trip by car from São Pedro do Sul to reach this site.

visits.text: A chapel inside a rock: in São Vicente, on the north coast, the Capela de São Vicente was built into a basalt boulder by the sea, near the river’s mouth. The rock protects it from the sea. Stop for 15 minutes to walk around it. The waves along this coast also attract surfers and bodyboarders.

visits.text: In 1387, King John I married the English princess Philippa of Lancaster in Sé do Porto, the city’s cathedral. They are the couple you just saw on horseback on the azulejos at São Bento. With its two square towers and battlements, the building resembles a fortified church. In the Gothic cloister, azulejos installed between 1729 and 1731 illustrate the Song of Songs, a love poem from the Bible. There is an admission fee for the cloister. The cathedral opens daily at 9 a.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Porto in 2 Days: Ribeira, Gaia Wine Cellars, and Foz do Douro

visits.text: Visit the Seia Interpretive Center, housed in the emblematic Casa Solar dos Botelhos, a listed heritage building and beautiful example of 16th-century Manueline style. This space offers an extensive journey through the municipality's history, revealing the cultural richness of this city at the gateway to Serra da Estrela.

Discover the Bread Museum, perhaps the largest in the world dedicated to this staple food. Opened in 2002 at Quinta Fonte do Marrão, this 3,500 m² space collects, preserves, and exhibits the heritage of bread in its various aspects: ethnographic, political, social, historical, religious, and artistic.

Explore the Toy Museum at Solar de Santa Rita, a fascinating space with about ten thousand toys from around the world. From the most common to the most original, including traditional Portuguese toys, all pieces have a story. Outside, admire the 300-year-old yew tree, classified as a tree of public interest.

Visit the Serra da Estrela Interpretation Center (CISE), an ideal place to explore mainland Portugal's largest mountain range through virtual reality. Participate in environmental activities such as hikes, themed outings, and wildlife and plant observation workshops.

Discover the Sanctuary of Nossa Senhora do Desterro, a Marian complex consisting of ten chapels built between the 17th and 19th centuries. According to popular tradition, the appearance of images of the Virgin, Saint Joseph, and the Child Jesus led to the construction of this sanctuary, where the beauty of the Rio Alva complements the built heritage.

Visit the village of Lapa dos Dinheiros, located at an altitude of over 700 meters with a superb view over the Mondego plateau. This mountain village has an extensive chestnut forest with rare species such as the whitebeam and Portuguese laurel, relics of forests from over 2 million years ago.

Explore the small town of Loriga, around half an hour's drive from the stopover town, nestled in a steep valley embraced by two rivers and surrounded by farmland laid out in imposing terraces. Wander the streets on foot, discover every corner and be sure to taste the award-winning Bolo Negro and the Broa de Loriga.

activities.text: Stroll through Seia's Historic Center admiring the Four Spouts Fountain from 1825, the Misericórdia Church built in 1571, the São Pedro Chapel classified as a National Monument since 1924, and the Parish Church referenced since 1136 in King Afonso Henriques' charter.

Visit the Natural Museum of Electricity, located in the century-old Senhora do Desterro Power Station. This museum showcases the technological heritage of hydropower in Serra da Estrela, including the original machinery and a 35-meter-long tunnel.

Cool off at the Loriga River Beach, around half an hour's drive from the stopover town, a place of rare beauty where the traces left by the glacier that carved the Loriga Valley are still visible. This beach, awarded the Golden Beach label, is the ideal spot for lovers of nature, calm and serenity.

Walk the Loriga Gorge trail as far as Eira da Pedra, discovering the characteristic shapes of the glacial landscape created by the erosive action of ice between 100,000 and 10,000 years ago. The highest areas of the mountain were covered by a layer of ice about 80 meters thick. Loriga is around half an hour's drive from the stopover town.

visits.text: Black sand, green cliffs, and Atlantic waves: Praia do Porto do Seixal formed naturally a few years ago beside the small harbor. This dark sand, made of volcanic rock, heats up quickly in the sun, so bring sandals. Showers, a bar, and kayak rentals are available on-site. Around the village, small vineyards cling to almost vertical terraces.

Miradouro do Véu da Noiva, the “bridal veil” viewpoint, overlooks the coast between São Vicente and Seixal. It faces a waterfall that plunges from the cliff above the old coastal road carved into the rock. Stay behind the barriers: water from the waterfall and falling rocks still land on this old road.

days_plan.itin_title: Madeira in 7 Days: Funchal, Levadas, and Pico Ruivo

places.name: Serpa

visits.text: Serpa smells of sheep's milk cheese from the town entrance—the queijo de Serpa DOP is one of Portugal's most renowned cheeses, creamy and slightly bitter, produced on surrounding farms. The castle ramparts, partially collapsed in an explosion in 1707, frame a perfectly preserved walled town. The aqueduct runs along the ramparts for several hundred meters—medieval in design, still intact.

The Museu do Relógio exhibits over 2,300 mechanical clocks in a 16th-century convent - from the oldest (1630) to the most recent, pendulum clocks, pocket watches, grandfather clocks, alarm clocks. António Tavares d'Almeida, a Serpa watchmaker, began collecting in the 1970s and opened the museum in 1995.

The aqueduct runs along the ramparts as if it had always been there—and it almost has: its route dates from the Middle Ages. It opens onto the Porta de Beja, the old town's main gate. The square inside the walls, Praça da República, contains the Igreja de Santa Maria and the Manueline Pelourinho—a granite pillory used to display convicted offenders.

activities.text: The queijo de Serpa DOP flows at room temperature—literally. In season (January–March), local cheesemakers sell fresh cheeses that are still runny. A traditional tavern in the old town serves Alentejo-style pork with a slice of cheese as a starter. Order red wine from Serpa with it.

If you pass through in January–March, cheese production is at its peak and the cheese is at its runniest. Off-season, Serpa cheesemakers still sell their cheese—ask for cheeses aged for 3–4 weeks, firmer but just as tasty. The Friday morning market on Praça da República sells it.

visits.text: The Parque Natural da Arrábida has covered about 17,000 hectares since 1976—including over 5,000 ha of marine area—a limestone massif peaking at 501 meters that drops straight into the Atlantic. The scenic N379-1 road follows the ridge, then descends to hidden beaches. The Mediterranean vegetation here is among the best preserved on the Iberian Peninsula according to ICNF. Drive carefully: tight bends and cliffs without barriers.

The Praia de Galapinhos surprises with its contrasts: turquoise water, white sand and limestone cliffs - 40 km from Lisbon. The final approach to the beach is a downhill walk. During the summer season, traffic and parking are regulated: check the access arrangements before coming. Bring water.

The Convento de Nossa Senhora da Arrábida is a 16th-century Franciscan monastery perched mid-slope, designed for total isolation - two chapels, a refectory, a kitchen, a library, and 40 small cells scattered in the surrounding hills. Acquired in 1990 by Fundação Oriente. Guided tours Wednesday to Sunday, €5 by prior reservation.

activities.text: If you're into diving or snorkeling, Arrábida is one of the best areas on Portugal's Atlantic coast—fully protected marine reserve, clear water, rich biodiversity. Several clubs in Setúbal offer half-day to full-day outings.

In Azeitão, on the road between Setúbal and Arrábida, stop for queijo de Azeitão DOP—creamy sheep's milk cheese—and Azeitão rolls and tarts (egg and almond pastries). Several producers are open to the public on rua Direita.

places.name: Serra do Pilar

visits.text: If you could keep just one view of Porto, choose the one from the terrace of Serra do Pilar Monastery, on the Vila Nova de Gaia bank. Across the river, Ribeira, the cathedral, and Luís I Bridge rise in tiers above the water. The monastery’s distinctive feature is that both its church and its cloister are round. In 1809, the future Duke of Wellington, a British general, used it as a base to retake Porto from the French. Just below, Jardim do Morro, a terraced garden, slopes down toward the river: return at sunset.

map_keywords: Mosteiro da Serra do Pilar Vila Nova de Gaia
Jardim do Morro Vila Nova de Gaia

visits.text: Sesimbra is a fishing village that hasn't forgotten its trade: the fish auction runs every morning at the port, trawlers return laden around 2pm, and restaurant signs advertise black scabbardfish and cuttlefish with freshly chalked prices. The village slopes steeply down to a sheltered beach—calm in rough seas, packed in summer. The old town remains intact between Cidade de Setúbal and 5 de Outubro streets.

The Castelo de Sesimbra dominates the bay from an altitude of 230 meters. Moorish origins, reconquered in 1165 by Afonso Henriques, given to the Templars then to the Order of Santiago in 1186. A walk around the entire circuit of ramparts takes 30 minutes, with a view extending to Sintra on clear days. Free access, parking at the summit.

Porto de Sesimbra, north side of the beach: fishing boats pull up to the quay in mid-afternoon, unloading black scabbardfish and conger eels in front of local buyers. Fifteen minutes in this small-scale fishing port is enough to see that Sesimbra isn't a beach resort in disguise.

activities.text: Eat grilled fish at Sesimbra port: Ribamar, A Nova Estrela, or the simpler taverns toward rua Cândido dos Reis. Black scabbardfish is the specialty, caught in deep water off Sesimbra. Expect to pay €12–18 per dish.

From Sesimbra, plan a round trip to Cabo Espichel to observe dinosaur footprints in the cliffs surrounding the Baía dos Lagosteiros. From the sanctuary, head to the viewpoints above, without descending onto the slabs at the foot of the cliffs. Bring binoculars and keep away from the edge; take care with children.

places.name: Sete Cidades

visits.text: If the crater is clear when you arrive, head straight to the Miradouro da Vista do Rei, the king’s viewpoint. It takes its name from the visit of King Carlos I and Queen Amélie on July 6, 1901. It overlooks a caldera measuring 6 km by 5 km, a large crater formed by the collapse of a volcano’s summit. Fog often covers the site: check the live webcams on the SpotAzores website before setting out. In summer, tour buses arrive between 9:30 and 10 a.m.: get there earlier.

A green-eyed princess and a blue-eyed shepherd: according to the legend of Sete Cidades, their love was forbidden, and their tears filled Lagoa Verde (Green Lake) and Lagoa Azul (Blue Lake). In reality, these two lakes form a single body of water, divided by a shallow channel crossed by a small bridge. The difference in color comes from the depth, reflections of the vegetation, and the angle of the light. It is easier to see from the viewpoints than from the bridge.

The village of Sete Cidades sits on the crater floor beside the lake, at an elevation of about 260 m. Around 700 people live here. Its Gothic Revival church of São Nicolau was inaugurated in 1852. A drainage tunnel, opened in 1937, allows the lake’s water level to be controlled. Park near the church, then walk to the water’s edge before leaving.

For us, this is the most beautiful view on the western side of the island: the Miradouro da Boca do Inferno, the “mouth of hell.” It overlooks the two large lakes and several smaller ones, including Lagoa de Santiago, which cannot be seen from Vista do Rei. Access is via a forest road starting at Lagoa do Canário, followed by a walk. When this road is closed to cars, allow 15 to 20 minutes of walking each way. Wear good shoes, as the ground is often slippery.

An aqueduct rather than a defensive wall, the Muro das Nove Janelas, the “wall of nine windows,” is hidden in the Serra Devassa forest. It carried water from Lagoa do Canário and neighboring lakes to Ponta Delgada, more than 10 km away. Its nine openings were cut to let the highland winds pass through instead of pushing against the wall. It is in the same area as Lagoa do Canário: combine the two and allow 10 to 20 minutes here.

activities.text: You can then walk along Lagoa Azul from the village of Sete Cidades, following a flat dirt path along the southern shore for several kilometers. In season, rental companies near the village also offer kayaks and paddleboards. Strong walkers can instead descend from Vista do Rei to the village along trail PR03 SMI: about 7.5 km and 2 hours, with no particular difficulty.

Miradouro da Boca do Inferno Sete Cidades

visits.text: The Igreja de Jesus de Setúbal is Portugal's first Manueline building—begun in 1490 by architect Diogo de Boitaca before he designed the Jerónimos. Twisted columns in local breccia marble, complex ribbed vaulting: the entire architectural vocabulary of the Manueline style is born here. The pink stone floor contrasts with the green marble columns. Classified as a national monument.

The Forte de São Filipe has dominated Setúbal and the Sado estuary since 1582—built by Philip II of Spain during the Iberian Union, on a star-shaped plan with four bastions. The fort is now partially converted into a pousada, and its ramparts remain accessible. Views of Tróia, the sandy peninsula opposite, and the dolphins that still populate the estuary.

The Mercado do Livramento dates from 1930: Setúbal's market has been selling its fresh fish here since 1930 under hand-painted azulejos depicting maritime scenes. Arrive before 10am for sardines, choco frito (fried squid, a local specialty) and seafood.

activities.text: Eat choco frito in a tavern on rua Antão Girão or around the market. Setúbal has made it its specialty: cuttlefish cut into strips, breaded, fried to order, served with lemon and fries. Expect to pay €8–12 per dish.

If you have time, cross by ferry to Tróia (20 min, €7 round trip on foot) to see the Roman fish salting remains - the Cetariae de Tróia, active from the 1st to 5th century, exported their garum widely in the western Empire. Site managed by the Tróia Resort foundation, ticket ~€3.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand Lisbon and Southern Portugal Tour in 15 Days

visits.text: Explore Silves, the former capital of the Algarve, usually overlooked by first-time visitors yet offering fascinating glimpses into the region's Moorish past. This typical medieval hilltop town is crowned by a partially restored castle that once rivaled Lisbon in importance before the devastating 1755 earthquake. Silves Cathedral and the Archaeological Museum just off the main square complement the castle experience.

Discover the charming village of Alte, approximately 28 km from Silves, a 25-minute drive away, one of the most picturesque traditional villages in the Algarve countryside, where time seems to stand still. Narrow cobbled streets wind between traditional white buildings adorned with colorful flowers and some of the finest street art in the region. The natural springs at Fonte Grande de Alte offer a refreshing swim in crystal-clear water—an unexpected experience in the inland Algarve.

Visit the beaches of Alvor, including Praia dos Três Irmãos and the small Praia da Prainha, linked by tunnels and passages through the cliffs; allow for a round trip by car from Silves. Walking barefoot through the tunnels, beneath natural arches and along narrow cliff passages reveals one surprise after another in this spectacular coastal landscape. The cliffside restaurant at Prainha, perched between the rocks, offers an utterly unique place to eat.

activities.text: Explore the Costa Vicentina, the less visited west coast of the Algarve, offering a wild, majestic landscape completely different from the popular eastern beaches; allow for a round trip by car within the day from Silves. Praia da Bordeira and Praia da Cordoama are favorites with surfers, but every small road leading to the coast rewards visitors with beautiful views. This natural, undeveloped coast offers authentic Atlantic beauty without the crowds.

places.name: Sines

visits.text: In Sines, everything starts with Vasco da Gama - born here around 1469, son of the castle governor. The Castelo de Sines now houses the Museu de Sines and Casa de Vasco da Gama, inaugurated in 2008, with a multimedia reconstruction of his voyages to India. The navigator's statue on the ramparts faces the ocean to the south. Open Tuesday to Sunday 10am to 5pm, free admission.

Pass by the Igreja Matriz where Vasco da Gama was baptized, then head to Largo dos Penedos da Índia for a panoramic view over the bay. The Centro Histórico de Sines consists of a few streets between the castle and the port—wandering without a plan is recommended. The old town takes 1 hour 30 minutes to explore on foot.

activities.text: The wind smells of the open sea at Largo dos Penedos da Índia, a natural terrace above the bay. It's also the best viewpoint over Sines' industrial port—a striking contrast with the three streets of the old town. Since 2015, an elevator has connected the center to the waterfront.

visits.text: Journey to Sintra, a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape where romantic palaces rise from forested hillsides in one of Europe's most enchanting settings. Portuguese royalty and aristocrats chose this misty mountain retreat for their summer residences, leaving behind an extraordinary concentration of architectural treasures. The town's fairytale atmosphere has captivated visitors from Lord Byron to modern-day travelers.

Explore the Palácio Nacional de Sintra, the medieval royal palace dominating the town center with its distinctive conical kitchen chimneys visible for kilometers around. This summer residence of the Portuguese monarchs preserves remarkable interiors, including rooms entirely covered in decorative azulejo tiles and elaborate Mudéjar ceilings.

Climb up to the Palácio da Pena, a flamboyant 19th-century palace crowning one of the peaks of the Sintra hills in an explosion of color and architectural fantasy. This Romantic masterpiece combines Gothic towers, Manueline decoration, Moorish elements and Renaissance domes in a riot of yellows, reds and blues. The surrounding park of exotic trees and hidden paths extends the magical atmosphere across the mountain.

Stand at Cabo da Roca, the westernmost point of mainland Europe, about thirty minutes' drive from Sintra. Here spectacular cliffs plunge into the Atlantic beneath a historic lighthouse. This windswept headland marks where the European landmass meets the ocean, a geographical landmark celebrated with a monument and a certificate for visitors. The raw power of the setting, with crashing waves, soaring cliffs and an endless horizon, creates a profound feeling of standing at the edge of the world.

End your trip in Cascais, an elegant seaside resort about thirty minutes' drive from Sintra, which has drawn aristocrats and artists ever since the Portuguese royal family made it their summer playground in the 19th century. The charming old town features cobbled pedestrian streets, whitewashed buildings and a picturesque fishing harbor still in use today. Sandy beaches, excellent seafood and a relaxed coastal atmosphere offer the perfect finale to your Lisbon adventure.

activities.text: Wander through Sintra's romantic gardens and parks, where winding paths lead past fountains, follies, and viewpoints revealing glimpses of palaces through the trees. The lush vegetation thrives in the unique microclimate created by Atlantic moisture collecting on the mountain slopes. These verdant landscapes were as carefully composed as any palace interior, creating outdoor rooms of botanical wonder.

visits.text: Not an inch of modern construction inside the ramparts of Sortelha. The medieval village, perched at 760 m, has kept its layout intact since the charter granted in 1228. Granite alleys 1.5 m wide, anthropomorphic graves carved into the rock, a Renaissance church, a Manueline pillory. The silence here isn't a cliché: there are few permanent residents.

Climb the ramparts for the view toward the Serra da Estrela on the horizon. The 13th-century castle, reached through the Porta da Traição (Gate of Betrayal), commands territory long disputed between Portugal and Castile. The granite formation called Cabeça da Velha—an old woman's face sculpted by erosion—is visible from the battlements.

activities.text: The Porta da Traição (Gate of Betrayal) gets its name from its discreet position: it was the secret exit in case of siege. Look for the medieval measures carved into the stone next to the Porta Nova—the cubit and the vara, standards from markets of old.

days_plan.itin_title: Portugal: Historic Villages & Serra da Estrela in 8 Days

visits.text: Discover the Monastery of São João de Tarouca, Portugal's first Cistercian monastery, founded in 1144. This enigmatic and very ancient monument retains its church, with paintings by Gaspar Vaz and the tomb of the Count of Barcelos. A place of spirituality and history where the Cistercian order began its transformative presence in the country.

Visit the Ucanha Toll Tower, a monument unique in Portugal that controlled passage over the medieval bridge spanning the Varosa River. This 12th-century defensive tower, with its fortified bridge, is an exceptional testament to medieval territorial organization and offers an unforgettable, photogenic setting.

activities.text: Explore the Monastery of Santa Maria de Salzedas, an imposing Cistercian monastic complex that was one of the richest in Portugal. Although partially in ruins, the grandeur of its church and cloister bears witness to the power and wealth that Cistercian monks accumulated in this wine-growing region over centuries.

visits.text: It is called the Ponte Romana, the “Roman bridge,” yet an archaeological study showed that the Romans did not build it. This seven-arch bridge connects the two banks of the Gilão, the river that divides Tavira in two. In 1989, a flood swept away two of its arches, and it was restored in 1992. Walk across it from Praça da República late in the day, when the facades are reflected in the water.

The Castelo de Tavira, built by the Moors, crowns the hill in the old town. Its ramparts offer views across all the rooftops. Right beside it, the Igreja de Santa Maria do Castelo was built in the 13th century on the ruins of a mosque, and its bell tower was rebuilt using the former minaret. It houses the tomb of Dom Paio Peres Correia, the Christian commander who retook the town from the Moors in 1242. His seven knights, killed during a truce, lie nearby. Church admission costs €4, including the climb up the bell tower.

In 1551, Tavira gained the Igreja da Misericórdia, whose Renaissance doorway is framed by columns and topped by Our Lady of Mercy. Inside, panels of azulejos, painted glazed ceramic tiles, have covered the walls since the 18th century. Tavira has 37 churches, but this one is on the climb up to the castle: stop in along the way.

A terracotta vessel with small human and animal figures lining its rim: this is the Vaso de Tavira, the star exhibit at the Núcleo Museológico Islâmico. This small museum is built around remains from the Muslim period. You can see a 12th-century rampart made of rammed earth, meaning soil compacted in layers inside formwork. Ask at the front desk for the translated visitor booklet to help you follow the exhibits.

If the sky is clear, head up the Torre de Tavira, the former water tower built in 1931. Slated for demolition, it was saved by local residents, who voted to preserve it in a referendum on June 13, 1999. At a height of 30 m, a camera obscura, a kind of periscope made of mirrors and lenses, projects a live image of the town onto a screen. The demonstration lasts about 20 minutes and takes place on weekdays from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m.

activities.text: Park at Pedras d’El Rei, cross the footbridge over the lagoon, then board the little train that travels 1.3 km through the dunes to Praia do Barril. On the sand, 203 rusty anchors form the Cemitério das Âncoras, the Anchor Cemetery. They held the nets of the almadrava, a maze of nets used to trap tuna, on the seabed. The fishermen left them there in 1964, when the fishing camp was abandoned. Their former huts now house cafés.

If you like octopus, have lunch in Santa Luzia, a fishing village west of Tavira. It is nicknamed the “octopus capital,” and its restaurants have made octopus their specialty. The village is on the road to Pedras d'El Rei: stop on your way to or from Praia do Barril.

visits.text: Angels, saints, and prophets carved in wood fill the Charola, the round church of the Convento de Cristo in Tomar. The Knights Templar, an order of warrior monks, built it in the 12th century, modeling it on the sanctuaries of Jerusalem. It has sixteen sides on the outside, with a drum, an eight-sided interior tower, rising at its center. In the 16th century, the vault and walls were covered with paintings, including depictions of the instruments of Christ’s Passion. Arrive when it opens at 9 a.m. to see it before the tour groups.

The Janela do Capítulo is the most symbolic of the five Manueline windows in the church of the Convento de Cristo. Manueline is a Portuguese decorative style from the early 16th century, rich in symbols associated with the Age of Discovery, the maritime voyages of the time. Diogo de Arruda designed its decoration. For the best view, look for the small cell facing it in the large dormitory. The convent has several cloisters, some of which reopened in 2026 after restoration: ask at reception which are open. Admission has been €15 since 2025.

If you have a car, drive five minutes from the convent to see the Aqueduto dos Pegões, the aqueduct that supplied it with water. It stretches for about 6 km and has 180 arches. In the Pegões valley, two tiers of arches rise to a height of 30 m. Designed by the Italian Filippo Terzi, it was completed in 1614, and water reached the main cloister in 1619. Admire it from the base of the arches: there are no guardrails at the top, and the structure sustained damage in the January 2026 storm.

You will then cross town to the Praça da República, Tomar’s main square, where a statue of Gualdim Pais stands prominently. This leader of the Knights Templar in Portugal laid the castle’s cornerstone in 1160, and the town celebrates him as its founder. Facing city hall, the Igreja de São João Baptista has an octagonal Manueline bell tower. Inside, look for the panels painted in the 1530s by Gregório Lopes. Look at the square’s paving, too: its patterns pay tribute to the Knights Templar.

In 1496, the expulsion of Jews from Portugal brought services at the Sinagoga de Tomar, built in the 15th century, to an end. Tomar’s tourist office describes it as the oldest synagogue in the country. Four columns support the vault, representing the four biblical matriarchs: Sarah, Rebecca, Leah, and Rachel. The twelve corbels on the walls, small stone supports, evoke the twelve tribes. Clay jars embedded in the walls improved the acoustics. It houses the Abraão Zacuto Museum, open Tuesday through Sunday.

Tomar’s most moving church is also its most unassuming: the Igreja de Santa Maria do Olival. This 13th-century Gothic church served as the pantheon of the Templar masters, meaning their burial place. The tombstone of Gualdim Pais, the town’s founder, is still there. The building stands on the site of a former Benedictine monastery. Opening hours vary: check with the tourist office before visiting.

activities.text: Finally, you will walk along the Nabão, the river that flows through Tomar. The Levada is a canal fed by the river. Along its banks, former grain mills and olive presses now form a cultural complex. A charter issued by Gualdim Pais in 1162 already mentions mills here. In Mouchão Park, on a small island, a wooden waterwheel dating from 1906 still lifts water in clay buckets. From the park, the view takes in the Ponte Velha and the Templar castle.

visits.text: At 1993 m, Torre is the roof of mainland Portugal. Legend has it that Dom João VI had a 2-meter cairn added in the 19th century to symbolically reach 2000 m—the official altitude remains 1993 m. In winter, the road is sometimes closed; in summer, the parking lot fills by 10 a.m.

Lagoa Comprida, a few kilometers from Torre, is the largest natural lake in the Serra. From its shore, the high plateau is utterly silent even in peak season—unlike the summit. Starting point for the trail to Covão dos Conchos.

activities.text: Bring a warm layer even in August—the wind at 2000 m is cold as soon as the sun passes behind a cloud. The Serra roads can close without warning in winter.

visits.text: The Torre dos Clérigos, or Clerics’ Tower, rises 75.6 m above central Porto. Designed by architect Nicolau Nasoni, it was completed in 1763. Nasoni asked to be buried in the crypt of the neighboring church, but no one knows exactly where his grave is. The 240 steps lead to the top, above the city’s rooftops. The €10 ticket includes the tower and museum. The site is open daily from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m., with last admission 30 minutes before closing.

visits.text: The marriage of Dom Dinis and Isabel of Aragon took place in Trancoso on June 26, 1282. Isabel was about 12 years old. Quickly neglected by her husband, she turned to charity—bread she distributed to the poor supposedly turned into roses when the king caught her. This Portuguese legend was later canonized. The chapel where the wedding was celebrated still stands.

Trancoso Castle overlooks the plain at 870 m altitude. The base of the watchtower is of Moorish origin—Visigothic work reclaimed by the Templars in 1173, then reinforced by Dom Dinis after 1282. The castle and ramparts have held their current form since that era.

Pass through the Porta d'El-Rei and lose yourself in the medieval grid of alleys inside the walls. Praça Dom Dinis at the center, lined with granite houses, has hardly changed since the 13th century. Local producers' shops are open in the morning.

activities.text: The complete ramparts, 1.2 km circuit with several medieval gates including the Porta do Prado and the Porta d'El-Rei, can be walked in 30 min at a leisurely pace. 360-degree views across the frontier plain from the battlements.

Look in the alleys within the walls for traces of the medieval judiaria—Trancoso sheltered one of the region's most important Jewish communities before the 1496 expulsion. A few lintels carved with Hebrew symbols survive on ordinary façades.

visits.text: More than 5 km of walls surround the Fortaleza de Valença, which guarded the Spanish border. It has two defensive enclosures, or sets of ramparts: the Magistral, the older of the two, and the Coroada, linked by the Porta do Meio. Construction began in 1641, during the war that restored Portugal’s independence from Spain. Work was completed in 1713. In 1809, Napoleon’s troops blew up the Porta do Sol. Park in the Coroada, to the south, then climb to the Baluarte do Socorro, the bastion with the best view of Tui.

The Igreja de Santo Estêvão, Neoclassical but Romanesque in origin, has a 1st-century milestone in its forecourt. This stone column marked distances along Roman road XIX, the road from Braga. Inside, a niche to the right of the altar holds a Virgin nursing the Child, a rare image in Portuguese religious art. Continue to the Igreja de Santa Maria dos Anjos, Valença’s main parish church, on a charming square in the old town.

activities.text: If you walk across the Ponte Internacional to Tui, Spain, set your watch forward one hour. Spain uses Central European Time, one hour ahead of Portugal. Built in 1886, this 384 m bridge carries trains on its upper level and road traffic below. Its lattice structure of intersecting iron beams recalls Gustave Eiffel’s style. Tui’s old town and fortress cathedral are about a 1.5 km walk away.

Allow 2 hours for the Ecopista do Rio Minho, the greenway along the former railroad between Valença and Monção. Opened in 2004, it was the country’s first greenway built on an abandoned rail line. In 2017, it placed third in the European Greenways Awards. It starts at Valença station and follows the river for 15 km through dense woods. Take an out-and-back walk; if you prefer cycling, ask the tourist office near the Porta do Sol where to rent a bike.

The cannons remain on the ramparts, but Valença now lives on trade. The fortress streets are lined with stores selling household linens, very popular with Spanish shoppers. On weekends, crowds fill the narrow streets. Shop early in the morning or late in the day, when the old town becomes quiet again.

places.name: Viana do Alentejo

visits.text: Viana do Alentejo Castle, classified as a national monument since 1910, encloses two Manueline churches within its pentagonal walls, both designed by Diogo de Arruda - the same architect behind Belém Tower. The larger one, the Igreja Matriz (1521), blends Gothic, Manueline and Mudéjar styles with a portal carved with vines and the Cross of the Order of Christ. Step into the courtyard: the ensemble is remarkably harmonious.

Three kilometers outside town, the Sanctuary of Nossa Senhora d'Aires rises from open countryside, its baroque ochre-and-white façade completed in 1804. Slip behind the choir: hundreds of ex-votos line a semi-circular ambulatory - family photos, accounts of miraculous healings, plaques of gratitude. Every April, pilgrims ride 150 km on horseback from Moita do Ribatejo to reach this shrine.

places.name: Viana do Castelo

visits.text: Explore the Minho region, Portugal's greenest area tucked into the northwest corner where the River Minho forms a natural border with Spain. The Lima Valley stretches from Peneda-Gerês to the Atlantic at Viana do Castelo, creating a corridor of lush landscapes. This peaceful region rewards visitors with authentic culture, excellent hiking, and refreshing local Vinho Verde wines.

Discover the Costa Verde stretching along the Minho's Atlantic shoreline with quiet, unspoiled beaches and traditional fishing villages. Unlike crowded southern resorts, this coastline offers authentic seaside experiences where fishing traditions endure. The dramatic meeting of green hills and Atlantic surf creates landscapes quite different from famous southern beaches.

Visit Viana do Castelo, an elegant port town at the Lima River mouth with rich maritime heritage dating to the Age of Discovery. The historic center features remarkable Manueline architecture, traditional markets, and the spectacular hilltop Santa Luzia sanctuary offering panoramic coastal views. This cultured city serves as the Minho's gateway to the sea.

activities.text: Walk the Rio Minho Trail, an eco-trail following the river along a former railway line through peaceful riverside landscapes and traditional villages. The gentle terrain makes this trail suitable for walkers of all abilities seeking natural beauty. The route near the Spanish border reveals the region's serene character. Allow for a round trip by car during the day from Viana do Castelo.

Canoe or kayak the rivers of the Minho region, where calm waters wind through lush valleys and past historic towns. The low-lying western area offers excellent conditions for paddling suitable for families and beginners. More experienced paddlers can seek white water rafting for adrenaline-pumping rapids.

Sample Vinho Verde, the region's signature wine, in local quintas and village tavernas throughout the Minho. This light, slightly sparkling white wine is lower in alcohol and perfectly refreshing after outdoor activities. The name means 'green wine' referring to the lush landscape where grapes are grown.

places.name: Vila Franca do Campo

visits.text: Vila Franca do Campo was São Miguel’s main town until October 20, 1522. That day, a powerful earthquake followed by a landslide buried the town and killed about 5,000 people. The seat of the island’s administration then moved to Ponta Delgada. The Igreja Matriz de São Miguel Arcanjo, a 15th-century church with a brick facade, preserves a 16th-century organ and a gilded chancel decorated with azulejos, painted ceramic tiles. Visit it before taking the boat.

Climb up to the Ermida de Nossa Senhora da Paz, the chapel overlooking Vila Franca do Campo. According to tradition, a shepherd found a statue of the Virgin Mary here. The current church dates from the 18th century. Its grand staircase, built in 1967, has ten flights of steps representing the ten Hail Marys in a decade of the rosary. Blue-and-white azulejos depict the life of Christ. Go up late in the day, when the heat subsides.

activities.text: A swimming pool inside a volcano, out at sea: the Ilhéu de Vila Franca is a former, almost circular crater about 150 m in diameter, connected to the ocean by a narrow passage. Seawater forms a calm lagoon inside. The islet is a nature reserve, and visits are limited to 400 people per day, with no more than 200 in the crater at a time. The Clube Naval boat leaves from the Vila Franca do Campo marina, and the trip takes about ten minutes. Crossings are seasonal: in 2026, Clube Naval offered them from June 12 to October 11. Outside that period, do not plan on taking this boat trip.

Cut white tissue paper wrapped around a small pastry: these are queijadas da Vila, the specialty of Vila Franca do Campo. They belong to the tradition of convent pastries. The earliest mentions date from the late 17th century, at the convent of Santo André de Vila Franca. To take some home, stop by the Queijadas de Adelino Morgado bakery in Vila Franca.

visits.text: Eight rectangular towers and an oval defensive enclosure beside the river: the Castelo de Vila Nova de Cerveira faces Galicia. The town received its charter from King Dom Dinis in 1321. Reinforced against Spain in the 17th century, the fortress prevented Napoleon’s troops from crossing the Minho in 1809. Above the old gate, the Nossa Senhora da Ajuda chapel dates from 1650. Walk around the walls for views of the river.

According to local legend, a “Cervo Rei,” or stag king, gave the lands of Cerveira their name. Sculptor José Rodrigues dedicated a large stag statue to him, set at an elevation of about 300 m on Alto do Castro, in the Serra da Gávea, the mountain overlooking the town. It can be seen from more than 10 km away. Head up late in the day for views of the town, the Minho River, and Spain.

Since 1978, Vila Nova de Cerveira has hosted the Bienal de Cerveira, an international contemporary art exhibition held every two years. Its organizer, the Fundação Bienal de Cerveira, lists current exhibitions on its website. Check it before you come to find out what will be open during your visit.

activities.text: You can see otters up close at the Aquamuseu do Rio Minho, in Castelinho Park beside the river. This municipal museum combines an aquarium, an otter enclosure, and a fishing museum. Admission costs €2. It is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. from April through October, closing at 5 p.m. in winter. It is closed on Mondays.

places.name: Vila Nova de Foz Côa

visits.text: From a distance, the Museu do Côa looks less like a museum than a large boulder emerging from the hillside. Its architects, Camilo Rebelo and Tiago Pimentel, tinted the concrete with mineral pigments to imitate the region’s rocks. Opened in 2010, it overlooks the point where the Côa flows into the Douro. Its seven galleries explain the valley’s rock art: images engraved on rocks in the open air. From November through March, it is closed on Mondays.

The first thing you notice about the Igreja Matriz de Vila Nova de Foz Côa is its portal: five carved arches nested inside one another. This is the Manueline style, the Portuguese decorative style of the early 16th century named after King Manuel I. In the chancel, the ceiling is divided into 27 coffers, square compartments painted with scenes from the lives of Christ and the Virgin Mary. Right beside the church stands the pillory, a stone column that symbolized municipal authority. Stop by toward the end of the day, on your way back from Penascosa.

activities.text: The 4x4 bumps along 6 km of dirt track between almond and olive trees, then stops beside the Côa at the Penascosa site. Between 22,000 and 10,000 BCE, the valley’s engravers mainly depicted horses, aurochs (now-extinct wild cattle), and wild goats. Here, one horse has three overlapping heads: as the light shifts across the rock, it seems to turn its head. The guided tour leaves Castelo Melhor, 15 km from Foz Côa, in the afternoon and costs €18.

“As gravuras não sabem nadar”—“the engravings can’t swim”: this slogan saved Canada do Inferno. This is where the first Côa rock engravings were spotted in late 1991. A dam was being built at the time, and its reservoir would have submerged them. In November 1995, the government abandoned the project. UNESCO added the valley to its World Heritage List in 1998. On rock No. 1, a horse has two heads. The goat on rock No. 14 serves as the park’s logo.

visits.text: Privatized in 1903, the Forte de São Clemente is no longer open to visitors—but the Praça da Barbacã in front of it is public and offers a direct view of the Mira estuary. The fort itself, built in 1602 against North African pirates, dominates the river mouth from a rocky point. It remains Milfontes' emblem, photographed by everyone from the square.

The fresh water of the Mira estuary smells different from the ocean—more of vegetation, calmer. The Praia da Franquia extends into this estuary, sheltered from the Atlantic wind: calm water, ideal for paddleboarding or for children to swim.

On the river side, the water is fresh and lukewarm; on the ocean side, cold and rough: Praia da Franquia and Praia do Farol are 15 minutes apart on foot and offer two different water temperatures. Praia do Farol is exposed to Atlantic waves and looks out toward the lighthouse. Surfers prefer the beaches to the north, Malhão and Aivados, accessible by car via the N393.

activities.text: Take the ferry boat in summer to Praia das Furnas, on the other side of the Mira. A few minutes' crossing to a wilder beach, less crowded than the village beaches. Off-season, car access via the bridge (10 minutes). The beach is in the Parque Natural protected zone.

Rent a kayak or stand-up paddleboard on Praia da Franquia to head up the Mira estuary toward Odemira: a few kilometers of calm river between reed-lined banks, far from the ocean. Several rental providers on the beach from June to September.

visits.text: Marvel at the sumptuous Mateus Palace, a jewel of Portuguese baroque whose silhouette adorns the bottles of the famous rosé wine. This 18th-century aristocratic manor, attributed to Nicolau Nasoni, features French-style gardens, a romantic lake, and refined interiors with period furniture and precious art collections.

Explore the mysterious Sanctuary of Panóias, a unique Roman archaeological site dedicated to Eastern cults. These granite rocks, carved with basins and Latin inscriptions, were used for ritual sacrifices nearly two thousand years ago. An enigmatic place that reveals the religious diversity of the Roman Empire in its most remote provinces.

activities.text: Discover Vila Real, a cosmopolitan city surrounded by an unspoiled natural setting. Climb to the Calvário viewpoint for a semicircular view over the city, encompassing the Marão and Alvão mountain ranges. Admire the numerous stones bearing coats of arms that lend distinction to the facades, testimony to the nobility that settled here alongside the marquises.

places.name: Vila Viçosa

visits.text: As soon as you arrive in Vila Viçosa, marble is everywhere - thresholds, fountains, stairways and pavements. More than 160 quarries surround the town and have been worked since the late Middle Ages. Facing the palace, an equestrian statue of João IV stands over 16,000 m² of white paving.

The Paço Ducal has been the seat of the Dukes of Bragança since 1501. The 110-meter Mannerist façade entirely clad in marble was commissioned by Dom Jaime - who returned from exile after his father was accused of treason. The palace contains 50 rooms: Baroque and Rococo furniture, Flemish tapestries, the ducal art collection. King Dom Carlos spent his last night here before his assassination in Lisbon on 1 February 1908. Book a guided tour.
Its interior is covered with 18th-century azulejos illustrating the life of Saint John the Evangelist.

activities.text: On the road toward Estremoz, detour to the marble quarries. Multi-ton blocks are extracted with diamond saws from excavations reaching up to 70 meters deep. Local operators offer guided tours - check availability in advance.

visits.text: Explore the city of Viseu, with more than two millennia of history linked to the Lusitanian chief Viriathus. Visit the impressive Cava de Viriato, a vast octagonal fortified enclosure evoking Lusitanian resistance against Rome. This city is a very important landmark in Portugal's history and holds secrets around every corner.

Marvel at Viseu Cathedral and the Grão Vasco National Museum, which houses masterpieces by the Portuguese Renaissance painter. The Romanesque-Gothic cathedral with its Manueline facade and the artistic treasures of the adjacent museum constitute the cultural heart of this city that has been an episcopal seat since ancient times.

activities.text: Discover Viseu's urban art on a walk through the city that reveals works by artists like AKA Corleone, Lord Mantraste, and Mariana, a miserável. This historic city has reinvented itself and presents a vibrant street art scene that harmoniously contrasts with the centuries-old heritage of its squares and monuments.

visits.text: Praia da Zambujeira is more beautiful than famous: fine sand in a steep-sided cove, black cliffs on each side, clear waters despite the Atlantic swell. At the top of the cliff, the Capela de Nossa Senhora do Mar watches over the inlet. Access via a steep staircase from the village—allow 10 minutes on foot.

Perched on cliffs about a hundred meters above the ocean, the village of Zambujeira do Mar hasn't budged since the 1980s. One main street, a few low houses, a restaurant terrace. What mass tourism has spared here is rare at this latitude. Book accommodation well in advance—few rooms available.

The Rota Vicentina passes through Zambujeira: two marked trails - the Trilho dos Pescadores follows the coast along the cliffs to Odeceixe, while the Caminho Histórico crosses the schist hinterland. Maps and trail guides are available at the Parque Natural reception in Vila Nova de Milfontes.

activities.text: South of the beach, the Praias dos Alteirinhos and do Carvalhal open into successive coves. The trail follows the cliff edge in the Parque Natural do Sudoeste Alentejano.

Book ahead: there are few rooms in the village, and the O Sacas restaurant on the cliff fills up in season. The food is simple, the terrace exposed to the wind, and the view of the cliffs is worth the wait.
